chapters.title: The Wealthy Patriarch
paragraphs: His Education in Sanskrit and Persian

Baburam Babu of Baidyabati was a man of great worldly ambition. He became famous through his many dealings in the civil and criminal courts. In those days, it was hardly an ancient custom to work diligently without taking bribes—Baburam followed that very custom. Skilled in his profession, he also managed to win over the English officials with flattery and obsequiousness. As a result, he amassed a great fortune in a short time.

In this country, wealth or position brings respect; learning and character do not command the same honor. Baburam Babu’s circumstances had once been quite poor—at that time, only one or two people in the village cared about him. But later, when he acquired a handsome mansion, gardens, estates, and other riches, the number of his followers, servants, and friends became countless. Whenever he had leisure and came home, his drawing room would be crowded with people, just as a sweet shop, when filled with sweets, is swarmed by flies—so too, when wealth arrives, people flock in. Whenever you went to Baburam Babu’s house, you would find him surrounded by people—great and small, all sitting around, speaking pleasing words; the clever ones would flatter him with practiced gestures, while the more boorish ones would babble on without restraint. In this manner, after some years, Baburam Babu retired on a pension and began managing his estates and trading from his own house.

No one is blessed with happiness in every way, nor is anyone wise in all matters. Baburam Babu devoted himself solely to amassing wealth. How might his property increase? How might ten people come to know his name? How might the villagers stand before him with folded hands? How might his ceremonies be the grandest?—these were his constant concerns. He had one son and two daughters. Being a descendant of Balaram Thakur, Baburam Babu, for the sake of preserving his caste, married off his two daughters as soon as they were born, spending lavishly on their weddings and ornaments. But the sons-in-law were Kulin Brahmins, who, having taken wives in many places, would not even glance at their father-in-law’s house in Baidyabati unless given a special reward.
His son, Motilal, was pampered from childhood and always indulged...

Sometimes he would say, “Father, catch the moon for me!”—sometimes, “Father, let’s fire the cannon!” When he began to wail and shriek, the people nearby would mutter, “Oh, that brat from the Bancks’ house is making it impossible to sleep!” The boy, pampered by his parents, would not even utter the name of the school. The household steward was entrusted with his education. When he was first taken to the tutor, Matilal would bawl and howl, scratching and biting the poor man. The tutor would go to the master and complain, “Sir, teaching your son is not my job.” The master would reply, “He is the apple of my eye, my precious Nilmoni—coax him, cajole him, stroke his back and teach him.”

Eventually, after much scheming, Matilal began to attend school. The tutor would sit with one leg crossed over the other, cane in hand, leaning against the wall and dozing, muttering, “Write, boy, write!” Meanwhile, Matilal would seize the opportunity to dance and wave a banana in front of his face—the tutor would be snoring, utterly oblivious to his pupil’s antics. If the tutor happened to open his eyes, Matilal would quickly sit by his palm-leaf slate, scribbling “the crow’s child, the tiger’s child.”

In the evening, when the tutor began to make the boys recite, Matilal would shout “Haribol!” with the rest, but would only recite the last syllables of “rhinoceros egg,” “old woman,” or “pawnshop,” and thus cheat his way through. If, in the midst of this, the tutor dozed off, Matilal would snip at his nose or toss a burning ember onto his dhoti, then dart away like an arrow.

At mealtimes, he would trick others into drinking lime-water, claiming it was buttermilk. The tutor soon realized the boy was incorrigible—Goddess Saraswati herself had abandoned him to his fate. He thought, “If even after so many canings he learns only the art of beating up his teacher, then it is best to free myself from such a pupil’s clutches.” But the master would not let him go, so he had to devise a plan.

Perhaps being a steward was better than being a tutor—at least the pay was two rupees, with food and clothing thrown in. As for extra perks, there was only the occasional palm-leaf, banana leaf, or a pair of clothes when fetching paper, but in the market, a steward’s job brought daily cash. With this in mind, he went to the master and said, “Matibabu has finished writing on all the banana leaves and paper, and has even filled a whole sheaf of estate documents.”
Baburam Babu, hearing this, was overjoyed. The courtiers nearby exclaimed, “Why wouldn’t he be? Can a lion’s cub ever turn into a jackal?”
Afterwards, Baburam Babu considered that his son should now be taught grammar and a little Persian.

Necessary. Having resolved thus, he asked the butter-worshipping Brahmin priest, “Well, how much grammar have you studied?” The priest, a thorough simpleton, thought to himself, “Whether I get rice or bananas, it never amounts to much—but perhaps, after all these years, this is finally a chance for some gain.” With this hope, he replied, “Yes, sir, I have studied grammar and such for five years at the tole of Ishwarchandra Vedantabagish of Queenmora. Alas, my luck is poor—despite all my studies, I have gained nothing. I only eat ginger water and study at the master’s feet.”
Babu Ram Babu said, “From today, you will teach my son grammar.” The priest, intoxicated by hope, began to teach a page or two of grammar, feeling as if he were floating on air.

Motilal thought to himself, “I have escaped from the hands of the old master, but how do I get rid of this rice-and-banana-eating Brahmin? I am the darling child of my parents—whether I study or not, they will never scold me. Studying is only for earning money, and my father has boundless wealth—what need have I for learning? As long as I can sign my name, that is enough. And if I do study, what will become of my airbox friends? This is the time for amusement—who wants the torment of studies now?”

Having made up his mind, Motilal said to the priest, “Hey Brahmin, if you dare come to teach me the alphabet again, I’ll throw your idol aside and make sure you never get your rice and bananas here again. But if you tell my father, I’ll give you such a thrashing from the rooftop that your wife will have to take off her bangles by tomorrow.”

The priest, stunned by the alphabet, remained dazed for a while, then reflected, “I have worked hard for six months and not received a single paisa. Again, ‘profit: only the slaughter of cows’—life is at stake. If I give it up now, at least I’ll escape with my life.”

While the priest was pondering all this, Motilal, watching his face, said, “Why are you sitting there thinking so hard? Want some money? Here, take this—but go tell my father I’ve learned everything.”
The priest went to the master and said, “Sir, Motilal is no ordinary boy—he has extraordinary intelligence; whatever he hears once, he remembers.” Babu Ram Babu’s...

chapters.title: The Spoilt Heir
paragraphs: Nearby lived a certain scholar—he declared there was no need to introduce Motilal. “That boy is a rare gem—if he lives, he’ll rule the world one day.”

Soon after, Baburam Babu began searching for a munshi to teach his son Persian. After much inquiry, he hired Habibullah Hossain, the grandfather of Aladi the tailor, for the princely sum of 140 rupees a month, plus oil and firewood. The munshi sahib had no teeth, a beard as white as ripe cotton, a moustache like hemp, and when teaching, his eyes would redden as he barked, “Arre, read, boy!” His mouth would twist into grotesque shapes as he pronounced “kaaf, gaaf, aayen, gaayen.” He had no particular passion for teaching, and with such a teacher, Motilal’s Persian lessons went about as well as you’d expect.

One day, Munshi Sahib was hunched over, poring over a book, waving his hands and chanting verses from the Masnavi in a sing-song tone. Meanwhile, Motilal crept up behind him and dropped a burning cigar stub onto his beard. Instantly, the beard went up in flames. Motilal shouted, “How’s that, you old glutton? Still want to teach me?” Munshi Sahib, slapping at his beard and crying “Toba! Toba!” fled the scene, shrieking in pain, “Never in my life have I seen such a rude and wicked boy—what kind of place is this? Even the air here is haram—toba, toba, toba!!!”
Motilal’s Attempt to Learn English and Baburam Babu’s Journey to Bally

Hearing of the munshi’s misfortune, Baburam Babu said, “Motilal isn’t really that sort of boy—he’s just a bit mischievous. He’ll turn out fine, you’ll see.” Then he thought to himself, “No one studies Persian anymore; better to have him learn English.” Just as a madman sometimes has flashes of sense, so too does the ignorant man occasionally stumble upon wisdom. Baburam Babu resolved to seek advice from someone learned. “I know English as well as the Baranasi Babus—‘Sarkar come, speak not’—and my associates are equally learned, so it’s best to consult a true expert.” As he ran through the names of his relatives and acquaintances, he remembered that the elder Babu of Bally was a most capable man. When business is at stake, one becomes diligent. So without delay, he took a servant and a guard and set off for the Baidyabati ghat.
In the months of Asharh and Shravan, the boatmen cast their nets for hilsa fish, and two...

At this hour of the day, most boatmen go to eat, so there was neither a ferry nor a passing boat at the Baidyabati ghat. Baburam Babu, with his nose marked with sandal paste, a tilak on his forehead, dhoti tied just so, shoes from the flower pond on his feet, a belly like Ganesha, a knotted chadar draped over his shoulder, and a cheek full of betel leaf, wandered about here and there, telling his servant, “O Hari! We must get to Bali quickly. Go hire a passing panshi boat for a few pice.”

The servants of great men are often insolent. Hari replied, “What a business, master! I was just sitting down to eat, but at your call I’ve left my rice and come running. If it were a ferry boat, it would be cheap, but now it’s high tide—rowing and pushing against the current will make the boatmen sweat black. If we take Gahana’s boat, maybe it’ll be a few pice, but hiring a passing panshi for four pice? That’s not my work—what do you think, I’m mixing sattu with spit?”

Baburam Babu glared with wide, angry eyes and said, “Your mouth’s grown too big. If you talk like that again, I’ll give you a tight slap.” Bengalis of the lower castes tremble at the slightest rebuke. Hari, chastened, shrank back and said, “Well, then, where will you get a boat now?” Just then, a boat was returning, rowing upstream. After much haggling and tussling with the boatman, a fare was agreed upon. Baburam Babu, along with his servant and footman, boarded the boat.

After they had gone a little way, Baburam looked around and said, “O Hari! Good, we’ve got a boat. Boatman! Whose house is that? Is that a sugar mill? Hey, shake out the flint and pack a chilum of tobacco, will you?” Then, puffing on the hookah with great relish, he watched the dolphins surface now and then. Baburam himself stood up high to look around, and, counting the oars, began to sing a love song: “I have seen, Shyam, your Vrindavan abode—only the name remains.” As the tide was ebbing, the boat sped along swiftly. The boatmen, now with some leisure, some sat at the prow, others, like foolish goats, stroked their beards and gazed around, and in a Chittagong tune began to sing, “The gold earring will fall from my ear at the sound of the flute.”

Before sunset, the boat reached the Deonagazi ghat. Baburam Babu’s body was nothing but a lump of flesh—the four boatmen had to heave and haul him up to the shore. Beni Babu, seeing his guest, greeted him with all manner of polite phrases: “Please come gently, please come gently.” The servant Ram at once brought out the tobacco.
Sajia brought it in. Baburam Babu, lost in his hookah reverie, took a few deep puffs and said,
—Hey, the hookah’s getting weak—Uncle, why aren’t you saying anything? When a wise man keeps servants, even the servants become wise.

Ram immediately gave the hookah a little shake, changed the water, packed some fine tobacco, fitted a big pipe, and brought the hookah back. Baburam Babu, having the hookah before him, seemed to take full possession of it—drawing long, thunderous puffs—blowing clouds of smoke like a monsoon—uttering little grunts of satisfaction.
Benibabu: Sir, wouldn’t it be good to get up and have a betel leaf?
Baburam Babu: Evening has come—let the water-drinking be, this is my house—must I be told what to do?
Look, Motilal’s wits have sharpened—just seeing the boy is a delight to the eyes. Lately, I wish to have him taught English—could you find a tutor for a modest monthly sum?
Benibabu: There are many tutors, but for twenty or twenty-five rupees a month, you can get someone of middling quality.

Baburam Babu: How much—twenty-five rupees! Oh, brother, every day there are household rituals—each day a hundred leaves are read—and before long, the boy must be married off. If I must spend so much, why did I bother hiring a boat to come to you?
Saying this, he slapped Benibabu on the back and burst out laughing.
Benibabu: Then let me enroll him in a Calcutta school. The boy can stay at a relative’s house, and his studies can be managed for three or four rupees a month.
Baburam Babu: Even that much? Can’t you bargain it down a bit more? Is studying at school better than studying at home?

Benibabu: If you can keep a wise teacher at home for the boy, that’s best, but such teachers aren’t found for a small sum. School has its merits—and its faults. When boys study together, they encourage one another, but bad company can spoil a boy, and with twenty-five or thirty boys in a class, there’s constant noise, and the teacher can’t give equal attention to each, so not all learn equally.

chapters.title: Frolics in Bali
paragraphs: Baburam Babu. Well, whatever it is—I’ll send Motilal to you. See to it, look after him, and do whatever is best for him. Of all those sahibs whose work I used to handle, not a single one remains—if they were still around, I could have easily gotten him admitted somewhere. And as for my son, as soon as he learns the bare minimum, that’s enough—if he studies too much, he’ll forget his own religion. Just make sure the boy grows up to be a decent human being—that’s all I ask, brother, the whole responsibility is on you.

Benibabu. If you want to raise a boy right, you have to keep an eye on him both at home and outside. The father has to see everything with his own eyes—he has to get down and dirty, be a boy among boys. Many jobs can be left to fate, but not this one—you can’t just let someone else chew your betel for you.

Baburam Babu. Yes, yes, that’s all true—but isn’t Moti your own son too? Right now, I have to go bathe in the Ganges, listen to the Purana, look after my property and affairs. Where do I have the time, brother? And my English is old-fashioned anyway. Moti is yours—yours—yours! Once I send him to you, my mind will be at peace. Do whatever you think best, but brother! Make sure it doesn’t cost too much—I’m a man with a big family to feed—you understand all that, don’t you?
After much more polite conversation, Baburam Babu returned to his house in Baidyabati.
3. Motilal’s Arrival in Bali and His Frolics Thereafter, and Later Residence in Bowbazar for English Studies

On Sundays, the gentlemen of the bungalow take things very easy—“It’ll happen when it happens, I’ll eat when I eat”—and so their bathing and meals are often quite late. Afterwards, some indulge in a long nap, some play cards, some go fishing, some beat the tabla, some pluck at the sitar, some lie in bed contemplating the lotus navel of Vishnu, some go out for a stroll, some read books. But as for studying or discussing anything worthwhile—well, that’s a rare occurrence. More often, the time is wasted in tall tales, petty squabbles, or endless debates about whether Shambhu ate three jackfruits or not. Benibabu of Bali, however, had a different way of thinking. The people of this country have a notion that once school is over, so is learning. But that is a great mistake—even if you strive your whole life, you’ll never reach the end of knowledge. The more you study, the more your wisdom grows.

Benibabu understood these matters well and acted accordingly. In the morning, after rising, he would oversee all the household affairs and then settle down with a book to pursue his studies. Meanwhile, a fourteen-year-old boy—wearing an amulet around his neck, earrings in his ears, bangles and armlets on his hands—came up and, with a thump, plopped himself down in front of him.

Benibabu, absorbed in his book, was startled by the sound of the boy’s shoes. Looking up, he said, “Come in, Motilal, come in—Is everything well at home?” Motilal sat down and recounted all the news of the household. Benibabu said, “Stay here tonight. Tomorrow morning, I’ll take you to Calcutta and get you admitted to school.”

After a while, Motilal finished his breakfast and found there was still plenty of time left in the day. Restless by nature, he found it torturous to sit in one place for long. So, he quietly got up and began to roam around the house and its surroundings. Sometimes he would step onto the rice-pounding mortar, sometimes he would go up to the roof and stomp about, sometimes he would pelt passersby with bricks and stones just for fun. Thus, he went rampaging around Bali village—plucking flowers from someone’s garden, picking fruit from someone’s tree, climbing onto someone’s water pot and jumping off, breaking someone’s water pitcher.

The people of Bali, all thoroughly exasperated, began to mutter among themselves, “Who is this brat? Just as a fire-ravaged house leaves Lanka in ashes, will our village be laid waste by him?” Someone, hearing the boy’s father’s name, said, “Ah, Baburam Babu’s son—why wouldn’t he be like this? ‘In the son, the father’s fame and fortune are manifest.’”

Evening fell—the howling of jackals and the chirping of crickets filled the village with sound. Many respectable people lived in Bali—almost every house had a sacred Shaligram stone, so there was no shortage of the sound of conch shells and bells. After his studies, Benibabu, wrapped in a gamcha, was enjoying his pipe when a commotion arose. Five or seven men came up and said, “Sir! The zamindar’s son from the Baidya house has thrown bricks at us.” One said, “He knocked over my basket.” Another said, “He pushed me to the ground.” Yet another, “He spat in my face.” Someone else complained, “He broke my pot of ghee.”

Benibabu, ever compassionate at others’ misfortune, soothed them with kind words and a little compensation, and sent them on their way. Then he thought, “This boy’s education will surely be a handful—he’s managed to shake up the whole village in just one day. If I can get him out of here soon, my bones will finally find some peace.”

From the village came Pranakrishna the cripple, old Bhagabati Thakurdada, and the sly Rajkrishna, who asked, “Benibabu, who is this boy? We had just finished our meal and were about to sleep—had to get up because of all the commotion—being woken from a deep sleep has left our bodies aching.” Benibabu replied, “Why even mention it? I’ve landed myself in a real mess. I have a certain zamindar relative—he knows neither short nor long, has no sense of anything, except for a pile of money. He’s sent this boy to me to get him admitted to school—but in just these few days, my bones have turned black—keep a boy like this at home for three days and you’ll have crows nesting in your house.”

As this conversation was going on, a few village boys came up behind Moti—shouting, “Praise to Nara, son of Shambhu!” Benibabu said, “There he is, babu—quiet now—or do you want another couple of whacks? If I could just get rid of this trouble, I’d be saved.” Seeing Benibabu, Moti bared his teeth in a sheepish grin and shrank back a little. Benibabu asked, “Where did you go, babu?” Moti replied, “Just went to see how big your gentlemen’s village is.”

Later, going inside the house, Moti told Ram the servant to bring him tobacco. Not content with Amburi or Velsa, he demanded stronger and stronger tobacco, smoking one after another. Ram could barely keep up—no sooner had he brought some, it was gone. With this constant demand for tobacco, Ram could do no other work.
Benibabu sat silently on the verandah, occasionally glancing back with a frown to see what was happening.

Mealtime arrived. Benibabu took Moti inside and treated him to fine rice, curries, and all sorts of delicacies, followed by betel leaves. Afterward, Benibabu went off to sleep. Moti, too, went to the bedroom, chewed betel, smoked tobacco, and crawled into bed. For a while he tossed and turned, then jumped up, paced the room a few times, and twice broke into song—either “The Tale of Niluthakur’s Friend” or “Ram Basu’s Longing.” The racket from his singing drove sleep from everyone in the house.

In the Chandimandap, Ram and Pelaram the gardener from Kashijora were sleeping. When you’ve worked hard all day, sleep is sweet, but if disturbed, it breeds nothing but irritation. The servant and the gardener were both jolted awake by the uproar of Moti’s singing.
Pelarām: Oh dear Rām! This cursed racket on the street won’t let me sleep. If I don’t get up, how will I go grind seeds in the garden?

Rām (wrapping his body with a cloth): Hey, it’s still the dead of night—why get up now? Babu has dug a good channel and brought water—this brat always finds some excuse—if he leaves, we’ll have peace.

The next morning, Benibabu took Motilal to the house of Becharam Bandyopadhyay in Bowbazar. Becharam Babu was the son of Kenaram Babu, a man of old lineage—quite a big shot, but with no children of his own. He was a simple, unassuming fellow, but had been a bit of a simpleton since birth—narrow-eyed and scrawny.
Seeing Benibabu, he asked in his usual nasal tone, “Well, what brings you here?”

Benibabu: Motilal Mahashay will stay at your house and attend school. On Saturdays, when there’s a holiday, he’ll go to Baidyabati. Since Baburam Babu has no closer relative in Calcutta than you, I’ve come to make this request.
Becharam: What’s the problem? This house or that house, it’s all the same. I have no children—just two nephews. Let Motilal stay here as he pleases.

Hearing Becharam Babu’s nasal voice, Motilal burst out laughing. At once, Benibabu began winking and shaking his head, thinking, “With a boy like this, there’s no peace anywhere.” Becharam Babu, hearing Motilal’s laughter, said, “Beni brother! The boy seems a bit unruly, doesn’t he? Perhaps he’s been a handful since childhood.”

Benibabu, ever the investigator—he knew all the old stories, and had suffered himself—but with his own tact, he covered it all up. If he revealed the secrets, Motilal would be ruined—he’d neither be able to stay in Calcutta nor study at school. Benibabu’s only wish was that the boy should learn something, somehow become a man.

After much more conversation of various kinds, Benibabu took his leave from Becharam Babu and brought Motilal to Mr. Sherborne’s school. Since it was a Hindu college, Mr. Sherborne’s school had fallen on slightly hard times, so the sahib was working day and night to keep it afloat. He was a stout man, with thick eyebrows, always chewing betel, cane in hand—he would pace the classroom once or twice, then sit on his bench and puff away at his hookah.
Benibabu enrolled Motilal in his school and returned to Bali.

chapters.title: The Police Station
paragraphs: When the English first came to Calcutta to trade, at that time the Seths, Basaks, and Babus were engaged in commerce, but not a single soul in Calcutta knew the English language. All dealings and conversations with the English were conducted through gestures. Such is human nature: when pressed, the mind finds a way. Gradually, through gestures alone, some English words began to be learned. Later, when the Supreme Court was established, the demands of law and justice led to an increased practice of English. In those days, Ramram Mishra and Anandirama Das had learned quite a few English words. Ramram Mishra’s disciple, Ramnarayan Mishra, worked as a clerk for a lawyer and wrote petitions for many people; he even had a school, where students had to pay a monthly fee of fourteen or sixteen rupees each. Later, Ramlochan the barber, Krishnamohan Basu, and many others also took up the profession of schoolmaster. The boys studied “Tom, Dick, and Harry” and memorized the meanings of words by rote. At weddings or feasts, the boy who could recite “John’s rod” would be gazed upon by all, and showered with applause and cries of “Bravo! Well done!”

Following the example of Fenko and Aratoon Petrus and others, Mr. Sharbhoron Sahib also started a school after some time. In that school, the sons of respectable families studied. If the boys truly had the desire, then no matter which school they attended, by their own effort they could certainly learn something or other. Every school has its faults and virtues, and there are also many boys who, declaring, “This school is no good, that school is better,” wander here today and there tomorrow—thinking that if they can just fritter away their days in confusion, they will have fooled their parents. Matilal, after attending Mr. Sharbhoron’s school for a day or two, enrolled in Mr. Kalus’s school.

The true purpose of learning is this: to cultivate good habits and upright character, to develop sound judgment, and to thoroughly learn whatever may be useful in life’s affairs. If children are educated with this aim, they become refined in every way, and can understand and perform all tasks, both at home and outside, with discernment. But to impart such an education, the care of both parents and teachers is required. The path the father walks, the son will follow. If you wish to make your child virtuous, first the parents must—

A father ought to be virtuous. If a father, sunk in drink, forbids his son to drink, why should the son listen? If a father, engaged in wicked deeds, preaches morality, the son will mock him as a hypocritical cat turned ascetic. The son of a father who walks the path of righteousness rarely needs much advice—the son’s good nature grows naturally from the father’s example. And a mother, too, must always keep a watchful eye on her child. Nothing softens a child’s heart like a mother’s sweet words, her affection, and her kisses. If a child knows for certain that by doing such-and-such he will not be taken into his mother’s arms and caressed, then good habits take root in him.

It is the teacher’s duty not to turn his pupil into a mere parrot by making him read a few books. Memorizing lessons may indeed sharpen the memory, but if it does not strengthen the intellect or impart practical knowledge, then such learning is only for show. Whether the pupil is young or old, he must be taught in such a way that his mind is truly engaged in his studies—this can be done only through the nectar and skill of true teaching, not by rote alone.

Living in the house at Baidyabati, Motilal learned not a whit of good conduct. Now, staying at Bohubazar, things have gone from bad to worse. Babu Becharam had two nephews, named Holodhor and Godadhor, who had never seen their father since birth. Out of fear of their mother and uncle, they would occasionally go and sit at the village school, but that was in name only. Mostly, they ran wild—racing about the lanes, the rooftops, and the fields. If anyone tried to restrain them, they would not listen. They would tell their mother, “If you do this, we’ll run away.” One was as bad as the other—and soon they saw that Motilal was just like them. Within a day or two, they became thick as thieves. They sat together, ate together, slept together. They would put their arms around each other’s shoulders, and whether inside or outside, at home or in the street, they roamed about hand in hand, necks entwined. Becharam Babu’s wife would sometimes look at them and exclaim, “Ah, as if they were three brothers born of the same mother!”

Whether child, youth, or old man—no one can remain silent or occupied with just one thing for long. Throughout the day and night, one must find ways to pass the time in various activities. For children, there must be such rules that... The Spoilt Child, Chapter 13

They will both play and study. To play constantly, or to study constantly—neither is good. The special significance of play is this: when the body is refreshed, the mind is more inclined to study. If one studies without pause, the mind grows weary, and whatever is learned merely floats on the surface—never truly sinks in. But there are rules to play as well: only those games that require physical exertion are beneficial. Cards, dice, and the like are of no use at all—they only breed laziness, and from that laziness, all manner of mischief arises. Just as constant study does not improve learning, so too does constant play dull the mind. For in play, only the body grows strong—there is no discipline for the mind. Yet the mind must always be engaged with something; if not led down the right path, who can say it will not stray into the wrong? Many boys have thus fallen into ruin.

Haldhar, Gadadhar, and Motilal roam about like Gokul’s oxen—doing whatever they please, heedless of anyone’s words, respecting no one. If not cards, then dice; if not dice, then kites; if not kites, then pigeons; if not pigeons, then bulbul fights—always busy with one amusement or another, with no time to eat, no time to sleep. When a servant comes to call them inside, they shout, “Go away, you rascal, we’re not coming!” If a maid comes and says, “Oh dear, mistress can’t sleep without you,” they retort, “Get lost, you wretch!” Sometimes the maid mutters, “Oh my, what sweet words they’ve learned!” Gradually, all the neighborhood’s wretched, good-for-nothing, half-starved, loafing lads began to gather around them. Day and night, there was a racket—the drawing room rang with shouts, bursts of laughter, and the clatter of hookahs, charas, and ganja; the smoke grew so thick, it turned the air dark. Who would dare pass that way? Who’s father would dare forbid it?

Becharam Babu, catching a whiff once or twice, pinched his nose and exclaimed, “Disgusting!” There is nothing more dangerous than bad company. Even with the utmost care from parents and teachers, all is lost to bad company; and in a place where there is no care at all, who can say how much worse it may become?

The companions Motilal found did not bring out his good qualities—on the contrary, his bad habits and wickedness only grew day by day. Once or twice a week, he would go to school, and even then, would sit there like a witness before the deity Sakhigopal, enduring it with great difficulty. Sometimes, with the boys, he would sneak out—

He acts the dandy—if not that, then he grabs a slate and sketches away at everything—never does he devote even five minutes to his studies. His mind is always flitting about, eager for the moment he can join his peers in boisterous fun and merriment! Yet, there are indeed some teachers who, by their skill and cunning, can coax a boy like Motilal into paying attention to his lessons. They know all sorts of methods for teaching—each child gets the approach that suits him best. But in the government schools nowadays, and in Mr. Kalus’s school as well, the teaching is all of a slapdash sort. No one pays equal attention to every boy in every class—no one bothers to see whether a child can properly understand the easy books before moving him on to the heavy tomes. The prevailing belief is that the more books and the more lessons assigned, the greater the glory of the school. As long as the boys can recite by rote, that’s enough—whether they understand or not is of no concern, nor does anyone consider whether what is taught will be of any use to them in future life. In such a school, a boy only learns anything by the sheer luck of his stars.

Motilal, as befitted his father’s son, as befitted the company he kept, as befitted the place he lived in, and as befitted the school he attended—his learning turned out just as weighty as all that. There is a certain kind of teacher who is rarely found in any school; some work themselves to death with tireless effort, while others, with a sly wink, just go through the motions. Bakreshwar Babu of Battala was Mr. Kalus’s golden wand and silver wand. He would visit the homes of all the big men and tell them, “I always keep a close eye on your son—why wouldn’t the gentleman’s son do well? He’s no ordinary boy, he’s the philosopher’s stone itself!” He was in charge of teaching the upper classes, but whether he himself understood what he taught was doubtful. If this ever came to light, it would be a terrible disgrace, so he kept it all under wraps. He would only make the boys churn through their lessons—if asked a question, he’d say, “Look it up in the dictionary.” Whatever translation the boys produced, he’d always have to make some corrections—if he let everything stand, how could he maintain his authority as a teacher? He’d cross out the word “action” and write “work,” or cross out “work” and write “action.” If the boys asked why, he’d snap, “You’re very insolent—how dare you question what I say?” Now and then, he’d lavish special attention on the sons of the wealthy and ask, “How much rent do you get from such-and-such property? How much profit from such-and-such estate?” In a few short days, Motilal became Bakreshwar Babu’s...

He became exceedingly beloved. One day it was a flower, the next a fruit, today a book, tomorrow a handkerchief—he would bring these little gifts, and Bakreshwar Babu thought to himself, “It’s not wise to let go of boys like Motilal—when they grow up, my brinjal patch will flourish.” Why bother with the petty details of supervising the school? Will such matters bear witness for me in the afterlife?

The time of the autumnal Durga Puja approached—the markets and every place were abuzz with excitement. In that very commotion, Motilal’s own house was filled with the sound of “Haribol!” If he had to stay at school, he grew restless—looking this way, then that, sitting down, then drumming on his desk—he could not sit still for even a moment. On Saturdays, he would come to school, plead with Bakreshwar Babu, and manage to get a half-day, then head home. On the way, he would buy a betel leaf, glance at the pigeon-sellers and kite-sellers’ stalls on either side as he walked along—his face untroubled, not casting a glance at anyone.

Just then, a police sergeant and a few constables came running and grabbed his hand. The sergeant said, “You are under arrest by the police—this is very serious, you must come with us.” Motilal began to protest and struggle. The sergeant, being strong, dragged him along with force. Motilal fell to the ground—his whole body scraped and covered in dust, yet he kept trying to break free and run. The sergeant, meanwhile, landed a few punches and blows. At last, lying in the street, Motilal remembered his father and began to weep, thinking more than once, “Why did I do such things—keeping company with rascals has brought about my ruin.”

A crowd gathered in the street—some asked, “What’s the matter?” A couple of old women began to mutter, “Ah, whose child is being beaten like this—the boy’s face is like the moon—hearing his cries makes our hearts ache.”

Before sunset, Motilal was brought to the police station, where he saw that Haldhar, Gadadhar, and from the neighborhood, Ramgobind, Dolgobind, Mangobind, and the like had also been brought in. All of them stood to one side, heads hung low. The magistrate was Mr. Bellacure—he would have to conduct the inquiry, but he had gone home, so all the accused had to remain in the lock-up.

chapters.title: The Assembly of Sycophants
paragraphs: “I couldn’t catch Shyam, oh friend—oh, I’m dying, dying here!”—tok-tok, patash-patash—the coachman Miyajan sings a line or two, throws in a mocking taunt, and, blaming the wretched ox for not moving, twists its tail and gives it a sharp slap. There’s a bit of cloud, a bit of rain falling—the two oxen, snorting, pull ahead and overtake a hackney carriage. In that carriage sits Premnarayan Majumdar—the vehicle sways in the wind—the two horses, descendants of some noble steed, perhaps the father of all horses, prance and clatter along—ting-ting, dong-dong—whip cracks fly, but no matter what, the pace refuses to quicken. Premnarayan, having just swallowed two mouthfuls of rice, sits as a passenger—his heart in his mouth from the jolting and lurching of the carriage. When the ox-cart overtakes him, his annoyance only grows.

But it’s hardly fair to blame Premnarayan for this—who isn’t a little touchy about their own dignity? Almost everyone thinks themselves important. If their pride is pricked even a little, some flare up like oil on fire, others sulk in silence. Premnarayan, irritated, begins muttering to himself—“Service is a misery—servants are no better than dogs—at a word, you have to run. Look at me! My whole life I’ve burned in Gada’s torment—never let me eat, never let me sleep—made up songs about me—always teasing, like the bite of tiny ants—set the street boys on me to drive me mad, and even joined in themselves, clapping and hooting behind my back. Who could bear all this and stay sane? Any decent man would go mad. The fact that I haven’t run away from Calcutta is my only claim to bravery—my only strength is that I still hold on to this government job. As for those street boys, as they sow, so shall they reap. Let them rot in jail now—may they never get out—but that’s just talk, for here I am, running around trying to get them released. Such is a servant’s lot—what choice is there? A man must do everything for his stomach.”

Baburam Babu of Baidyabati sits enthroned in all his babu glory. His wife is massaging his feet. On one side, a couple of Bhattacharyas are engaged in a learned debate—today it is whether bottle gourd is permissible to eat, tomorrow it will be about brinjal, or whether eating milk with salt is as sinful as eating beef. They are grinding away at these topics like a pestle pounding rice, making a great racket over nothing.
Elsewhere, a few men are playing chess. Among them, one player sits with his head in his hands, deep in thought—ruin is upon him, and with the next move, he will be checkmated.
In another corner, a couple of singers are tuning their instruments, coaxing their tanpura to the right pitch.

Nearby, the clerks are busy with their ledgers, writing away. In front of them stand a crowd of debtors, tenants, and moneylenders—many are having their accounts settled, others dismissed. The drawing room is packed to the brim, bustling with people.

The moneylenders complain, “Sir, it’s been three years for some, four for others—we’ve supplied goods all this time, but haven’t seen a paisa. We’ve run around endlessly—our own work has come to a standstill.” The petty moneylenders—the oil seller, the wood seller, the sweetmeat vendor—are wailing, “Sir, we’re finished! We’re as fragile as little fish—how can we survive like this? Chasing after our money, our legs are worn to the bone—our shops are shut, our wives and children are starving.”

The Dewanji replies curtly, “Go away for today—you’ll get your money, won’t you? Why all this fuss?” If anyone dares to speak out of turn, Baburam Babu immediately turns his face, rains down abuse, and has them thrown out.

Bengali gentlemen of means borrow goods from everyone in the land, but when it comes time to pay, they’re struck with a fever. The cash sits locked in their chests, but unless there’s a grand commotion in the drawing room, unless the place is teeming with people, it doesn’t feel like real babu-dom. Whether the poor, suffering moneylender lives or dies is of no consequence; what matters is that such grand behavior upholds the family name.

There are other sorts of so-called gentlemen too—polished and shiny on the outside, rotten within. Outwardly, their dhotis are starched and spotless, but at home, their wives are patching up old clothes. If they try to spend according to their means, they feel as if Yama himself is strangling them—so, no garden, no real babu lifestyle. They put on a show just to dazzle the moneylenders, take loans or goods on credit, and if pressed too hard, pawn things off here and there. When the summons finally arrives, they transfer their property to someone else’s name and disappear without a trace.

Babu Ram Babu was exceedingly attached to his money—his hand grew heavy whenever he had to take cash out of the big iron chest; it was a terrible ordeal. He was haggling and squabbling with the moneylenders, when Premnarayan Majumdar arrived and whispered all the latest news of Calcutta into his ear. Hearing this, Babu Ram Babu sat stunned—it felt as though a thunderbolt had struck his head. After a moment, he collected himself and summoned Mokajan Miyan.

Mokajan was a master of court affairs. Many landlords, indigo planters, and the like were always consulting him. Forging documents, arranging witnesses, bringing police inspectors and clerks to heel, swallowing up ill-gotten gains, orchestrating riots and disturbances, turning falsehood into truth and truth into falsehood—there was no one to match him in these arts. Everyone affectionately called him Thokchacha, and he melted at the sound, thinking, “I must have been born under a lucky star—Ramzan, Eid, Shab-e-Barat, all my prayers have borne fruit. If only the Pir would tie a charm on my arm, my powers would grow even greater.” With such thoughts, he was performing his ablutions with a brass lota, when Babu Ram Babu’s urgent summons forced him to hurry over and listen to all the news in private.

After pondering for a while, he said, “What’s the worry, Babu? I’ve swept away hundreds of such cases—this is nothing! I have some seasoned men—I'll take them along, and with their testimony, we’ll win the case. Don’t be afraid—I’ll come at first light, just wait.” Babu Ram Babu took heart at these words, yet anxiety gnawed at him.

He loved his wife dearly; whatever she said was law. If she declared, “This is not water, but milk,” he would, even seeing it with his own eyes, agree, “Yes, indeed, this is not water—it is milk. Why else would the mistress say so?” Other men may love their wives, but they can still judge which of their words to heed, and to what extent. A true gentleman loves his wife with all his heart, but if he were to obey her every word, he might as well don a sari and stay inside the house. Babu Ram Babu would rise if his wife told him to rise, and sit if she told him to sit.

A few months ago, his wife had borne him a son—she now sat cradling the infant, showering him with affection. On either side, his two daughters sat, chatting about household matters and other affairs. At such a moment, the master of the house entered, sat down gloomily, and said, “Wife, my fate—”
I had cherished the hope that, once Mati grew into a responsible man, we would entrust him with all our affairs and retire to live in Kashi. But it seems fate has dashed that hope.
Wife: Oh dear—what is it? Tell me quickly, my heart is pounding just hearing your words—my Mati is well, isn’t he?
Master: Yes—he is well—but I heard that today the police dragged him away and locked him up.

Wife: What are you saying? They dragged Mati away and put him in jail? Oh, why did they imprison him? Alas, how many bruises must cover my poor child’s body, perhaps my boy hasn’t even eaten—hasn’t even slept! Oh, what will become of us? Bring my Mati back to me at once.
Saying this, the wife began to weep—the two daughters wiped their tears and tried in various ways to console her. Seeing their mother cry, the baby in her lap too began to wail.

In the course of conversation, the master gradually discovered that Matilal had been coming home and, by various tricks, extracting money from his mother. The wife had never revealed this—who knows, perhaps the master would have grown angry—and the boy was so pampered, if scolded, who knows what might have happened. It is always best for women to tell their husbands everything concerning the children. Concealing an illness never does any good. After much discussion with his wife, the master sent letters that very night to several relatives, asking them to be present the next day at the place in Calcutta where he would be going.

The night of happiness seems to slip away. When the mind is sunk in a sea of worry, the night feels interminably long. It seems as though dawn has come, but the dawn never arrives, no matter how long you wait. Baburam Babu’s mind was beset with a thousand thoughts—a thousand schemes—a thousand strategies—a thousand solutions. He could not remain still in the house; before daybreak, he took Thakchacha and others and boarded a boat. With the ebb tide, the boat drifted and moored at the Baghbazar ghat. The night was nearly over—the oilmen had yoked their bullocks to the presses—the cowherds were leading their cattle—the washerman’s donkey was plodding along—the fish and vegetable boats were coming in with a whoosh—the Brahmin scholars...

With their bathing pots in hand, the women made their way to the ghat, lining up in rows and exchanging the secrets of their hearts. One complained, “My life is ruined by that wretched Thakurji’s nagging.” Another said, “My mother-in-law, that old witch, is always picking on the eldest daughter-in-law.” Yet another sighed, “Sister, I have no desire to live any longer—my husband’s aunt tramples me underfoot, and my son says nothing; she’s turned the poor boy into a sheep.” Someone else lamented, “Ah, what a cursed fate I have—she sits on my chest day and night, making me cook rice.” Another said, “My son in my lap is already ten years old—who knows whether I’ll live or die, but I should marry him off while I still can.”

A brief shower had just passed; here and there, ragged clouds still lingered in the sky. The roads and ghats were slick and muddy. Baburam Babu, after smoking a hookah, tried to hire a carriage or a palanquin, but none could be had—the fares seemed outrageously high. A crowd of young loafers had gathered on the street. Observing Baburam Babu’s predicament, one of them called out, “Hey Babu, why not ride on a porter’s back? That’ll only cost you two paisa! Hasn’t your father’s ancestral home been ruined?” At this, Baburam, about to rush at the boy in anger, slipped and fell with a crash. The boys burst into laughter, clapping their hands from a safe distance.

With his head hung low, Baburam Babu quickly bundled himself into a rickety old carriage, taking along Thakchacha and the others, and with a clatter and a jangle, they arrived at the house of Bansharam Babu of Simla.

Bansharam Babu was a regular fixture in the drawing rooms of lawyers and butlers, a master of lawsuits and legal wrangling. His monthly salary was fifty rupees, but his actual earnings knew no bounds; rituals and ceremonies were held at his house every day. In his drawing room, Beni Babu from Bali, Becharam Babu from Bahubazar, and Bakreshwar Babu from Battala were already waiting.

Becharam spoke up, “Baburam! You raised a snake on pure milk. I sent word to you again and again, but you paid me no heed—now you’ve lost both this world and the next because of your son. Mati drinks liquor by the gallon, gambles, eats all sorts of filth. He was caught gambling and nearly beat the watchman to death. Hala, Gada, and the other boys were with him. I have no children of my own. I thought Hala and Gada might at least bring me a pot of water in my old age, but now even that hope is dashed. What more can I say about these boys? Bah!”
Baburam replied, “It’s hard to say who’s at fault here—let’s talk about what can be done now.”

Becharam: Do whatever you wish—I’m fed up with it all. At night, he sneaks into the prayer room and drinks bottles of liquor. He’s blackened the rafters with the smoke from his charas and ganja. He’s stolen silver and gold things and sold them off. And then he says, one day he’ll burn the sacred Shalgram stone, grind it to powder, and chew it with his betel leaf. And I’m supposed to pay money to get them out of trouble again? Nonsense!
Bakreshwar: Motilal isn’t all that bad—I’ve seen him myself at school, his nature is quite good. He’s not a child, nor is he made of stone, so why he’s turned out like this, I can’t say.
Thakchacha: I say, what’s the use of all this idle chatter? Does talk of oil and hemp fill our bellies? Let’s get to the root of this lawsuit and settle it once and for all.

Banchharam: (Inwardly delighted—thinking, perhaps, the flattened rice and curd are ready to eat) If you’re not a businessman, you won’t understand business talk. What Thakchacha says is what needs to be done. We’ll need to properly instruct a couple of reliable witnesses. We must hire our Butler Sahib as the lawyer—if we don’t win the case, we’ll take it to the higher court. If that doesn’t work, we’ll go to the counsel. If even that fails, we’ll take it all the way to England! Are we to be beaten by children? But without our Butler Sahib, nothing will happen. He’s a clever fellow—he’s resolved many cases by setting traps in the sky, and he trains witnesses as if he’s teaching birds to fly.
Bakreshwar: When trouble strikes, that’s when you need wit and wisdom. We must certainly pursue the case. Is it good to stand by and lose, and then get clapped at?
Banchharam: I’ve never seen a smarter lawyer than Butler Sahib. I’m in awe of his intelligence. He’ll blow away this whole case in three words. Let’s get up at once and go to his house.

Beni: Gentlemen, forgive me. Even if I lose my life, I won’t do anything unrighteous. For the sake of friendship, I can do anything, but I cannot risk my afterlife. If there’s truly fault, it’s better to admit it—truth is undefeated. If you take the path of lies in trouble, the trouble only grows.
Thakchacha: Ha-ha-ha! Lawsuits aren’t for bookish men—

chapters.title: The Mother’s Sorrow
paragraphs: They slip away at the slightest hint of trouble. If we act like them, we’ll be in the grave before long—how delightful!

Banchharam: You’ve spent so long getting ready, the festival is over. Benibabu is as steady as a rock—he’s the Jagannath Tarkapanchanan of moral philosophy. You can go to Bali with him one day and have a debate. For now, get up and be on your way.

Becharam: Beni brother! Your opinion is my opinion—I’ve lived through three ages, now I’m in the fourth. Even if it costs me my life, I won’t do wrong—why should I do wrong for anyone else? Those rascals have already wrung my bones—should I spend more money on them? Should I give false testimony for their sake? If they go to jail, in a way, I’m saved. Why should I feel sorry for them? Just the sight of their faces makes my blood boil—get lost!
6. Motilal’s Mother’s Worries, A Conversation Between the Sisters, A Discussion on Principles Between Beni and Becharam Babu, and the Introduction of Bardaprasad Babu.

At the Baidyabati house, the peace of the evening lulled everyone to sleep. Before sunrise, Sridhar Bhattacharya, Ramgopal Churamani, and others sat down to their prayers. Some offered tulsi leaves, some picked bilva leaves, some made a humming drone as they recited their mantras, some declared, “If this doesn’t bring good fortune, I’m no Brahmin,” while others threatened, “If things go badly, I’ll throw away my sacred thread!” The whole house was in a flurry—no one felt the least bit of happiness.

The mistress of the house sat by the window, anxiously calling upon her chosen deity. The little boy in her lap sucked on his pacifier, kicking his arms and legs as he played. Glancing at the child now and then, the lady thought to herself, “Oh fate! Who can say what will become of you? The pain of not having a child is one thing, but having one brings a hundred more troubles. If the child falls even a little ill, the mother’s heart flies out of her chest. She pours her whole being into making the child well—eating, sleeping, everything is forgotten. Days and nights blur together, she loses all sense of time. If, after all this suffering, the child grows up to be a good person, then it’s all worth it. But if not, it’s like dying while still alive—nothing in the world brings joy, and it’s shameful to even show your face to the neighbors.”

I have no desire—my proud face shrinks, and I wish the earth would split in two so I could slip inside. Only Guru knows how much effort I put into raising Moti—now the boy has learned to fly and is dressing me down. Hearing of Moti’s misdeeds, I am fried—living in sorrow and disgust. I don’t tell Master everything; if he heard it all, he might go mad. Away with it! I can’t bear to think anymore! I am but a woman—what can I do by thinking? Whatever is written in fate, that will be.
A maid came and took the child away. The mistress sat down to perform her daily prayers.

Such is the nature of the mind: when it is engrossed in one thing, it cannot suddenly forget and turn to another. That is why, though the mistress sat down to her prayers, she could not concentrate. Time and again she tried to focus on her chanting, but her mind would not go that way. Thoughts of Moti kept arising—like a fierce current, who could resist it? Sometimes she felt as if an arrest warrant had been issued for him—they were binding him and taking him to jail—his father stood nearby, head bowed in grief, weeping. Sometimes she imagined her son coming close and saying, “Mother, forgive me—I have done what I have done, but I will never cause you pain again.” And again, she felt as if Moti was in grave danger—he would have to go into exile for life. The mistress’s composure broke, and she began to mutter to herself—“It’s broad daylight—am I dreaming? No—this is not a dream. Then what delusion is this? Who knows why my mind is so restless today.”
Saying this, she wiped her tears and slowly lay down on the floor.
The two daughters, Mokshada and Promoda, were sitting on the roof, drying their hair.

Mokshada: “Hey Promoda! Let your hair down properly—your hair is so tangled and wild! Well, why wouldn’t it be? In seven lifetimes, not a drop of oil touches it—people’s bodies thrive on oil and water, but you bathe all year round without oil, what illness will you not catch? Why do you worry so much? You’ve worried yourself into a rope!”

Promoda: “Sister! Do you think I worry for pleasure? My mind just can’t rest, what can I do? When I was a child, father caught hold of a Kulin’s son and married me off to him—I heard about it only when I grew up. My husband has married in countless places, and—”
With such a character as his, I have no desire to even look at his face. Better to have no husband at all than one like that.
Mokshada: Hush, dear! Don’t say such things—whether a husband is good or bad, it’s better for a woman to have one.

Promoda: Then listen to this—last year, when I was suffering from that recurring fever, bedridden day and night, too weak even to stand, my husband came to see me. Since I became aware of the world, I have never seen a husband as poor in affection as he is. I thought that if he sat by me and spoke a few words, my suffering might ease a little. But sister, you said not to expect anything—he is my... Standing close by, he immediately said—“It’s been sixteen years since I married you—you are my only wife—I’ve come to you now because I need money—I won’t stay long—I went to your father, but he dodged me—now take off your bangles and give them to me.” I said, “Let me ask my mother—whatever she says, I’ll do.” No sooner had I said this than he forcibly pulled the bangles off my wrist. I tried to resist a little, but he kicked me and walked away—at that, I fainted on the spot. Afterwards, my mother came and fanned me for a long time until I regained consciousness.
Mokshada: Promoda! Hearing your tale of sorrow brings tears to my eyes. See, at least you still have him left—I don’t even have that.

Promoda: Sister! Such is a husband. By fortune, I stayed at my uncle’s house for some time, so I learned a bit of reading, writing, and handiwork. All day, I keep myself busy with chores, studies, and crafts to cover up the sadness in my heart. If I ever sit alone and start thinking, my mind immediately catches fire.

Mokshada: What can you do? In a previous life, we must have sinned so much that we’re suffering so now. If you keep yourself busy, your body stays healthy, and your mind too. But if you sit idle, worries, evil thoughts, sickness—everything comes and grabs hold of you. My uncle told me this—I have eased much of my widow’s pain by keeping busy, and I always think that everything is in God’s hands. To keep your mind on Him is the real work. Sister! If you start thinking, you’ll drown in a sea of thoughts. There’s no shore to it. What’s the use of thinking? Do your religious duties—serve your parents—take care of your two brothers, and when they have children, raise them as your own—they are our children too.

Promoda: Sister! What you say is true, but our eldest brother has gone completely astray. He spends his days in bad company, bad deeds, and worse talk. His character, his devotion to our parents, his affection for us—none of it is as it should be. The love a sister has for her brother, a brother doesn’t have even a hundredth part of that for his sister. Sisters wear themselves out for their brothers, but brothers always think they’ll be free once their sisters are married off. We’re the elder sisters—if Mati ever comes near and says a kind word or two, it soothes the heart, but you know what his behavior is like.

Mokshada: Not all brothers are like that. There are some brothers who look upon their elder sisters as mothers, and their younger sisters as daughters. Truly, there are such brothers who treat their sisters just as they do their brothers. Unless they spend a few moments talking with their sisters, they feel no satisfaction; and if any trouble befalls the sister, they rush to help her with all their might.
Promoda: That is true, but as ill luck would have it, we have the very sort of brother our fate deserves. Alas! There is not a single kind of happiness for us in this world!
A maid came in and said, “Mother is crying”—hearing this, the two sisters hurriedly went downstairs.

It was a moonlit night. The river Ganges shimmered with the glow of the moon—gentle breezes were blowing—mingled with the fragrance of wildflowers, wafting now and then, delighting the senses—the waves were dancing. From the nearby thicket, birds were calling out in various cries. Beni Babu sat at Deonagazi’s ghat, looking this way and that, singing a kheyal in Kedara ragini: “Shikeho.” Immersed in the song, he kept time with his hands.
Just then, from behind, a voice called out, “Beni Bhaiya, O Shikeho!” Beni Babu turned to see that Becharam Babu of Bowbazar had arrived. At once, he rose in haste and respectfully seated him nearby.
Becharam: Beni Bhaiya! Today you spoke very rightly to Baburam. I had come to your village for an invitation—I am greatly pleased with you—for that reason, I wished to see you once before leaving.

Beni: Becharam Dada, we are but poor souls, living hand to mouth by our labor. Wherever there is discussion of knowledge or religion, there we go. There are many wealthy relatives and acquaintances, it is true, but we only go to them out of shame, compulsion, or necessity—rarely out of affection. And even if we do go, our hearts find no joy, for the rich only respect the rich. If we go, at most they’ll say, “It’s so hot today—how’s your work going? Hey, bring a hookah.” If, by chance, they smile and speak a word, it’s as if we’ve become kin to their fathers. Nowadays, money is all that matters—neither learning nor religion has any worth. And flattering the rich is a tiresome business. There is a saying, “The love of the great is a sandbank’s dam—now it’s a rope in your hand, now it’s the moon in the sky.” But people do not understand—such is the enchantment of money that people gladly suffer kicks and still go near to bow and scrape. That—
Be that as it may, keeping company with the high and mighty is a peril to one’s afterlife; today’s incident nearly tore my afterlife to shreds!

Becharam: Judging by Baburam’s ways and means, it seems his prospects are bleak indeed. Ah, what a minister he’s acquired! That fellow, a sly dog, goes by the name Thokchacha. He’s the king of all swindlers. Trickery runs in his very bones. He’s a man from Bancharam the lawyer’s quarters! Just like a sneaky, rain-soaked alley cat, he slinks about, quietly pocketing whatever he can. Whoever falls under his spell is finished, plain and simple. And then there’s Bakreshwar, the schoolmaster—teaching morals, yet the very crown prince of double-dealing and sly talk. Bah! Anyway, tell me, did you acquire all this religious wisdom from reading English books?

Beni: What religious wisdom do I really have? To say so of me is mere kindness on your part. Whatever little sense of right and wrong I possess, I owe entirely to Bardabubu of Badarganj. I lived with that great man for many days. Out of his kindness, he offered me a few words of advice.
Becharam: Who is Bardababu? Tell me his story in detail. I love to hear such tales.

Beni: Bardabubu’s home is in Etakagomari, a village in Bengal. When his father passed away, he came to Calcutta—he suffered great hardship for food and clothing—nothing like the comfort we have today. From his childhood, he was always absorbed in spiritual matters, so even though he endured hardship, he never felt it. He lived in a humble thatched hut—the two rupees he received from his uncle each month were his only support. He had acquaintance with one or two honest men—apart from them, he visited no one, nor did he rely on anyone. He could not afford servants—he did his own marketing, cooked his own meals, and while cooking, he would study. Whether morning, noon, or night, he meditated on the Lord with single-minded devotion. He went to school in torn and soiled clothes, and the sons of the wealthy mocked and ridiculed him. Even when he heard it, he paid no heed, and would calm everyone with sweet words, calling them brother or friend. When one studies English, many become envious—they look upon the world as their own tavern. But envy could never find a place in Bardababu’s heart. His nature was exceedingly gentle and humble, and his learning...

After completing his studies, he left the school. No sooner had he left than a post worth thirty rupees opened up at the school. With this, he brought his mother, wife, and his uncle’s son to live with him at home, and took great pains to ensure their well-being.

There were many poor and destitute people living near his house, whom he always looked after—giving charity as much as he could, visiting anyone who fell ill, and bringing them medicine. The children of these poor folks could not afford to attend school, so every morning he himself would teach them.

When his uncle fell ill, his cousin became gravely anxious, and our gentleman would sit by his side day and night, nursing him until he recovered. He had an extraordinary devotion to his aunt, whom he regarded as a mother. Many people, when faced with loss or calamity among friends or family, are suddenly seized by a fit of renunciation, as if the world is empty and only God is real. But in Bardababu’s heart, that feeling is ever-present; it is evident in his speech and actions, though he never makes a show of it before others.

He is not a man of quick temper—he does nothing for the sake of display or to win applause. Whatever good deeds he performs, he does so in secret. He helps many people, but only the person helped knows of it; if others find out, he is exceedingly embarrassed. He is learned in many subjects, yet not the least bit proud. Some people, after learning a little, strut about like a fish jumping in shallow water, thinking, “I am the wisest—no one can write as I do—no one possesses knowledge like mine—whatever I say is the final word.” Bardababu is of a different sort; his knowledge and intellect are profound, yet he never disregards even the words of the humblest, and if he hears an opposing view, he is not at all annoyed; rather, he listens with pleasure and reconsiders the merits and faults of his own opinion.

To recount all the virtues of this gentleman would be a heavy task—let it suffice to say that no one has ever seen a man as humble and God-fearing as he; even in the face of death, he would never stray from righteousness. In the company of such a person, one receives more good counsel than from reading a hundred books.
Becharam: Hearing of such a man is soothing to the ears. It’s late at night, and the road across the river is long—I must be on my way home. Let us hope we meet again at the police station tomorrow.

chapters.title: Storm on the River
paragraphs: Job Charnock would pass through the area of Batanagar; there was a large tree under which he would rest and smoke his hookah. Many traders would gather in the shade of that tree. So enamored was he by the shade of that tree that he decided to establish his factory right there. The three villages of Sutanuti, Gobindapur, and Kalikata were bought outright and began to be settled. Later, for the sake of trade, people of various races came and settled, and gradually Calcutta grew into a bustling city.

The city of Calcutta began in the year 1689. Three years later, Job Charnock died. At that time, the Maidan and Chaurangi were jungles. Where the Permit Office now stands, there was once a fort, and the place now called Clive Street was where all the trading took place.
Earlier, Calcutta was plagued by terrible epidemics, so much so that the English, to ward them off, would gather every year on the 15th of November and recite their Tuesday prayers together.

One of the chief virtues of the English is that wherever they live, they keep the place exceedingly clean. As Calcutta gradually became tidier, the incidence of disease also steadily declined—but the Bengalis, even after all this, refuse to understand. To this day, there is such a ditch near Lakshmipati’s house that the stench makes it unbearable to go near!

The administration of Calcutta’s goods, courts, and criminal justice—these three responsibilities—used to rest on a single Englishman. Under him served a Bengali official, and this Englishman was called the ‘zamindar’. Later, to curb the excesses of various courts and the growing influence of the English, a Supreme Court was established; and the duties of the police were separated and began to run smoothly. In 1798, Sir John Richardson and others were appointed as Justices of the Peace. Afterwards, in 1800, Mr. Blacquire and others were assigned to that post.

The orders of those who became Justices of the Peace were enforced throughout the land. Those who were only magistrates, and not Justices of the Peace, needed the help of the local court to issue orders beyond their own jurisdiction. For this reason, many magistrates in the mofussil have recently become Justices of the Peace.

It has been about four years since Mr. Blacquire died. People say he was born of an English father and a Brahmin mother. He received his early education here, and later went to England for further study. When he was appointed Police Magistrate, his authority shook the very city of Calcutta—everyone trembled in fear. After some time, he gave up the work of investigation and arrests, and focused solely on adjudication. He was a master of judgment, for he understood the language, customs, and all the subtle nuances of this country—he knew the criminal law by heart, and having served as an interpreter in the Supreme Court for many years, he had acquired excellent knowledge of how to conduct a case.

Time flows like water—before one knows it, Monday arrives—the church clock strikes ten with a resounding clang. Sergeants, sepoys, darogas, naibs, guards, chowkidars, and all manner of people filled the police station. Here and there, groups of landladies and prostitutes sat, spitting out betel quid; elsewhere, some men, having been beaten, stood with bloodied clothes; in another corner, a few thieves sat with downcast faces—

Sitting on the side, someone is deep in thought—elsewhere, a couple of English-knowing scribes are writing out petitions for a fee—somewhere, the plaintiffs are scurrying up and down the stairs, making a commotion—somewhere, the witnesses are whispering conspiratorially among themselves—somewhere, the professional bailers are sitting like crows at a pilgrimage, waiting for their chance—somewhere, the touts of the lawyers are lying in wait, casting their nets—somewhere, the lawyers are whispering mantras into the ears of the witnesses—somewhere, the clerks are shuffling files and pushing along the cases—somewhere, the sergeants are strutting about, chest puffed out, showing off their authority—somewhere, the head clerks are gossiping: “That sahib is a fool—this sahib is clever—that one is soft—that one is strict—the verdict in yesterday’s case was no good.” The police are prowling about—it's a veritable abode of Yama—who knows whose fate will turn out how—everyone is anxious.

Baburam Babu arrived in haste, accompanied by his lawyer, advisor, and relatives. Thakchacha had a turban wound messily on his head, a long tunic on his body, slippers on his feet, a rosary of glass beads in his hand—murmuring the names of saints and prophets, stroking his beard now and then, as if counting his prayers, but it was all just for show. It's hard to find a trickster as clever as Thakchacha. As soon as the police arrived, he began whirling about in all directions like a spinning top. One moment he’s here, the next he’s there—whispering in the ears of the witnesses—dragging Baburam Babu by the hand—arguing with Butler Sahib—explaining things to Bancharam Babu. All eyes among the police were fixed on Thakchacha. Many whose fathers and grandfathers were thieves and rascals, their descendants, out of weakness of character, believe them to have been extraordinary and famous men, and so, when introducing themselves to others, they blurt out, “I am so-and-so’s son, so-and-so’s grandson.” Whoever came to speak with Thakchacha, he would immediately declare, “I am Abdur Rahman, son of Gulmohammad, and grandson of Golam Hossain of Ampak.”

A sharp-tongued government man retorted, “Arre, just tell us what work you do—maybe a couple of loafers in your neighborhood know your father and grandfather’s names, but who in Calcutta cares? Did they work as stable boys?”
Hearing this, Thakchacha’s eyes turned blood-red and he said, “What are you saying, you policeman, if this were anywhere else, I’d have leapt on you and bitten you!” Saying this, Baburam...
Taking the Babu by the hand, he stood upright and showed the officer, in no uncertain terms, just how much respect and honor he commanded.

Meanwhile, a commotion arose near the police steps. A carriage came rattling up and, as soon as the door opened, out stepped a frail, withered old Englishman. The surgeons immediately doffed their hats and bowed, and everyone exclaimed, “Mr. Blackier has arrived!” The sahib seated himself on the bench and settled a few cases of assault before calling up Motilal’s case.

On one side stood Kale Khan and Fate Khan, the complainants; on the other, Baburam Babu of Baidyabati, Benibabu of Bali, Bakreshwar Babu of Battala, Becharam Babu of Bowbazar, Bansharam Babu of Outer Simla, and the butler of the clubroom—all arrayed in a line.

Baburam Babu, dressed in a double-breasted coat, a Khirkidar turban on his head, a tilak on his nose, and a sacrificial mark above that, stood with folded hands, gazing at the sahib with a pitiful expression—convinced that the sight of his tears would surely awaken the sahib’s compassion. Motilal, Haldhar, Gadadhar, and the other accused were brought before the sahib. Motilal, his head bowed in shame, stood silent; the sight of his gaunt, starved face nearly broke Baburam Babu’s heart.

The complainants declared that the accused had been gambling at the wrestling ground and, when they tried to apprehend them, had been beaten severely and the culprits had escaped. They bared their bodies to show the marks of the beating. Butler Sahib cross-examined the complainants and their witnesses at length, trimming away much of the testimony relating to Motilal. Such trimming is hardly surprising—after all, that’s the lawyer’s craft, and the groundwork had already been laid; what can’t be accomplished with money? “Even an old man can be married off with coins.”

Then Butler Sahib called his own witnesses. They claimed that, on the day of the beating, Motilal was at the Baidyabati house. But under Mr. Blackier’s sharp questioning, they began to falter once or twice. Thakchacha saw the way things were going—not at all favorable—a slip and they could fall flat. When it comes to lawsuits, people often lose all sense of direction; one must twist and turn the truth to enter the court—victory depends only on cunning. For this reason, he himself stepped forward and testified that, on such-and-such day, at such-and-such hour, he had been teaching Motilal Persian at the Baidyabati house. The magistrate questioned him at length, but Thakchacha did not waver.

Dolbar is not one to be trifled with—he’s a master of legal wrangling, and under no circumstances would he let the main point of his case slip away. At once, Mr. Butler began to deliver a speech. After pondering for a while, the magistrate pronounced his judgment: Motilal was acquitted, while the other accused received one or two months’ imprisonment and a fine of thirty rupees each. No sooner was the verdict announced than cries of “Haribol!” rang out, and Baburam Babu shouted, “O incarnation of righteousness! What subtle justice! May you soon become Governor!”

As everyone gathered in the police courtyard, Haldhar and Gadadhar, upon seeing Premnarayan Majumdar, began singing his teasing song right into his ears: “Premnarayan Majumdar, eat your bananas, you’ve got no work to do—just go home! We suspect you’re Hanuman himself, so why not leap freely by the seashore?” Premnarayan retorted, “Well done, you rascals! May shamelessness be far from you! Even as you’re being sent to jail, you can’t stop your mischief!” With that, they were led away to prison.

Beni Babu, a man of religious scruples, stood silent and stunned, witnessing the defeat of virtue and the triumph of vice. Uncle Thakchacha stroked his beard and, with a boastful laugh, said, “Well, what do you say now, Bookish Babu? If you’d followed this gentleman’s advice, we’d all have been finished!” Bancharam stormed over, waving his right hand, and exclaimed, “What’s this, a child’s game?” Bakreshwar replied, “He’s no child—he’s a stone from Paresh!” Becharam Babu said, “Nonsense! I want no part in such unrighteousness—I don’t even want to win the case—nonsense!” With that, he grabbed Beni Babu’s hand and marched out indignantly.

Baburam Babu, after offering prayers at Kalighat, boarded a boat. Bengalis are always proud of their caste, but when it comes to action, even a Yavana turns into his father’s priest! Baburam Babu now regarded Thakchacha as a veritable Bhishma, and, putting his arm around his neck, became absorbed in talk of their courtroom victory—who cared now for betel, water, ablutions, or evening prayers? All was forgotten. At times, he declared that there was no one like Mr. Butler and Bancharam Babu; at others, he claimed he’d never seen fools the likes of Becharam and Beni. Motilal looked around restlessly—sometimes standing at the prow, sometimes tugging at his beard, sometimes sitting atop the umbrella, sometimes grabbing the oar to strike the maidservant. In the midst of this, Baburam Babu would say, “Motilal, my boy, what’s this? Sit still!” At the bow, the gardener from Kashijora was rolling tobacco—seeing Baburam’s delight, he too felt a surge of joy—
Someone asks, “Go on, sir! Will there be a Bakule Jatra at this house during the Puja this year? Is this the price of a shell bangle? How much have the others offered?”

Nothing ever happens in the same way—just as anger, when suppressed in the mind, must burst out at least once, so too, when the summer is fierce and the air is still, a storm is almost certain to follow. The sun is setting—the evening approaches—look, a dark cloud has risen in the west. In a matter of moments, a deep gloom spreads in all directions. The wind howls—so fierce that you can’t see the person at your side—cries of “Hold on!” ring out. Lightning begins to flash, and thunder crashes again and again with a rattling, rumbling roar, filling everyone with terror. The rain pours down in torrents—who could possibly stand outside in this deluge? The waves rise higher and higher, then come crashing down upon the boat. Within a short while, two or three boats are lost. Seeing this, the boatmen of the other boats try to steer for the shore, but the force of the wind drives them off in another direction.

Uncle Thakchacha’s scolding ceases—he is stunned, senseless at the sight and sound. Now and then, he clutches his rosary and mutters prayers—now he begins to invoke both Muhammad Ali and Satya Pir. Baburam Babu is beside himself with anxiety; the punishment for his misdeeds begins right here. Who can keep a calm mind after committing wrong? You may cover up your sins with cunning before others, but no deed is ever hidden from your own heart. The sinner feels as if someone is pricking his soul with needles—always anxious, always afraid, always unwell—the little laughter he manages is nothing but a forced, toothy grin. Baburam Babu, terrified, begins to weep and says, “Uncle Thakchacha, what will become of us? I see death by accident before my eyes—surely this is the punishment for our sins. Alas, I brought my son back from jail, but could not take him to his mother—if I die, my wife will die of grief as well. Now I remember my brother Beni’s words—perhaps it would have been better to stay on the path of righteousness.”
Thakchacha is afraid too, but he is an old sinner—his mouth is bold. He says, “Why fear, Babu? If we drown, I’ll carry you on my back to the other side—danger is for men to face, after all!”
The storm grows fiercer and fiercer—the boat rocks and nearly capsizes, everyone clings to each other and cries out for help. In his heart, Thakchacha mutters, “Uncle, save yourself first!”

chapters.title: The Lawyer’s Office
paragraphs: Butler Sahib has arrived at the office. He’s flipping through the records to see how much work has been done this month. Nearby, a dog is lying down; every now and then, the sahib hisses at it. Occasionally, he stuffs snuff up his nose and snaps his fingers. Sometimes, his eyes wander over the account books; sometimes, he stands with his legs apart; sometimes, he worries about the expenses in several court offices—so much money will have to be paid.
