Not a paisa has been arranged yet, and if the money isn’t deposited before the term opens, all work will come to a halt. Just then, Howard the lawyer’s clerk arrives and hands him two papers. The moment he gets the papers, the sahib’s face lights up with delight. Immediately, he calls out, “Bensharam! Come here quickly!”
Banchharam Babu throws his shawl over the chair, tucks a pen behind his ear, and rushes in.
Butler: “Bensharam! I am very pleased! Two cases have been filed against Baburam—one for ejectment and another for something else. Howard Sahib has sent me both the notice and the subpoena.”

The moment Banchharam hears this, he claps his armpits in glee and says, “Sahib, just watch what a clever manager I am! If I can bring Baburam here, there’ll be enough sweets and cream for everyone. Hand me those two papers at once; I’ll go to Vaidyabati myself—this isn’t a job for just anyone. Now’s the time for some real bluster and bravado. If I can just climb this tree, money will rain down; but for now, our oven is hot and empty—very greedy—have to strike quick and bring something home for Alal.”

At the house in Vaidyabati, the ceremonial bodhon has begun—the drums are beating, “dhadha gur gur dhadha gur gur.” Mushundadi is sitting on a decorated stool, singing the morning raga. In the hall, the svastyayana has started for Motilal. On one side, the Chandi is being recited; on another, Ganges clay is being prepared for Shiva worship. In the center, the shalgram stone is placed and offered tulsi leaves. The Brahmins, hands on their heads, are deep in thought, muttering among themselves, “Our divine Brahminhood has been revealed for cash alone—never mind Motilal’s release, now even the master—”

He went with him. If he had boarded the boat yesterday, there is no doubt that the boat must have perished in the storm—whatever happens, the household is utterly ruined—now there will be nothing but the wailing of beggars—who knows what will become of the Young Master—perhaps our share of the spoils is lost forever. Among those Brahmins, one began to speak softly, “Oh, why are you all so worried? No one can deprive us of our dues—we are like the saw on the greens—cutting both ways, coming and going. If the master has indeed passed away, then there will be a grand funeral feast—the master was old—if the mistress starts squabbling over money, people will smear her face with soot and lime. Another said, ‘Oh brother! That eggplant patch is gone, but the radish patch remains. What I want is that it should drip like the goddess of the earth—every day I get, every day I eat—will one downpour quench a lifetime’s thirst?’

Baburam Babu’s wife was a most virtuous woman. From the moment her husband left, she had given up food and water, and was beside herself with anxiety. From the window of the house, she could see the Ganges—she sat at the window all night. Whenever the wind howled fiercely, she shrank back in terror. Sometimes she cast her gaze upon the storm, but the very sight made her heart tremble. At times, the sound of thunder reached her ears, and she would grow restless and cry out to the Lord in anguish. Thus some time passed—the movement of boats on the Ganges had nearly ceased. Whenever she heard even the slightest sound, she would rise and look. Sometimes, from afar, she saw a faint, flickering light, and thought perhaps it was the lamp of a boat—after a while, a boat would come into view, and she would hope it might come to the landing. But when the boat, instead of mooring, passed straight by, the pain of disappointment struck her heart like an arrow. The night was nearly over—the storm and rain gradually subsided. After the turmoil of creation, calm is all the more beautiful. Stars appeared in the sky—the moonlight seemed to dance upon the Ganges, and the earth grew so silent that even the rustle of a single leaf could be heard distinctly.

Such sights stir many thoughts in the mind. The mistress looked around again and again, and, growing impatient, spoke to herself, “O Lord of the Universe! I have never wronged anyone—never committed a sin—must I now, after all these years, suffer the agony of widowhood? I have no use for wealth—no use for jewels—”

It would be better to remain a beggar-woman with nothing—at least that sorrow would not feel so bitter. But this—this alms, O God, grant me only that I may die with my husband and son’s faces before me. Such thoughts made the mistress of the house exceedingly anxious. She was a wise and reserved woman—if she were to weep, her daughters would surely break down as well, so she held herself together with great effort.

In the last hours of the night, the morning band began to play in the house. That music, it’s true, usually draws the hearts of ordinary folk, but to a tormented soul, such music only unlocks the floodgates of sorrow. Thus, upon hearing it, the mistress’s grief seemed to flare up anew.

Just then, a fisherman came to the Baidyabati house to sell fish. When questioned, he said that during the storm, near the Bashberia sandbank, a boat had nearly capsized—he believed it had finally sunk. There had been a fat gentleman, a Muslim, a young boy, and several others aboard. This news struck the household like a bolt of lightning. The music stopped at once, and the family burst into loud, wailing cries.

Later, as evening fell, Bancharam Babu bustled into the Baidyabati house’s drawing room and asked, “Where is the master?” Upon hearing the news from a servant, he sat down, clutching his head, and exclaimed, “Alas! The great man is gone.” After lamenting for a long while, he told the servant, “Bring me a hookah.” When someone brought him tobacco, as he began to smoke, he mused, “Babu Ram Babu is gone—soon I too shall follow him. I came here with such high hopes, but all was dashed the moment I arrived. The house is in mourning, the idols are being rattled in the shrine—I have no idea what to do or where to begin. If only I could have gotten hold of that money with a little trickery, it would have served many purposes—some I would have given to the sahib, some I’d have kept for myself, and then I’d have shifted the blame from one head to another. Who knew disaster would fall from the sky and land squarely on my head?”

Bancharam Babu, for show, began to weep a little in front of the servants, but his tears were only for the lost money. Seeing him, the household priests came and sat nearby. The Brahmins of the Swastyayani clan are a cunning lot—hard to get the better of them. Some began to extol Baburam Babu’s virtues, some lamented, “We are now orphans,” and others, unable to restrain their greed, said, “This is no time for mourning; we must do all we can to ensure his soul’s welfare in the next world—he was not a man of few means…”

Weren’t you there? Bancharam Babu is smoking his hookah and exclaiming, “Ha, ha!”—he doesn’t show much affection in his words—he knows well, what does a crow care for a ripe bel fruit? You, meanwhile, are so heartbroken that you cannot even lift your feet to leave—you agree to whatever you hear, muttering “Hmm, yes” to everything—you don’t know what to do, whose head to bite off—you can’t come up with any plan at all. At times, you think that if you don’t make some effort, you might lose a good property or two—if you inform the family, money will come out immediately. Then again, you think, in such fresh grief, any talk will be swept away. Thus, your mind is tangled with all sorts of thoughts, when suddenly a commotion rises at the door—a hired servant arrives and hands over a letter—the address is in Baburam Babu’s handwriting, but the man can say nothing more, having brought the letter inside the house. The mistress, flustered, opens and reads it. The letter reads:

“Last night I was in grave danger—the boat lurched forward as we tried to dock, the boatmen couldn’t make sense of anything, the storm was so fierce that the boat capsized completely. As the boat was sinking, I was terrified more than once, and more than once I remembered you—you seemed to stand by me and say, ‘Do not fear in times of peril—call upon the Lord with all your heart and soul—He is merciful, He will surely save you from danger.’ I did just that. When I fell from the boat into the water, I found myself on a sandbank—knee-deep in water. The boat was torn to shreds by the force of the storm. I spent the entire night on the sandbank and arrived at Basberia in the morning. Motilal, having been in the water for a long time, fell ill. After some rest, he is feeling better; I believe we will reach home tonight.”

As soon as the letter was read, it was as if water had been poured on a raging fire—the mistress, after pondering for a moment, said, “Could such misfortune befall this poor woman?” No sooner had she spoken than Baburam Babu, along with his son and Thakchacha, arrived at the house. All around, a great commotion broke out. The family’s hearts, clouded by the gloom of sorrow, now saw the sun of joy rise. The mistress, holding the hands of her two daughters, gazed upon her husband and son and wept tears of relief—she had intended to reproach Motilal, but now all that was forgotten. The two daughters clung to their brother’s hand and fell at their father’s feet, weeping. The youngest son, seeing his father, felt as if he had found a priceless treasure—many

chapters.title: The Path of Vice
paragraphs: For a while, she clung to his neck—she would not come down from his lap. The other women began chanting auspicious verses from behind the curtain. Baburam Babu, overwhelmed by emotion, could not speak for some time. Motilal thought to himself, “Saved by the boat capsizing—otherwise, I would have lost my life facing my mother.”

Outside, in the courtyard, the Brahmins who had performed the svastyayani ceremony, seeing the master, blessed him and then said, “Nach daibat param balam”—there is no strength greater than fate. Sir, you are already virtuous, and now fate itself has favored you—what harm could possibly befall you? Had it not been so, we would not be true Brahmins.”
At these words, Thakchacha burst out, “If all the trouble was warded off by their incantations, then what of my hard work? Did I just sit there twiddling my thumbs?”

At once, the Brahmins softened and tried to appease him, saying, “Oh, just as Krishna was Arjuna’s charioteer, so you were the master’s charioteer—it is by your wisdom and strength that all was accomplished. You are an avatar of sorts; wherever you are, wherever we are, misfortune flees in terror.”

Banchharam Babu, who had been like a snake bereft of its gem, now began to weep a little, just enough to show Baburam Babu, with a sly glance, that he was deeply moved. At this, his chest swelled with pride, and he became firmly convinced that if he so much as cast a line, a fish would bite. Hearing the Brahmins’ words, he rushed forward, waving his right hand, and exclaimed, “What, am I to be beaten by a child? If misfortune were to befall the master, would I be cutting grass in Calcutta?”
9. The lack of proper education and good upbringing led to Motilal’s gradual decline, and, finding many companions, he became a full-fledged babu and began to mistreat respectable young women.

Once a boy goes astray, it is almost impossible to set him right again. It is the duty of guardians to instill good habits from childhood, so that noble tendencies may gradually ripen and, instead of inclining toward vice, the mind is drawn powerfully toward virtue. But if, in childhood, a boy falls into bad company or receives poor guidance, the restlessness of youth may overturn everything. Therefore, as long as a child’s mind is immature, it is essential to cultivate in him all manner of good habits. If such training continues until the age of twenty-five, there is little chance of him straying onto the wrong path. By then, his mind becomes so pure that even the mention of wrongdoing provokes anger and disgust.

It is exceedingly difficult for children of this country to receive such an education. Firstly, there are no good teachers; secondly, there are no good books. What is needed are books that, when read, instill noble feelings and sound judgment, which gradually become steadfast. But the common belief is that true education consists merely in learning the meanings of a handful of words. Thirdly, very few people understand by what means noble feelings are born in the mind. Fourthly, the kind of company children keep makes it nearly impossible for them to develop good character. One child’s father may be a gambler or a drunkard; another’s uncle or elder may be addicted to vice; perhaps someone’s mother knows nothing of reading or writing and takes no care at all in her children’s education, while other members of the family and the servants impart all sorts of bad lessons. Or, in the neighborhood or at school, the company of other boys leads to bad associations and evil deeds, resulting in utter ruin. Wherever even one of the above causes is present, it gravely hinders the imparting of good counsel to children. When all these causes come together, the effect is terrifying—like fire catching on dry straw. Whichever way it burns, it is as if someone pours ghee on that side, and in no time the flames spread and consume everything in their path.

Many had thought that, since the police matter was resolved, Motilal would return home, chastened. But a boy in whose mind not a trace of good upbringing has taken root, who feels no fear of honor or disgrace, cannot feel shame in any situation. Good or bad sense arises from the mind; thus, it is only through the mind that such feelings are connected. How can a mere physical blow or hardship change the course of the mind? When the sergeant had dragged Motilal along the street, he did feel a momentary discomfort and humiliation, but it was fleeting. Being sent to the lock-up caused him not the slightest worry, fear, or sense of shame. He spent the whole night and the next day singing songs and howling like a jackal or a dog, tormenting those nearby to such an extent that, covering their ears and invoking Lord Ram, they declared that being imprisoned with this boy was far worse than being in jail itself. The next day, when he stood before the magistrate, he did lower his head a little, like a chastened child, to show his father, but in his heart he felt nothing at all—whether he went to jail or was put in chains, he was not afraid in the least.

Those boys who have no fear, no shame, no sense of propriety—who are engaged only in mischief—their malady is not a trifling one; it is a disease of the mind. Only the right medicine, applied in earnest, can gradually cure it. But Baburam Babu had no inkling of such matters. He was firmly convinced that Motilal was a very good boy; at the slightest hint of criticism against him, he would flare up in anger. Yet, though others did not refrain from speaking, he himself would neither listen nor pay heed. Later, after seeing and hearing certain things, a faint suspicion began to stir in his mind, but for fear of losing face before others, he kept it bottled up, never confiding in anyone. He merely whispered to the household doorman that Motilal should not be allowed to leave the house.

By then, the disease had grown severe, and no suitable remedy was administered. What can come of simply confining or keeping someone under watch? Once the mind is corrupted, even blows of iron cannot restrain it; rather, such measures only sharpen its cunning.

Motilal soon began to scale the walls and slip outside. Haldhar, Gadadhar, Ramgovinda, Dolgovinda, and Mangovinda, having been released, gathered at the Vaidya’s house and set up their haunt. Soon, others from the neighborhood—Kabelram, Banchharam, Bhajakrishna, Harekrishna, and the likes of Sreedam and Subal—joined the group. In the company of these boys, Motilal lost all his fears; his dread of his father gradually vanished.

A boy who, even in childhood, does not learn innocent games or wholesome amusements, inevitably finds pleasure in base amusements. English boys, guided by their parents, learn various innocent games to keep body and mind healthy—some take to drawing, some to flowers, some to music, some to hunting or athletic pursuits—each according to his taste, all harmless pastimes. But the boys of this country merely imitate what they see: their constant desire is to don gold, jewels, pearls, and coral, to roam gardens with sycophants and courtesans, and to revel in ostentatious display and extravagance. Show and splendor are the prerogatives of youth, but if not checked early, such desires only grow and give rise to all manner of vices—vices that, in the end, ruin both body and mind.
Motilal, in time, became a thorough scoundrel, so cunning that he could throw dust in his father’s eyes while engaging in all sorts of rude and immoral acts. Always in the company of his cronies...
People would gossip, “That old fellow’s son—just close his eyes for a moment, and he’ll play the grand gentleman to his heart’s content.”

Whenever Motilal asked his parents for money, they had to give it to him—if there was any delay, he would threaten, “I’ll hang myself, or swallow poison and die.” His father and mother, terrified, would think, “Whatever is written in our fate will come to pass. For now, if the boy stays alive, we live—he is the lamp of our Shivaratri—let him live, at least we’ll have a sip of water in our old age.”

Motilal was always caught up in extravagance—there was never a moment’s peace at home. Sometimes he was drunk on picnics—sometimes obsessed with joining the theater troupe—sometimes organizing a group for storytelling—sometimes bellowing and bantering with the poets and singers of the Saker’s club—sometimes running about for the neighborhood puja—sometimes off to watch a dancing girl’s performance—sometimes caught up in pointless brawls, riots, and mayhem. Siddi, charas, ganja, pills, liquor—these flowed endlessly at his side—the “guruk palai” call rang out. The young gentlemen were always decked out—wild hair on their heads, black tooth powder on their teeth, Dhakai dhotis with a sepoy’s border, boots with high heels, a velvet or hempen coat on their backs, a gold-embroidered cap on their heads, a perfumed silk handkerchief and a fancy cane in their hands, English shoes with silver buckles on their feet. There was no time for a proper meal, but rich kachoris, fine sweets, barfi, nikhuti, manohara, and rose-flavored betel were always at hand.

If bad habits are not checked at the start, they only grow with time. In the end, one becomes almost animal-like—unable to tell good from bad, just as with opium: once you start, the dose must always increase. So too, when one indulges in vice, the urge to commit graver sins arises of its own accord. The amusements that once delighted Motilal and his band of young gentlemen soon seemed trivial—they no longer brought any special satisfaction, so they began to seek out heavier pleasures. After dusk, the young men would form a gang and head out—sometimes breaking into someone’s house to loot and plunder, sometimes setting fire to someone’s haystack, sometimes going to a courtesan’s house to raise a ruckus, pulling her hair, burning her mosquito net, or stealing her clothes and jewelry—sometimes trying to ruin the virtue of some respectable woman. The whole village was in a state of alarm, cracking their knuckles and muttering, “May you all meet your end soon!”

Thus some time passed—a few days ago, Babu Ram Babu, in the midst of his usual exploits... At someone’s request, he had gone to Calcutta. One evening, near the house at Baidyabati, a covered palanquin was passing by. The young dandies, as soon as they saw the palanquin, rushed over and surrounded it from all sides, and began to beat the bearers. Terrified for their lives, the bearers dropped the palanquin and fled. The young gentlemen opened the palanquin and discovered inside a most beautiful young woman. Matilal lunged forward, grabbed her by the hand, and dragged her out of the palanquin.

The young lady, trembling violently with fear, looked around at the empty surroundings and, weeping, called out to the Lord in her heart—“O Lord! Protect this helpless orphan—let my life be lost, but let my virtue not be destroyed.” As they all pulled and tugged at her, the girl fell to the ground, but still they dragged her forcefully into the house. The sound of her crying reached the ears of Matilal’s mother, who hurriedly came outside. At once, the young men scattered in all directions.
Seeing the mistress of the house, the young woman fell at her feet and cried out in anguish, “Mother!”

chapters.title: The Wedding Plot
paragraphs: “Protect my virtue—you are a true woman.” Only a virtuous wife can understand the perils that befall a virtuous wife. The mistress lifted her daughter, wiped the tears from her eyes with the edge of her own sari, and said, “My child! Don’t cry—there is nothing to fear—I will hold you close to my heart, you are as dear to me as my own flesh and blood. The wife who is devoted to her husband, her virtue is guarded by the Lord Himself.” With these words, she comforted her daughter, reassured her, and then took her along to her father’s house, where she left her in safety.

Description of the market at Baidyabati, the arrival of Becharam Babu, the tangle of Matilal’s marriage in Baburam Babu’s assembly, the journey to Monirampur to arrange the marriage, and the ensuing commotion.

The evening worship at Nistarini’s shrine in Sheorapuli is ringing out—ding, ding, ding. Becharam Babu, catching sight of the goddess’s temple, is walking along on foot. On either side of the road are shops—here, piles of potatoes from Bandipur and Gopalpur; there, puffed rice, sweet balls, rice, and lentils for sale; somewhere else, an oil-presser sits by his wooden mill, reading the Ramayana aloud—when the oxen circle round, he sings out a taunt, and when the oil flows again, he bursts out, “O Ram, we are monkeys, Ram, we are monkeys!” Nearby, a fisherman’s daughter, with a basket of fish and a lamp beside her, calls out, “Will you buy some fish?” Elsewhere, a cloth merchant is conducting a grand ceremony for Vyasa’s funeral feast. Becharam Babu is taking in all these sights as he walks along. When one strolls alone, the mind is always crowded with the same old thoughts that bubble up unbidden. In those days, Becharam Babu was always amused by devotional songs. As he left the bustle behind and passed through a lonely stretch, he remembered a tune by Manohar Sahi. The night was dark—hardly a soul on the road—only the occasional bullock cart creaking and groaning its way home, and here and there a dog barking at nothing. Becharam Babu began to hum the tune with great gusto—his nasal voice no sooner reached the ears of a couple of rustic women nearby than they cried out in alarm. In the villages, it has always been believed that the voice of a nasal man...
He only keeps talking about ghosts. Hearing all that commotion, Becharam Babu, a little flustered, hurried straight to the Baidyabati house.

Baburam Babu was sitting in the midst of a lively gathering. Beni Babu from Bali, Bakreshwar Babu from Battala, Bansharam Babu from Outer Simla, and many others were present. Thakchacha was seated on a chair near the cushion. Several Brahmin scholars were engaged in scriptural debates. Some were picking holes in the Nyaya Shastra, some were busy arguing over the Tithi-tattva, others were engrossed in the intricacies of the Malmas-tattva, some were explaining verses from the Tenth Canto, and some were locked in a fierce quarrel over Bahuvrihi and Dvandva compounds.

A man from Kamakhya, sitting beside Dhekial Phukan Karta, was puffing on a hookah and saying, “You are a very fortunate man—you have two sons with loose tongues and two with owl-shaped heads. This year there’s a bit of a mess, but if you perform a yajna, all the red Phukans’ machangs will be yours and they’ll all be under your sway—”

Just then, Becharam Babu arrived. As soon as he entered, everyone stood up and began to say, “Welcome, sir, welcome!” Becharam Babu had been rather annoyed ever since the police incident, but who can resist courtesy and sweet words? With repeated “At your service, sir,” his heart softened a little, and he sat down beside Beni Babu with a smile.

Baburam Babu said, “Sir, you haven’t chosen the best seat—come, sit on the cushion. When like-minded people gather, it’s a perfect match.” Baburam Babu insisted, but Becharam Babu would not leave Beni Babu’s side.
After some general conversation, Becharam Babu asked, “Where has the marriage proposal for Motilal come from?”

Baburam replied, “Many proposals had come. Haridas Babu from Guptipara, Shyamacharan Babu from Nakashipara, Ramhari Babu from Kanchrapara, and many others from various places had brought proposals. Leaving all those aside, now the marriage has been fixed with the daughter of Madhab Babu from Manirampur. Madhab Babu is a man of means, and we might even get ten rupees from them.”
Becharam said, “Beni brother! What do you think about this? Tell me frankly.”
Beni replied, “Becharam dada, speaking frankly is a risky business—dumb men have no enemies. And when the matter is already settled, what’s the use of stirring it up?”
Becharam: Oh, you must tell me—I want to know the deep truth of every matter.

Beni: Then listen—Madhab Babu of Monirampur is a quarrelsome fellow—he has no genteel manners, only a kind of piety that comes from slaughtering cows and making shoes—he can give money and goods at marriage, but is it right to look only at money when arranging a marriage? First, one should look for a respectable family, then seek a good girl, and after that, if there are gifts or dowry, well and good—and if not, so be it. Ramhari Babu of Kancharapara is a truly good man—he lives contentedly on whatever he earns through his own labor—never even glances at other people’s affairs—his circumstances are not very good, it’s true, but he is always careful to give good advice to his children, always thinking about how his family will fare and how they will grow wise. If one were to form a relationship with such a man, it would be happiness in every way.

Becharam: Baburam Babu! On whose advice did you arrange this match? It’s clear you went after the money! What can I say to you?—this is the failing of our generation. Whenever marriage is discussed, people immediately start asking—“How much will they give in cash? Will they give a pearl necklace?” Oh, you blockhead, first see if the family is respectable or not—find out if the girl is good or bad—those are small matters, apparently—if you get ten rupees, that’s all that matters—nonsense, utter nonsense!
Banchharam: We want pedigree, we want beauty, we want wealth. If you completely disregard money, how will a household run?
Bakreshwar: Of course—you must consider wealth. What’s the use of talking to a poor man? Can you fill your belly with talk alone?

Thakchacha, tumbling off the bench, says—Why all this mockery at my expense? Did I say to make this marriage? If you don’t bring a daughter from a well-known family, it’s a great shame before people. I’ve kept my eyes open day and night and seen that Madhab Babu of Monirampur is a fine man—at the very mention of his name, even the cows in the field drink water respectfully—when there’s trouble, he can gather a gang of toughs, and in court, he’s a man of real influence—if calamity strikes, he can help in a thousand ways. Ramhari Babu of Kancharapara is the safest...
A man—he just sits around, scratching his belly all day—what’s the use of playing or working with someone like that?

Becharam: Baburam! You’ve found yourself a fine minister!—If you keep listening to such a minister, you’ll be off to heaven in the flesh—what sort of son have you got anyway?—And now you want to get him married? Beni, brother, are you anything like this?

Beni: My way is this—first, a father should properly educate his son, and do his utmost to ensure the boy grows up virtuous in every way. When the boy reaches a suitable age for marriage, then the father should lend his special support. If you marry him off too early, it only brings all sorts of trouble for the boy.

Hearing all this, Baburam Babu jumped up in a fluster and hurried inside the house. The mistress was already deep in conversation with the neighborhood ladies about the wedding. The master came close, relayed everything he’d heard outside, and stood there bewildered, saying, “So, should Motilal’s wedding be postponed for a while?” The mistress replied, “What nonsense are you talking—may ashes fall on the enemy’s mouth! Motilal is already sixteen—does it look good to delay his marriage any longer? If you start fussing over this now, the auspicious hour will pass us by—what are you doing, will a good man’s caste be ruined?—Take the groom and go quickly.” At the mistress’s advice, the master’s agitation melted away—he stepped outside and ordered the kitchen fires to be lit; at once, the drums, the rosun chowki, and the English band struck up, and Baburam Babu, taking the groom by the hand and accompanied by Thakchacha, friends, relatives, and all the respectable folk, set off in grand procession, swaying and swaggering along. From the rooftop, the mistress gazed at her son’s face. The other women exclaimed, “Oh, Moti’s mother! Just look how handsome your boy has become.” All the groom’s friends marched along, and behind them, the mischief-makers went about singeing people’s backs with firecrackers, hurling squibs near someone’s house, setting off sparklers at someone’s feet. The poor and the wretched looked on in dismay, but no one dared say a word.

After a while, the groom reached Monirampur. The crowd lining the road broke into a frenzy at the sight of the groom—women whispered among themselves, “The boy is handsome, no doubt, but if only his nose were a little straighter, he’d look even better.” Someone else said, “His complexion is a bit pale—if it were a touch brighter, he’d shine all the more.” The wedding will be at a very auspicious hour, but at night…

chapters.title: The Wedding Poets
paragraphs: Was it not yet ten o’clock? Madhab Babu arrived, bringing along the doorman and a lantern, to fetch the bridegroom’s party. Meeting the wedding procession on the road, nearly half an hour was spent in mere courtesies—one gentleman insisted, “Sir, please proceed ahead,” while the other replied, “No, sir, you go first.” At last, Beni Babu of Bali stepped forward and said, “Whichever of you it may be, let one of you go ahead. We cannot stand here in the cold all night.” Thus resolved, everyone proceeded to the bride’s house and entered within, while the groom went and took his seat in the assembly. The drummers, the musicians, and the hired singers surrounded the gathering on all sides—village drummers and various other performers began their chatter. Thakchacha stood, negotiating the terms—much haggling over the share of sweets, but when it came to the fruit, only a token amount was offered. Among the musicians, a burly fellow suddenly charged forward and shouted, “Who is this barber’s son, eh? Get out of here, boy! Why is a Muslim meddling in a Hindu ceremony?” At once, Thakchacha’s temper flared. Stroking his beard and glaring, he began to hurl abuses. Haldhar, Gadadhar, and the other young gentlemen watched the scene, each hoping to see what would happen next. They saw the clouds gathering—there might be a storm. Some abandoned their seats, some adjusted their turbans, some tossed coins into the air, some flung things over each other’s heads. Two men from the bride’s side, witnessing this commotion, uttered a few strong words, and it nearly came to blows. Matilal, seeing the quarrel, thought to himself, “Perhaps marriage is not in my fate—maybe I’ll have to return home with the sacred thread in hand, as a bachelor.”
11. On the Occasion of Matilal’s Wedding: Poetry and the Professors of Agarpara

The professors of Agarpara were seated in the evening under a tree, having spread out their mats. Some were taking snuff, some smoking hookah, some coughing and clearing their throats, while others exchanged a few light-hearted stories and jokes. Among them, one asked, “How is Vidyaratna these days?”

“A Brahmin, driven by hunger, went to a feast in Monirampur and ended up breaking his leg!” replied another. “Ah, just yesterday he was hobbling along with a stick to bathe. Seeing him, my heart was filled with sorrow.”
Vidyabhushan: “Vidyaratna is well. With a little lime, turmeric, and a warm compress, the pain…”
It has diminished a great deal. On the occasion of the invitation at Monirampur, the poem composed by our dear Kavikankan brother is quite colorful—let me recite it for you.

Dimiki, the nahabat rings out with a clatter and a clang. Madhab Bhavan. Devendra Sadan. The one who reigns over the world resides here. A wondrous assembly. The glow of lights. The brilliance of chandeliers shining in between. All around, flowers of every kind. Both banks overflowing with blossoms. The music’s tumult resounds with zest. Marigold garlands in hair buns. Red saris, silver bangles. At last, the wedding hall is decked out in splendor. The awnings flutter and flap. Their folds are many-layered. Water drips and trickles in a constant stream. Sturdy lathiyals. Doorkeepers like Rajputs. Strange shouts and cries echo about. Luchi, sweets, and other delicacies—piled high in the pantry. The floor is adorned with intricate alpana patterns. How many bards detained! Hundreds recite verses. The rhythms twist and turn in varied measures. The poet from Agarpara, in his creative fervor, suddenly brings in the groom’s party with a flourish. Haldhar and Gadadhar whisper and mutter. Fidget, fidget—they can hardly sit still. Uncle Thakchacha, still green, listens to the gossip. Haldhar and Gadadhar are busy eating their mashed fare. Rustle, rustle—the sound of tearing and ripping. Munch, munch—they gnaw and gobble, stuffing themselves. Clang, clang—the chandeliers tremble and ring. Scurry, scurry—everyone dashes about in a hurry. Motilal sits and swings, watching the scene unfold. Is there a thread of fate tied to my forehead, I wonder? Bakreshwar and Bokeshwar are masters at flattery. They push and shove, elbowing their way through the crowd. Bancharam, forever scheming, is lost in thought. After a slap and a taste of pickle, he’s left bewildered. Becharam, seeing everything go awry, tiptoes away. “Go away, go away!” he mutters without end. Beni Babu eats and eats, with no hope of deliverance—like a river stuck in the Ganges’ current. Huff, puff, gulp, gulp—the quarrel swells and grows. Baburam tries to hold everyone back—“Stop, stop!” he pleads. Thump, thump—he trembles and nearly collapses.

Uncle Thakcha-cha shouts, “Save me! Save me!” and tries to flee in haste. Muslim scoundrels, a whole basketful, are everywhere. They slink away slowly, faces wrapped in cloth. Everyone says, “There you go, that’s the root of all the trouble.” Reo Bhat grabs his shirt and drags him down. “Slap him! Slap him! Slap him! Slap him!” they cry, tearing out his beard. The poor fellow wails, “Oh! Oh! I repent! I repent!” “My life is gone, alas! Spare me, father!” He clasps his hands, begging, “Let me go, please!” “I’m a good man, I know nothing, I just came to watch.” “What business have I here, what a mess I’m in!” “I’m exhausted, distressed, dying of disgrace.” “Without knowing, without understanding, I sat with these Hindus.” “I only came and sat for the sake of friendship.” “My aunt, my uncle, everyone warned me not to come to this party.” “But I didn’t listen, didn’t heed their words.” “My life is going, my beard is going, soon my head will go too!”

In the midst of this great chaos, the lathi-wielders arrive, With a clatter and a crash, they come storming in. Whack! Whack! The canes rain down on backs. “Help! I’m done for!” everyone cries out. Bride’s party, groom’s party—everyone scatters in every direction. “Hit him! Grab him!”—the shouts grow louder. Madhab Babu, taking the groom, flees into the inner chambers. The assembly is shattered, utterly destroyed. Everyone shouts, “Thak, uncover your face!” “Tear his beard! Tear his beard! Tear it off!” The babus, terrified, begin to flee. Who knows where the shawls and sashes have gone? Clothes are torn, falling off, And in the wind, the scraps flutter and dance.

No shawl, no wrap, not a stitch on my back. Stumbling and bumbling, though my legs are sound. I walk and I talk, my head hanging low— I’m sunk, I’m drowned in a sea of sorrow. Hunger and thirst are splitting my chest; No sweets, no puffed rice, not a crumb to be had. Night falls thick and heavy as doom, The wind in my breath grows fierce and wild. Storms rage and howl on every side, The wind itself seems the god of death, arrived in haste. What am I to do, alone, not a soul in sight? Death will soon come, dreadful and near. I have no heart to walk or speak; If Fate is my foe, what can I do? Who knows if my wife, hearing of my death, Will waste away in grief and pain? Was the marriage a blessing or a curse? Beaten and battered, I nearly lost my life. Why did I ever tie this knot? I’m trapped, both in pride and in soul. As he walked, he spotted a shop— Without a thought, he slipped right in. On a mat in the corner, sprawled in a heap, Lay an old, restless, wretched cheat, tossing in sleep. “How did you get here?” Baburam asks. “You left me alone and came away! Is this the way a friend should behave? In trouble and danger, true love is revealed.” The cheat says, “Sir, hush your mouth! The shopkeeper might be their spy, no doubt. If you get caught, the whole plan’s blown. If you survive, our friendship will be known.”

chapters.title: The Good Brother
paragraphs: At dawn, both hands set forth. Composed the verse—Sri Kavikankan.

Tarkabagish Baburam Babu is a stubborn old man; the moment he hears poetry, he flares up and exclaims—"Ah, I die! What poetry—Saraswati herself incarnate—or perhaps Kalidas has been reborn—Kavikankan’s learning is immense—such a boy is a rare find! Even the meter is marvelous. The floor’s mud, stone bowls, cool mats, coconut cuttings—everything is perfect." A Brahmin scholar, always singing the praises of the great and powerful—what a disgraceful habit! Criticizing is not a gentleman’s work—so saying, he stormed off in a huff from the gathering. Everyone cried out, "Oh, wait! Please, sit down!" and with much insistence, they managed to seat him again.

Another professor, eager to smooth things over, quickly changed the subject and began to lavish praise on Baburam Babu and Madhab Babu instead. "Brahmins are often rather thick-headed—never able to grasp the heart of a matter. After all that logic and scripture, all they have is a legalistic mind—no sense for the ways of the world." Tarkabagish, mollified, soon joined in the merriment of the conversation.
12. Benibabu’s Visit to Becharam Babu; The Reason for Ramalal’s Virtuous Character, Brother of Motilal; The Topic of Bardaprasad Babu—A Method for Cleansing the Mind.

Becharam Babu of Bowbazar is seated in his drawing room. Nearby, a few men are singing kirtan. Babu orders one after another—Ghoshti, Daan, Maan, Mathur, Khandita, Utkanthita, Kalahantarita—each in turn. The kirtan singers, with their sweet, honeyed voices, perform in various melodies; hearing these, some listeners are so overcome they fall to the ground, rolling about in ecstasy. Becharam Babu sits motionless, like a painted idol. At this moment, Benibabu of Bali arrives. Becharam Babu immediately halts the kirtan and asks, "Well, tell me, Beni-bhai! Still alive, are you? Baburam’s fire is like a wolf’s—never lets go, even when it seems to. Yet, whatever business we undertake with him ends up in utter ruin. We learned our lesson well from the affair at Monirampur—there’s a saying: the enemy within the house is the first to join the wedding procession."

Beni: Don’t even mention Baburam Babu anymore—he’s become utterly hopeless. Sometimes I feel like leaving this house of sand and walking out the door. “Aparamba king bhavishyati”—who knows what fate still has in store!

Becharam: Well, that’s the state of Baburam—just as he is, so are his ministers, his companions, his sons, and all his affairs. But how is it that his youngest son is turning out well? It’s like a lotus blooming in a heap of dung!

Beni: You might well ask that. It does seem impossible, but there’s a reason behind it. Earlier, I introduced you to Baradaprasad Biswas Babu—you may remember. For some time now, that gentleman has been residing at Baidyabati. I thought to myself, if Baburam Babu’s youngest son, Ramlal, turns out like Motilal, then Baburam’s lineage will surely be wiped out. But this boy has a chance to be good—he’s had a fortunate opportunity. Considering all this, I took Ramlal with me to Biswas Babu. The boy has developed such sincere devotion to Biswas Babu that he always stays with him, hardly ever at his own home, and regards him as a father.
Becharam: You did praise Biswas Babu’s virtues before, but I’ve never heard of so many qualities in one man. Now that he’s in a good position, how did he become so humble instead of proud?

Beni: A person who inherits wealth from childhood and never faces hardship, who grows up surrounded only by riches, rarely becomes humble. Such a person cannot understand the feelings of others—what pleases or displeases them means nothing to him. He remains intoxicated by his own comfort, always thinking himself superior, and his relatives mostly respect him for his wealth alone. In such circumstances, pride becomes dangerous—humility and compassion can never take root. That’s why the sons of Calcutta’s rich men rarely turn out well. First, they inherit their father’s property, then they hold high positions, so they go about looking down on everyone. Unless they face adversity—unless they suffer some blow—their minds never settle. Humility is essential for a person. Without humility—
If one remains absorbed in oneself, one’s faults are never judged or corrected—without humility, a man cannot even advance in religion.
Becharam: How did Borda Babu become such a good man?

Beni: Borda Babu suffered hardships all through his childhood. Through those hardships, he constantly meditated upon the Lord. This constant meditation has so deeply impressed upon his mind the conviction that only those actions which are dear to God are worth doing. Whatever is displeasing to Him, even at the cost of one’s life, must never be done. He lives his life according to this principle.
Becharam: But how has he determined which actions are pleasing or displeasing to God?

Beni: There are two ways to gain such knowledge. First, one must restrain the mind. For this, it is necessary to sit still and meditate, and to increase the mind’s capacity for reflection. With a steadier mind, through meditation, one can turn the mind inside out, so to speak, and the power of discernment between good and bad begins to operate. As this power grows stronger, a person becomes averse to actions displeasing to God, and devoted to those that please Him. Second, by reading and reflecting upon the writings of holy men, this power gradually becomes habitual. Borda Babu has spared no effort to improve himself. To this day, he does not spend his time merely laughing and idling about like ordinary people. Rising early in the morning, he regularly worships the Lord. The feelings that arise in his heart at that time are revealed by the tears in his eyes. Afterwards, he calmly reviews what good and bad deeds he has done—he never credits himself with any virtue, but if he finds even the slightest fault, he is deeply grieved. Yet, when he hears of another’s virtues, he is delighted; if he learns of another’s faults, he expresses only a brotherly sorrow. Through such habits, his mind has become pure and tranquil. Is it any wonder that a person who so restrains his mind should progress in religion?
Becharam: Beni brother! My ears are soothed just hearing about Borda Babu. I must meet such a man at least once. What does he do during the day?

Beni Babu. He does indeed engage in worldly affairs during the day, but not in the same way as others. Many people, once involved in matters of property and business, think only of rank and wealth; but he does not attach much importance to these. He knows very well that rank and wealth are like the waves of the sea—pleasant to look at, pleasing to hear about—but they do not accompany one after death. In fact, unless one treads carefully, these two can give rise to wickedness. His principal reason for engaging in worldly affairs is to guide and test his own sense of duty. When one is involved in such matters, greed, anger, envy, injustice, and the like become powerful, and many are destroyed by the tyranny of these vices. The one who can withstand them is truly virtuous. It is easy to speak of virtue, but unless one demonstrates it through action, mere words are nothing but hypocrisy. Borda Babu always says that this world is a school, and if one cultivates good habits of mind through worldly work, virtue remains unshaken.
Becharam. Then does Borda Babu disregard wealth?
Beni. No, no—he does not despise wealth—but in his view, duty comes first, wealth after. That is, one must earn wealth while upholding virtue.
Becharam. What does Borda Babu do at home at night?

Beni. After dusk, he spends time in pleasant conversation and study with his family. Observing his upright character, all the members of his household strive to emulate him. He is so affectionate towards his family that his wife prays to be blessed with such a husband in every birth, and his children grow restless if they do not see him for even a moment. Borda Babu’s sons are as good as his daughters. In many households, brothers and sisters are constantly bickering and quarreling. But Borda Babu’s children never speak harshly to one another—whether they are writing, reading, or eating, at all times they converse with each other affectionately. If the parents are not good, the children cannot be good.
Becharam. I have heard that Borda Babu is always roaming about the neighborhood.

Beni. That is true—if he hears of someone’s distress, misfortune, or illness, he cannot remain quietly at home. He helps many people nearby in various ways, but never breathes a word of it to anyone, and when he helps others, he feels as though he himself has been benefited.

chapters.title: The Wise Counselor
paragraphs: Becharam: Beni brother! I have never, in my life, even heard of such a person, let alone seen one with my own eyes—such people, it would be better to keep even an old man near them—the boy is bound to turn out well. Ah! If only Baburam’s youngest son turns out well, it would be a great joy indeed.

Babu Bardaprasad’s Advice—His Wisdom, Piety, and Method of Instruction. His Counsel to Ramlal, His Father’s Anxieties, and Uncle Thakchacha’s Wounded Advice. Changing Opinions about Ramlal’s Qualities, and His Elder Sister’s Illness and Death.

Babu Bardaprasad possessed a rare discernment in matters of education. He understood human nature well. He knew the powers and inclinations of the mind, and how, by directing those powers and inclinations in the right way, a person could become intelligent and virtuous—on this subject, he had particular expertise. The work of a teacher is no easy task. Many, having picked up a smattering of knowledge here and there, and finding no other employment, set themselves up as teachers—but from such people, true education cannot be expected. To be a real teacher, one must thoroughly understand the workings and moods of the mind, and must carefully consider, listen, and learn how instruction can be made effective in practice. Without this, if one teaches in a hurried and careless manner, it is like striking a stone with a pickaxe—one may strike a hundred times and not dislodge even a handful of earth.

Babu Bardaprasad was a man of wide experience—having devoted himself for many years to the subject of education, he knew well the proper methods of instruction. The way he taught imparted true knowledge. Nowadays, in government schools, the real aim of education is not fulfilled, for the powers and inclinations of the mind are not properly directed. The students only learn to memorize by rote, which merely awakens their memory, while their powers of reasoning remain dormant, to say nothing of the development of their finer feelings. The chief purpose of education is that, according to the age of the students, all the powers and inclinations of the mind should be equally exercised. It is not right to overdevelop one faculty and neglect another. Just as the body becomes strong when all its limbs are equally exercised, so too, true intelligence is developed when all the powers of the mind are equally cultivated. The faculties of the mind, too...

It is necessary to govern one’s faculties in a balanced manner. Guiding one quality does not mean all qualities are guided. One may develop reverence for truth, yet lack even a trace of compassion; or, having an excess of compassion, may be utterly devoid of common sense in matters of debt and credit. It is not impossible for a person to be upright in financial dealings, yet be neglectful and unloving towards parents, wife, and children. Conversely, one may be affectionate towards parents and family, yet possess not a shred of honesty. Thus, Babu Bardaprasad well understood that the root of governing the mind’s faculties lies in devotion to the Almighty. As that devotion grows, so too does the governance of all the mind’s faculties; without it, such efforts are as futile as drawing lines upon water.

By a stroke of fortune, Ramlal became Bardababu’s disciple. The governance of all Ramlal’s mental faculties and powers began to proceed beautifully. The cultivation of the mind’s faculties comes more from the company of virtuous people than from mere instruction. Just as by grafting, a branch of a jamun tree can become a branch of a mango tree, so too does association transform the mind—one kind of mind becomes another. Such is the greatness of a virtuous mind that when its shadow falls upon a baser mind, the latter gradually assumes the nature of that shadow.

In Bardababu’s company, the mold of Ramlal’s mind began to take after his own. Ramlal would rise early in the morning and, to strengthen his body, would walk and take in the fresh air in an open field—he became firmly convinced that without bodily strength, there can be no strength of mind. Afterwards, returning home, he would engage in worship and self-reflection, and would read only those books, or converse only with those people, who could enrich his intellect and mind. Upon hearing of a virtuous person, he would immediately seek out their company, never inquiring into their caste or station.

Ramlal’s understanding became so clear that in conversation, he would speak only of necessary matters—never indulging in idle talk. If others spoke frivolously, he would, with the strength of his own intellect, extract the essence, like a swan separating milk from water. In his mind, he was ever pondering how to increase his devotion to the Almighty, his sense of morality, and his wisdom—he considered this his sole duty. Living thus, his nature, character, and actions all became increasingly praiseworthy.

Virtue can never remain hidden—the whole neighborhood would say amongst themselves, “Ramlal is the Prahlad among demons.” In times of trouble or misfortune, Ramlal was always the first to step forward. Whether by toil, by money, or by wit—whatever means were needed to help someone, he would do just that. Be it the old, the young, or the children, everyone became devoted to Ramlal, regarding him as their own kin. To hear a word spoken against Ramlal was to feel an arrow pierce their ears; to hear his praise brought them immense joy. The elderly women of the neighborhood would say to each other, “If only we had such a son, we would never let him out of our sight—ah! What great merit his mother must have earned to be blessed with such a child.” The young women, seeing and hearing of Ramlal’s beauty and virtues, would secretly wish, “May such a man be my husband.”
Ramlal’s honest nature and good character gradually began to reveal themselves in many ways, both at home and outside. In his household, no one ever failed in their duties.

Ramlal’s father would sometimes think to himself, “The younger son is a bit lax in Hindu customs—he does not serve the tilak, nor does he perform worship with all the ritual paraphernalia, nor does he chant the garland of Harinam. Yet, he worships in his own way and is never engaged in any unrighteous act. We, on the other hand, tell basketfuls of lies—the boy knows nothing but the truth. He has special devotion to his parents, and, moreover, he never agrees to do anything wrong at our request. I have much property and influence—I want both truth and falsehood. In other households, there are festivities like Dol and Durga Puja—how will all this be maintained? Motilal may be wayward, but at least he keeps up the Hindu customs—perhaps, with age, his faults and virtues will balance out.”

Ramlal’s mother and sisters were daily moved by his virtues. Just as joy arises at the sight of light after utter darkness, so too did happiness fill their hearts. They had been dispirited by Motilal’s misconduct, finding no joy in their hearts, and would hang their heads in shame before others. But now, thanks to Ramlal’s good qualities, their minds were at peace and their faces brightened. The servants, who previously received nothing but abuse and beatings from Motilal and would flee at the sound of his call, now, softened by Ramlal’s gentle words and kindness, became more attentive to their duties.
Motilal, Haldhar, and Gadadhar—Ramlal’s...

Seeing his antics, people would whisper among themselves, “The boy has gone mad—must have something wrong with his head. Tell the master and have him sent to the asylum—he’s just a slip of a lad, yet all day and night he talks of religion. It doesn’t suit a boy to mouth the words of old men.”

Among themselves, Mangobind, Ramgobind, and Dolgobind would say, “Moti Babu, you are truly fortunate—Ramlaal’s prospects don’t look good. He’ll soon be finished off in the name of religion, and then you alone will inherit the whole estate and can sit back with your feet up, enjoying life to the fullest. And even if he survives, he’ll be nothing more than a living corpse. Oh dear! Like guru, like disciple—couldn’t find a better teacher in the whole world! Got his spiritual mantra from some Bengali and now goes around preaching religion to everyone. If he carries on like this, we’ll throw both him and his guru out for good. Oh my! The little brat goes around saying, ‘Brother, it would be best to give up bad company’—and then again, ‘Brother, it would be good to visit Bardababu.’ Bardababu—the very pinnacle of stupidity. A paragon of virtue, that uncle! Beware, Moti Babu, don’t you ever lose heart and go to him. Are we to become his students now? If he wishes, let him come and learn from us. What we want now is fun—pleasure—luxury!”

Uncle Thak was always hearing praise of Ramlaal and would sit and ponder. Thak, whenever he got the chance, would try to take a bite out of Baburam’s property. So far, many cases had ended in confusion—he hadn’t yet had the chance to strike, but he never failed to cast his fishing line whenever he could. The way Ramlaal was turning out, it didn’t seem likely he’d catch any fish—if a snare was set, Ramlaal would warn even his own father against getting caught. So Uncle Thak saw serious obstacles ahead and thought, “The moon of hope seems to be sinking behind clouds of despair, never to rise again.”

After much consideration, one day he said to Baburam Babu, “Babu Sahib! Your younger boy’s ways are causing me great distress. It seems to me he’s gone mad—he’s very angry with me, goes around telling everyone that I’ve led you astray—hearing such things, my heart is deeply wounded. Babu Sahib! This is very bad—if he says such things to me, he could say worse to you. The boy will be alright—he’ll soften up. But he’s become insolent and wicked, he needs a cure. And as for all this religious study, I can’t see how it helps with managing the estate.”

A man who lacks great intelligence becomes easily unsettled by the words of others. Just as a boat in a storm, when steered by an inexperienced boatman, rocks and sways—never quite reaching the shore—so too does such a person see only darkness on all sides, unable to decide what is good or bad. Now, Baburam Babu was not exactly a man of sharp wit, and to him, Thakchacha’s words were like divine wisdom. Thus, he sat there, bewildered, staring blankly like a gentleman lost in thought. After a while, he asked, “What is to be done?”

Thakchacha replied, “Sir, the boy is not bad by nature, but it’s that elder Babu who is the root of all evil. If you separate him, the boy will turn out well. Babu Saheb! A Hindu boy ought to observe Hindu customs and rituals—that is proper. But if you want to live in this world, you need both sense and cunning. The world is not true—what will I achieve by being the only honest man? If you hear words that match your own inclinations, they seem most agreeable to you. Thakchacha knew well that talk of preserving Hindu ways and family honor would hit the mark, and indeed, that was the very chord he struck.
Baburam Babu, hearing this advice, said, “That’s true indeed. If this is your opinion, then act quickly—whatever money is needed, I shall provide, but all the arrangements are up to you.”

Thus began the endless discussions and deliberations regarding Ramlal. Every sage had a different opinion—some said the boy was good in this respect, others said he was lacking in that. Some claimed that, for want of one essential virtue, it was as if a single drop of cow dung had fallen into a pot of milk. Others declared the boy was endowed with every quality. In this way, some time passed.

By chance, Baburam Babu’s eldest daughter was struck by a grave illness. Father and mother summoned the best physicians to tend to her. Motilal did not come to see his sister even once. Instead, he went about saying, “For a widow in a respectable house, it is better to die soon than to live on.” At that time, his merriment and amusements only increased. But Ramlal, forsaking food and sleep, devoted himself to serving and nursing his sister, deeply anxious and attentive to her recovery.

Yet, the sister could not be saved from her illness. In her final moments, she placed her hand on her younger brother’s head and said, “Ram! If I am born as a girl again after death, may I have a brother like you. I cannot express in words all that you have done for me. May God keep you as happy as your heart is pure.” With these words, she breathed her last.

chapters.title: The Quack Doctor
paragraphs: Motilal and his companions, each more flamboyant than the next, engaged in all sorts of antics, but to say which prank would be their last is a difficult guess indeed. Their thirst for pleasure and amusement grew day by day. One kind of entertainment might please them for a day or two—after that, it becomes stale, and unless a new flavor is found, restlessness sets in. Thus Motilal and his gang passed their days. In turn, each one had to open a new fountain of amusement for the group. For this reason, one day, Haldhar, wrapping Dolgovinda in a quilt and teaching the rest of the fellows their parts, led them all to the house of Brajanath the Kaviraj.

At the Kaviraj’s house, there was a flurry of medicine-making—here, Rasasindhu was being prepared, there, Madhyam Narayan oil was being boiled, elsewhere, gold was being incinerated into ash. The Kaviraj himself, with a medicine jar in one hand and a bottle of some sticky oil in the other, was just about to step outside when Haldhar appeared and said, “Rai Mahashay! Please, come quickly—at the zamindar’s house, a boy has been struck by a terrible fever. It seems the patient is at death’s door, but perhaps his life—and your reputation—may yet be saved. If you administer your famous medicine, he might recover. If you succeed, you will be handsomely rewarded.”

Hearing this, the Kaviraj hurried to the patient’s side. All the young gentlemen who were present cried out, “Please, Kaviraj Mahashay, save us! Dolgovinda has been bedridden with fever for ten or fifteen days—burning thirst, terrible restlessness, no sleep at night—he just tosses and turns, Mahashay, please—”

After smoking his hookah and tobacco, he examined the patient’s hand carefully. Brajanath Ray was an old man, not much educated—he managed his own affairs in a haphazard way, always agreed with whatever his elder brother said—so, he was not self-reliant, could not make any decisions or take any action on his own. Ray Mahashay’s body was frail, he had no teeth, his words came out slurred, but his moustache was still impressive—though even that had turned grey, yet out of affection he would never shave it off. After examining the patient’s hand, he heaved a sigh and sat silently. Haldhar asked, “Kaviraj Mahashay, why are you so quiet?” The kaviraj did not reply, but kept his eyes fixed on the patient. The patient, in turn, kept glancing at him now and then—stuck out his tongue a few times—chattered his teeth a few times—showed off his labored breathing a few times—and once or twice, even tugged at the kaviraj’s moustache. Ray Mahashay edged away, the patient rolled over and started pulling at his bottle of oil. The boys asked, “Ray Mahashay! What’s this?” He replied, “This illness is dreadful—seems like it’s a feverish delirium and has turned to heat. If I’d been informed earlier, I might have been able to help, but now, even Shiva himself could do nothing.” Saying this, the patient snatched the oil bottle, poured out a handful, and smeared it all over himself. The kaviraj, seeing that if he lingered any longer he’d lose both his reputation and his bottle, quickly grabbed the bottle, screwed the cap on tightly, and got up to leave. Everyone called out, “Mahashay, where are you going?” The kaviraj replied, “The crisis seems to be worsening rapidly, it is no longer proper to keep the patient here—now, efforts should be made for his soul’s welfare in the next world.” Hearing this, the patient suddenly sat up with a start—the kaviraj, seeing this, gave him a sharp slap—the whole crowd of village healers ran after him—the kaviraj, after going a little distance, stopped in utter bewilderment—the young gentlemen gave the kaviraj a good shove, hoisted him onto their shoulders, and with cries of “Haribol!” carried him off to the banks of the Ganges. Dolgovinda came up and said, “Kaviraj uncle! You had ordered me to go to the Ganges—now the burden is on your own neck—come, uncle! Now we’ll give you your last rites and put you on the pyre.” Like a man punished by a madman, he changed his tune again after a while and said, “Will you send me to the Ganges again? Go, uncle! Let the son of the house return home, but leave the oil bottle behind.” Saying this, he grabbed the oil bottle, and everyone began vigorously oiling themselves, then with a splash, jumped into the Ganges. The kaviraj, seeing and hearing all this, was left utterly stupefied. Now, to escape— As soon as he thought, “If only I could escape!” and was about to step away, Haldhar, swimming in the pond, shouted out, “Hey, Kaviraj uncle! My bile has increased a lot, you’ll have to give me two doses of Pan Rasasindhu—don’t run away! If you do, uncle, I’ll have to make aunt take off her iron bangles!” The Kaviraj, flinging away his box of medicines, hurriedly left for home, muttering “Father, father!” as he went.

In the month of Phalgun, the trees and plants begin to sprout, and the fragrance of flowers spreads all around. Borda Babu’s house stood by the banks of the Ganges—there was an eight-pillared verandah in front, and gardens all around. Every afternoon, Borda Babu would sit in that verandah, taking in the air, pondering various matters, and, if any relatives were present, conversing with them. Ramlal was always nearby; it was with him that Borda Babu shared his innermost thoughts. In this way, Ramlal received much advice—whenever he got the chance, he would prod his guru with questions about how to attain true knowledge and purify the mind.

One day, Ramlal said, “Sir! I have a great desire to travel the country. Staying at home, I’m fed up with my brother’s harsh words and Uncle Thakchacha’s evil counsel. But the affection of my parents and sister binds my feet—because of them, I cannot bring myself to leave home. I don’t know what to do.”

Borda: “There is much benefit in traveling the country. Without travel, a person does not gain broad experience; seeing different lands and different people makes the mind generous. By closely observing the customs and manners of people from other places, and investigating why their circumstances are good or bad, one receives much instruction. And by associating with people of various races, the mind’s tendency toward hatred is diminished, and the sense of possibility grows. Sitting at home and reading leads only to bookish knowledge—reading is necessary, but so is the company of good people, engagement with affairs, and conversation with all sorts of people. Through these several pursuits, the intellect is clarified and one’s sense of possibility increases. But before setting out to travel, one must know what to investigate and how to inquire; otherwise, wandering about is no better than the aimless roaming of an ox. I do not mean to say that such wandering is entirely useless—no, that is not my intention. Some benefit is always gained from travel, but if a person does not know what to inquire into while traveling, and cannot make those inquiries—”

His travels do not always bear the desired fruit. Among Bengalis, many journey from one land to another, but how many, when asked about the true nature of those places, can give a satisfactory answer? This fault is not entirely theirs—it is a flaw in their education. Unless one learns to observe, inquire, and reason, wisdom does not simply descend from the heavens. Children must be trained in such a way that, at first, they are shown the sketches of various objects—when they see all these pictures, they will compare one with another: this one has hands, that one has no feet; this one’s face is like this, that one has no tail. By making such comparisons, both their powers of observation and of reasoning will be exercised. After some time, this habit of comparison will become second nature, and then they will be able to consider why different things differ from one another; after that, it will become easy to understand which object belongs to which category. Giving such instruction cultivates the habit of inquiry and sharpens the intellect. But such education is rare in this country, and so our minds become muddled and superficial—when a question arises, it is not immediately clear which point is essential and which is not, nor do many understand how to investigate a matter so as to arrive at a sound conclusion. Therefore, it is not untrue to say that many of our travels are, in fact, false journeys. But given the kind of education you have received, I believe that if you travel, you will benefit greatly from it.
Ramlal: If I go abroad, I must stay for some time in the place where I settle. But with what sort of people, and of what character, should I associate most closely?

Borda: That is not an easy question—you must answer it with care. In every nation, there are both good and bad people—if you find good people, associate with them. You know well enough the marks of a good person; there is no need to repeat them. By keeping company with the English, one becomes courageous—they worship courage. An Englishman who acts without courage cannot enter polite society. But to be courageous does not mean one is virtuous in every way—courage is indeed necessary for all, but only that courage which springs from a sense of righteousness is true courage. I have told you before—

And I still say, always pursue the higher truth; otherwise, whatever you see, whatever you hear, whatever you learn—these will only serve to inflate your pride. And man always wishes to do what he sees others do. Especially Bengalis—after mingling with the sahibs, they pick up all sorts of useless airs and become puffed up with conceit, and whatever they do, it is always out of vanity—let it be remembered, there is no harm in that.

While such conversation was going on, a few policemen came marching in from the west side of the garden and surrounded Borda Babu. Casting a glance at them, Borda Babu asked, “Who are you?” They replied, “We are police officers. There has been a complaint against you regarding the murder of a cow. You must go to the magistrate’s court in Hooghly and answer the charge. Meanwhile, we will search the premises for the cow.”

No sooner had he heard this than Ramlal sprang to his feet, read the warrant, and began trembling with rage at the false accusation. Borda Babu took his hand and made him sit down, saying, “Do not be agitated. Let us look into the matter thoroughly—many kinds of troubles occur in this world. When calamity comes, one must not lose composure. To become flustered in times of danger is the act of a fool. And as for the charge against me, I know very well I am innocent—so why should I be afraid? But the order of the court must be obeyed, so I shall present myself there without delay. For now, let the police search my house and see for themselves that I am hiding no one.”

Receiving this permission, the policemen searched all around, but found no trace of the cow. Afterwards, Borda Babu had a boat brought and began making preparations to go to Hooghly. Just then, Benibabu of Bali happened to arrive. Taking him and Ramlal along, Borda Babu set off for Hooghly. Benibabu and Ramlal were somewhat anxious, but Borda Babu, with a smiling face, kept them calm with cheerful conversation of various kinds.

chapters.title: The Magistrate’s Court
paragraphs: Bardababu, along with Benibabu and Ramlal, has spread a blanket under a tree and is sitting there. Now and then, a couple of clerks approach him, speaking in hushed, conspiratorial tones about settlements, but Bardababu pays them no heed. To intimidate him, they say, “The Sahib’s orders are very strict—all the work is in our hands—we can do whatever we wish. Taking statements is our job—with a flick of the pen, we can turn everything upside down. But you need influence—if you want to make a move, now is the time. Once an order is passed, even we can do nothing to help.”

Hearing all this, Ramlal feels a twinge of fear now and then, but Bardababu, utterly fearless, replies, “Do what you must—I will never give a bribe. I am innocent—I have nothing to fear.” The clerks, annoyed, wander off to their own corners.

A couple of lawyers approach Bardababu and say, “We can see, sir, that you are a very respectable gentleman—certainly you have fallen into trouble. But make sure the case doesn’t go against you. If you need witnesses, we can arrange them right here—a little expense, and all conveniences can be managed. The Sahib is about to arrive—whatever needs to be done, do it now.”

Bardababu replies, “I am grateful for your kindness, but even if I have to wear shackles, so be it—it will not trouble me. I will indeed be humiliated, but I am prepared to accept that humiliation. But even if my life is at stake, I will not walk the path of falsehood.”
“Ah! Sir, you must be a man of the Golden Age—perhaps King Yudhishthira has been reborn!” they say, mocking him with a slight laugh, and then walk away.

In this manner, two o’clock passes—still no sign of the Sahib. Everyone is waiting with the longing eyes of pilgrims at a holy place. Someone asks a learned Brahmin, “Hey, astrologer, tell us, will the Sahib come today or not?” Immediately—

The Acharya is saying—“Name a flower, let’s see?” Someone says hibiscus—The Acharya, counting on his fingers, replies, “No, the sahib won’t come today—there’s work at home.” Trusting the Acharya’s words, everyone began packing up their books and exclaimed, “Thank heavens! Let’s go home and be at ease.” Thakchacha was sitting amidst the crowd, with three or four people around him—a paper bundle tucked under his arm, a cloth over his mouth—his eyes blinking rapidly, his beard hanging down, his head bowed as he walked along. At that moment, Ramlal’s gaze fell upon him. Ramlal immediately said to Borda and Beni Babu, “Look, Thakchacha is here—perhaps he’s involved in this case—otherwise, why would he turn his face away when he sees me?” Borda Babu looked up and replied, “I was thinking the same thing—he glances at us sideways, and if our eyes meet, he turns his head and starts talking to someone else—maybe Thakchacha is the ghost in the mustard seeds.” Beni Babu, ever the smiling face, often probed mysteries with his wit. Unable to stay silent, he began calling out, “Thakchacha!” at the top of his voice. Five or seven calls went unanswered—Thakchacha was busy unwrapping his paper bundle, looking very preoccupied—he heard but pretended not to, didn’t even lift his head. Beni Babu went up to him, nudged him, and asked, “What’s the matter? Why are you here?” Thakchacha said nothing, just kept shuffling through his papers—embarrassment was written all over his face—but he had to nudge Beni Babu aside too. Without answering, he said, “Babu! The sea is very rough today—are you all going to Surat for this?” “All right, but why are you here?” “Oh, why do you keep pestering me about that? I have a lot of work, after a little while I’ll talk to you—let me finish this cross-examination and come back,” saying this, Thakchacha hurriedly moved away and got busy in idle chatter with another fellow.

Three o’clock struck—everyone was growing restless, pacing back and forth, there was no end to the work in the suburbs—people’s lives are wasted walking the corridors of the court. The office had already dispersed when the sound of the magistrate’s carriage wheels began to be heard, and immediately everyone cried out, “The sahib is coming!” The Acharya’s face went pale—a few people said to him, “Sir, your predictions are remarkable!” The Acharya replied, “Today I ate some rather harsh food, that’s why my calculations were off.” The clerks… The bailiffs took their places. As soon as the sahib entered the court, everyone bowed their heads low to the ground and saluted him. The sahib, after giving a nod, seated himself on the bench—the hookah attendant brought in the hookah—he stretched out both legs on the table, reclined on the couch, and began to draw on the hookah, while dabbing his face with a lemon-scented handkerchief taken from his pocket.

The office of the nazir filled up with people—scribes were busily taking depositions, but as always, money talks—the head clerk, resplendent in his double-breasted coat, and the doorkeeper with his turban, recited the petitions before the sahib in a singsong, almost musical tone, leading a procession of supplicants. The sahib, meanwhile, perused the newspaper and wrote his own important letters; after each petition was read, he would ask, “Well, what happened?” The head clerk would explain however he pleased, and whatever verdict the head clerk gave, the sahib would echo as his own.

Borda Babu stood to one side with Beni Babu and Ramlal. Observing the proceedings, he was utterly bewildered. The way his deposition had been recorded by the scribe left no hope for his case—any favor from the head clerk was equally impossible; at this moment, he was truly at the mercy of fate. These thoughts ran through his mind when suddenly his case was called.

Thakchacha, who had been sitting inside, immediately puffed out his chest and, gathering his witnesses, marched up before the sahib. When the petition was read, the head clerk declared, “Khodayawand, the accused is clearly guilty of cow slaughter.” At once, Thakchacha shot a triumphant glance at Borda Babu, glaring fiercely, as if to say, “Now you see what comes of your actions.”

In most other cases, after the petition was read, the accused were not questioned at all—the proceedings resembled nothing so much as a goat sacrifice. But by chance, before pronouncing judgment, the sahib’s gaze fell upon Borda Babu, and, out of respect, he asked Borda Babu to explain the entire matter in English. Borda Babu replied that he had never seen the person accused of cow slaughter, and that when the police had searched his house, they had not found that person; at that time, both Beni Babu and Ramlal were present with him. If their testimony were kindly accepted, it would prove the truth of his statement.
The sahib, impressed by Borda Babu’s genteel appearance and reasonable words, felt inclined to investigate further—Thakchacha...

chapters.title: The Trickster’s Wife
paragraphs: He kept making many signals to the serestadar, but the serestadar, seeing Bhojkat, feared he might have to cough up some money, so, casting aside his fear of the sahib, he said, “Huzoor, there is absolutely no need for this case to proceed.” The sahib, at the serestadar’s words, leaned back and began biting his nails, lost in thought. At this moment, Borda Babu quietly and patiently explained the real facts of his case once again. No sooner had the sahib heard this than he took the testimony of Beni Babu and Ramlal, and from their statements, the complaint was revealed to be entirely false and was dismissed. Before the order was even pronounced, Thakchacha, with a “cho!” bolted out at a run. Borda Babu, saluting the magistrate sahib, came out of the court. When the session ended, everyone began to praise him, but he paid no heed to their words, nor did he feel any elation at winning the case; instead, he quietly took Beni Babu and Ramlal by the hand and boarded the boat.
16. Introduction to Thakchacha’s House, His Wife, and Their Conversation, Including Baburam Babu’s Summons and Their Discussion on Safeguarding Their Interests

Thakchacha’s house was on the outskirts of the city—on either side, lotus ponds, and in front, a pir’s shrine. Inside the compound stood a granary, and in the yard, ducks and chickens roamed about day and night. From early morning, all sorts of shady characters would swarm to that place. To get his work done, Thakchacha would don many guises—sometimes soft, sometimes stern, sometimes smiling, sometimes sullen, sometimes displaying piety, sometimes showing off his strength. When the day’s business was over, he would bathe, eat, and then sit beside his wife, puffing away at the bidri hookah with a deep “bhoror,” filling the air with tobacco smoke. At that time, husband and wife would share all the joys and sorrows of their lives.

Thakchachi was highly respected among the womenfolk of the neighborhood—they believed she was well-versed in spells, charms, enchantments, love potions, death curses, exorcisms, talismans, magic tricks, and all sorts of occult arts. For this reason, women of all kinds would always come to her, whispering and confiding in her. Like husband, like wife—both Thakchacha and Thakchachi were a perfect match: the husband earned by his wits, the wife by her knowledge.
