...earns money. A woman who earns her own living always has a bit of pride; it’s hard for her to give her husband unqualified respect. That’s why Thakchacha had to endure a scolding or two from his wife now and then. Thakchachi, sitting on a cane stool, asked:

“You wander here and there every day—what good does that do for me or my Lerkabala? You’re always saying you have a lot of work in hand, but does that fill our bellies? My heart longs to strut about, decked in gold and silver, among the best of the courtesans, but I don’t see a single coin, not even a rupee. You’re always coming and going like a debtor—then just sit quietly in the house. Thakchacha, a little irritated, replied:

“What can I say about my efforts? You can’t even imagine how much I scheme—how many tricks, how many plots, how many plans! Sometimes the prey is almost in my grasp, then slips away again. Of course, if the prey came quickly—”
While this conversation was going on, a maid arrived and said, “Someone has come from Baburam Babu’s house to call you.”
Thakchacha immediately looked at his wife and said, “See, Babus call for me all the time—nothing gets done without my advice. I’ll seize my chance when the time is right.”

Baburam Babu was sitting in the drawing room. Nearby sat Banchharam Babu of Simla, Benibabu of Bali, and Becharam Babu of Bowbazar, chatting together. Thakchacha entered and took his seat as the chief guest.

Baburam: “Thakchacha! Good that you’ve come—the matter just isn’t getting resolved. With all these lawsuits, we’re getting entangled in endless troubles. Now, what’s the way to save our property and estate?”

chapters.title: The Second Marriage
paragraphs: Thakchacha: A man’s job is to fight his case—once the suit is won, all troubles will vanish! Why are you so scared at the slightest thing?
Becharam: Oh dear! What kind of advice are you giving? If we follow your counsel, Baburam is sure to be ruined—there’s not a shred of doubt about it. Well, Beni brother, what do you say?

Beni: In my opinion, it’s best to sell off a couple of properties to pay off the debts, and arrange things so that expenses don’t exceed income. Also, it’s necessary to settle the lawsuit with proper understanding. But all we do is sit and wail in the bamboo grove—whatever Thakchacha says, that’s what goes.

Thakchacha: I say this with my chest out—if the case is handled by me, it will be won, no question about it. I’ll cut off all the trouble at the root. If you’re a real man, you must fight—what’s there to fear?

Becharam: Thakchacha! You’ve always shown your valor. We saw your prowess during the boat wreck. At the time of the wedding, it was because of you that we suffered so much, and you showed great heroism by filing false complaints against Borda Babu. And whatever business you’ve handled for Baburam has always ended up in disaster. I bow to your feet. Just remembering all your exploits makes my blood boil—what more can I say to you? Enough!! Beni brother, let’s get up—I have no wish to sit here any longer.
The Barber and His Wife’s Conversation, Baburam Babu’s Second Marriage Discussed, and What Happened After

A heavy shower has just passed—the roads and lanes are all muddy and slippery. The sky is filled with blue-black clouds, rumbling now and then. Frogs are croaking all around. Shopkeepers and hawkers have opened their shutters and are smoking tobacco. Because of the rain, people’s comings and goings have almost stopped—only the cart drivers are shouting and singing as they go, and the porters are trudging along with heavy loads, lost in the song, “Hango Biskha se jibe Mathura.”

To the west of Baidyabati Bazaar, a few barbers’ families live. Among them, one barber is sitting on his veranda because of the rain. He glances at the sky now and then and counts something on his fingers. His wife brings their child on her hip and says, “There’s still housework left—”

I can’t manage, I tell you! Someone take the boy for a moment—here, the dishes aren’t washed, there, the room hasn’t been swept, and then there’s still the cooking left to do—how can I, a lone woman, handle all this? Which way should I turn? Do I have four hands and four feet?
At that, the barber, ever the clown, tucked his towel under his arm and jumped up, exclaiming, “Now’s not the time to hold the child—I must leave at once, Baburam Babu’s wedding is tomorrow!”

The barber’s wife, startled, cried out, “Oh dear, what will I do? The old man will start up again! Ah, such a mistress—such a virtuous, blessed woman—and now they’ll saddle her with a co-wife—what could be worse than death itself! Oh, menfolk are capable of anything!” The barber, lost in the winds of hope, paid no heed to her words, gave her a tap on the head, and strode off with a flourish.

That day passed in a heavy downpour. But the next morning, the sun broke through—as when a fire, hidden in a dark room, suddenly flares up, its heat feels all the more intense. So too, the sun’s rays blazed fiercely; the trees and plants seemed to come alive again, and the fields and gardens echoed with the calls and songs of animals and birds.

At the Baidyabati ghat, a crowd of boats was gathered. Baburam Babu, Thakchacha, Bakreshwar, Bancharam, and the household staff had all boarded one. Just then, Benibabu and Becharam Babu arrived. Thakchacha, seeing them, acted as if he hadn’t; he simply shouted, “Loosen the ropes!” The boatmen protested, “But master, the water hasn’t risen yet—how can we go, pushing with poles or pulling with ropes?”
Baburam Babu, spotting his two relatives, said, “It’s good you’ve come; now let’s all go together.”
Bancharam: “Baburam! Who advised you to take a wife at your age?”

Baburam: “Becharam da! Am I so old? I’m much younger than you. If you say my hair is gray and my teeth are falling out—well, that happens to many at a young age. That’s not the main thing. I have to look after everything, from every side. Look—one son is lost, another has gone mad, one daughter is gone, another is nearly a widow. If I have a child or two from this marriage, the family line will be preserved. And besides, I’m under great pressure—if I don’t marry, the bride’s father’s honor will be ruined—they have no other family left.”
Bakreshwar: That’s true, but do you think the master has embarked on this course of action without considering everything? Who has more sense than him?
Banchharam: We are kulin people—we must protect our lineage with our very lives, and when it comes to the call of money, well, then there’s nothing left to say.
Becharam: Ashes to your lineage, and ashes to your money too! A handful of people have come together and ruined a whole household—shame! Beni brother, what do you say?

Beni: What can I say? All we can do is cry in the wilderness. This whole affair is deeply distressing. To marry another wife while the first is still alive is a grave sin. A person who wishes to uphold their religion could never commit such an act. Even if there’s some scripture that says otherwise, it is never right to follow it. There’s no doubt that such a scripture is not a true scripture, and if people start following it, the bond of marriage will become terribly weak. A wife’s heart will no longer be steadfast towards her husband, nor the husband’s towards his wife. If such chaos is allowed, family life can never follow the path of virtue, so even if the scriptures permit it, that rule should be rejected. Be that as it may—Baburam Babu’s marrying again while his wife is still alive is a great sin—I had never even heard a whisper of such a thing before—now I hear it.

Thakchacha: These bookish gentlemen have to poke their noses into everything. Seems like they have nothing better to do. I’m old—my hair’s turned white—why should I get into arguments with these youngsters all day long? Do these bookish babus even know how much silver will come into the house from this match?

Banchharam: Oh, you money-obsessed devil! All you ever think about is cash—don’t you have anything else to say? You’re a great sinner—I have nothing more to say to you—shame on you! Beni brother, let’s go.
Thakchacha: Nephew, you can follow if you want—we can’t wait any longer. If you want to leave, go quickly.

Becharam took Beni Babu’s hand, stood up, and said—We won’t attend such a wedding, not while we’re alive, but if you have any religion left, don’t you dare come back in one piece. Your advice will bring ruin—you’ve enjoyed plenty at Baburam’s expense—what more can I say to you? Shame!

chapters.title: News of the Remarriage
paragraphs: With a Poem on the Subject.

The sun was setting—the western sky adorned in a riot of colors. On water and land alike, the restless glow of the day’s charioteer seemed to smile gently; a soft breeze was blowing. Who wouldn’t wish to step outside at such an hour? Along the winding lane of Baidyabati, a group of young gentlemen advanced with much hullabaloo—“Hey! Ho! Mind your step!”—one tumbling onto another’s shoulder, one nearly breaking another’s back, one shoving and sending a friend sprawling, another knocking off someone’s basket, yet another snatching away someone’s food, one singing at the top of his lungs, another barking like a dog. The people on both sides of the road fled in panic, crying out for mercy—everyone shrank back in terror, thinking, “If I survive today, I’ll live a long life yet.” Just as a storm rages in all directions with a wild roar, so did this band of new babus sweep along. Who were these paragons of virtue? Who else! They were none other than those illustrious souls—Motilal, Haladhar, Gadadhar, Ramgovinda, Dolgovinda, Mangobinda, and other second incarnations of Nala and Yudhishthir. They paid no heed to anything—utterly intoxicated, heads heavy with pride, rolling along as if about to collapse. Each was lost in his own world—when suddenly, old Majumdar of the village, his tuft of hair tied tight atop his head, came hobbling along, a stick in one hand and a couple of brinjals in the other, thumping his way right into their midst. Instantly, they surrounded him and began their mischief. Majumdar was somewhat hard of hearing—they asked, “Hey, tell us, how’s your wife?” Majumdar replied, “She’ll have to be roasted and eaten”—at which they burst into peals of laughter, “Ha ha! Ho ho! Lick! Fick!” filling the air with their mirth. Majumdar tried to slip away, but there was no escape. The young babus seized him and made him sit by the ghat of the Ganges. After making him smoke a chilam of gurak, they said, “Majumdar, tell us in detail about the master’s recent troubles—you’re a poet, your words are always so sweet; if you don’t, we won’t let you go, and we’ll go straight to your wife and tell her you’ve met with a fatal accident.” Seeing there was no way out, Majumdar set down his stick and brinjals and began to speak. What more can I say of our misfortunes? I learned a good lesson after accompanying the master.

It was evening when our boat docked at the Bolagarh ghat. A few women had come to fetch water; seeing the master, they pulled their veils a little tighter, exchanged sly smiles, and began whispering among themselves—“Oh my! What a handsome groom! Whoever gets him for a husband will wear him in her hair like a champa flower.” Among them, one said, “Old or young, at least a woman will get to see him with her own eyes, right? That’s something. My luck is so wretched—let no one else suffer as I have. I was married at six, but I never even set eyes on my husband. I’ve heard he’s married fifty or sixty times, over eighty years old—a tottering old man, but if there’s money, he’ll still come to marry. If it weren’t for some great sin, no woman would be born into a kulin Brahmin’s house.”

Another said, “Hey, are you done drawing water? Let’s go—no point gossiping at the ghat. At least your husband is alive. The man I was married to was already on his deathbed. Do kulin Brahmins have any religion or conscience? What’s the use of talking about all this? Best to keep such things to yourself.”

Hearing the girls’ conversation, I felt a pang of sorrow, and memories of Beni Babu from the other day came flooding back. Later, after getting off at Bolagarh, we tried hard to find a palanquin, but not a single soul was to be found. Since the auspicious hour was slipping away, everyone had to set off on foot. Stumbling and slipping through the mud, we finally reached the bride’s father’s house.

What a sight we must have made! If you’d sat the master on a bullock, he’d have looked just like Lord Shiva, and Thakchacha and Bakreshwar like Nandi and Bhringi. We’d heard there would be plenty of gifts, but when we reached the verandah, it was all a disappointment—nothing but sand in the sugar. With our hopes dashed, Thakchacha wandered here and there, muttering and grumbling. I just smiled to myself and thought, “Best to keep quiet in a place like this.”

The groom went to perform the customary rites. Many girls, young and old, gathered around, their bangles jingling, and shrieked in surprise at the sight of the groom. When their eyes met his, the master had to quickly put on his spectacles. The girls burst into peals of laughter and started teasing him. The master, losing his temper, called out for Thakchacha. Thakchacha tried to make a run for it inside the house, but at once the bride’s people caught him and, in a most playful manner,— There they lay him down—Bancharam Babu rises up in a fury, and he too receives a sound thrashing. Bakreshwar, under the crescent’s onslaught, becomes a pigeon with a swollen neck. Witnessing all this commotion, I slipped away from the groom’s party and mingled with the bride’s side. After that, who went where, I cannot say, but I had to leave behind poor old Thakchacha. As the saying goes, greed leads to sin, and sin to death. Now, listen to the poem I have composed on this occasion.
Thakchacha Mahashoy, ever so grand, Whispers mantras in Baburam’s ear. Baburam, the great fool, has become a Bhimarathi, He takes Thakchacha’s words as gospel, as law, as scripture.
Ever drunk on the thought of wealth, He knows not virtue from vice, How will his fortune last or grow? Always this restlessness, never a thought for good deeds, Now he sets his mind on marriage.
Everyone cries, “Shame, shame! At your age, what folly! Why dig a canal to bring in water now? Your family shines bright, a grandson you already have, What want or lack can you possibly claim?”
He listens to no one, makes up his mind, Determined to score a grand coup with this wedding. He hires a boat, sets off in haste, With kith and kin and all his people in tow.
If Jeni Babu objects, who heeds his words? He goes home and eats his rice alone. Becharam is always irritable, calls Thakchacha a sly old fox, And shoos him away with a “Get lost! Get lost!”
In the village of Gandagram, Rama and the rest set their traps, Mocking with gestures and sly remarks. Baburam fidgets and squirms, seeing great peril ahead, Afraid he might be caught in a snare.
He takes up a mirror, looks at his face with trembling fear, Why do Rama and the others put obstacles in his way?

His hair is tied up thick and high, he slaps his shoulder with his hand, Marches along, brimming with cheer and swagger. If he slips, it’s a grand commotion—he tumbles like a pumpkin, His heart full of excitement and delight.

Family and folks, seeing this, think it’s the summons of doom, Their faces smeared with mud, these poor souls. When the groom arrived, bones and all, he offered up his neck, All hopes and dreams of fortune dashed in a moment.

Where is the silver, where the gold? Only the name of gold remains, Where is the pearl necklace now? The trickster stirs up quarrels, makes a grand show of “mine and yours,” All are seething with anger inside.

The groom is led away by his wife’s customs, while Rama jingles along, The groom, seeing this, spits in disgust and shouts. “Shame, shame, shame! Is that drum of a man really the girl’s groom? Take him away, Fomaram, he’s a joy to behold in his old age!

What black hair he has, what a fine wrinkled face, and on his nose, With spectacles perched, he looks like a goblin! The girl is a golden vine—oh, what has fate done? Cursed be the ways of the high-born, shame, shame, shame!

The old groom, feverish and frail, shivers and trembles, His eyes darting wildly, making a strange, hissing sound. He utters not a word, clutching his aching head and calling out, ‘Uncle Trickster, what is this mess? Save me, please!’

He leaps and jumps, causing an earthquake, the trickster bounces about, The doorkeeper rushes in, brandishing his stick. Falling to the ground, rolling over, his mustache and beard cover his face, His nose ring clatters like a stone, slipping off as he falls.

Seeing this scene, everyone shrinks away and flees, Bowing in farewell, grateful to escape this ordeal. Majumdar, seeing the door, makes for it at once, ‘Hit him, catch him, surround him!’—the commotion grows.

chapters.title: The Death of Baburam
paragraphs: In the morning, after his walk, Beni Babu was seated in the pavilion of his own garden, glancing here and there, humming a Ramprasad song—“Now the night of fireworks is over.” On the western side, amidst a tangle of vines, a sound began to emerge—“Beni bhaiya, the night of fireworks is truly over.” Beni Babu started in surprise and saw Becharam Babu of Bowbazar hurrying towards him in great agitation. Advancing to meet him, he asked, “Becharam da! What’s the matter?”

Becharam Babu replied, “Throw a shawl over your shoulders, come quickly—Baburam is gravely ill—you must see him at once.” Beni Babu and Becharam hurried to the physician’s house, where they found Baburam burning with fever and delirium—tormented by thirst, tossing restlessly on his bed. Slices of cucumber and rags soaked in rosewater lay before him, but he was vomiting constantly, unable to keep anything down.

The entire village had gathered around, all in a commotion over his illness. Some said, “For us, eating greens and fish, leeches, purgatives, and poultices might do more harm than good. For our kind, the vaidya’s (traditional doctor’s) treatment is best; if that doesn’t work, then we can call the doctor in due time.” Others insisted, “The hakim’s (Unani physician’s) method is far superior—they feed and comfort the patient, and their medicines taste as delightful as sweetmeats.” Yet others declared, “Say what you will, these fevers are cured as if by magic with the doctor’s treatment—without it, recovery is nearly impossible.”

The patient, meanwhile, kept pleading for water, “Water, give me water!” But Brajanath Ray, the local kabiraj (herbalist), seated at his side, declared, “This is a severe sannyipat (malignant fever)—giving water repeatedly is not good. Squeeze out a little juice from the vishvapathra (a medicinal herb) and give him just a drop or two. We are not his enemies, that we should give him as much water as he asks for at such a time.”

Such was the confusion around the patient. In the adjoining room, the village Brahmin pundits had assembled in force, each insisting that the foremost duty was to perform Shivasvastayana, offer arghya to the sun, make a hundred thousand hibiscus offerings at Kalighat, and so on—divine rituals above all else.
Beni Babu stood by, listening to it all, but who was listening to whom? Each sage had his own doctrine, each was certain of his own wisdom. Once or twice, Beni Babu tried to offer his own opinion—

He tried to begin—but barely had he started the invocation when his words got hopelessly tangled. Somehow, with no other way out, Becharam took Babu outside to the verandah. Meanwhile, Thakchacha, limping and shuffling, arrived before them.
Thakchacha was deeply anxious about Baburam’s illness—he kept thinking all his schemes were about to fall apart. Seeing him, Beni Babu asked, “Thakchacha, have you hurt your foot?”
At once, Becharam piped up, “Brother! Haven’t you heard about what happened in Balagarh? That pain is punishment for his evil plotting. Did you forget what I said on the boat?”

Hearing this, Thakchacha tried to wriggle out of the situation. But Beni Babu grabbed his hand and said, “Whatever the case, what’s being done for the master’s illness? There’s utter chaos inside the house.”

Thakchacha replied, “When the fever started, I brought Hakim Ekramuddin right away—gave him all sorts of purgatives and medicines, drove the fever away and fed him khichuri. But as soon as the fast ended, the fever came back. Now Brajanath the Kabiraj is seeing him, but the illness seems to be getting worse every day—I’m an old man, I can’t keep up with all this.”
Beni Babu said, “Don’t be offended, Thakchacha—you should have sent us word about all this. Well, what’s done is done, but now it’s essential to bring a clever English doctor as soon as possible.”

As this conversation was going on, Ramlal and Bardaprasad Babu arrived. Ramlal’s face was pale from sleepless nights, the strain of nursing, and constant worry—his only thought was how to keep his father comfortable and help him recover. Seeing Beni Babu, he said, “Sir! We are in dire trouble, the house is in turmoil, but there’s no one to give sound advice. Bardababu comes morning and evening to look after things, but no one listens to what he says. Now that you’re here, please do whatever is necessary.”

Becharam Babu gazed at Bardababu for a moment, then, with tears in his eyes, took his hand and said, “Bardababu! If you didn’t have so many virtues, why would everyone revere you? This Thakchacha, by advising Baburam, has filed complaints against you and, for no reason, subjected you to all sorts of harassment and injustice. But when Thakchacha was ill, you yourself gave him medicine, looked after him, and nursed him back to health. Now Baburam is ill again—”

You never hesitate to give good advice or take care of others, but if someone utters a single harsh word to another among you, it instantly sparks a quarrel and breeds enmity. Even after a thousand reconciliations, the bitterness never truly fades. Yet you, even when gravely insulted or wronged, easily forget your own humiliation and injury—towards others, you feel nothing but brotherly affection, never any other sentiment, Bardababu. Many people talk of religion, but I have never seen anyone whose religion is like yours. What can ordinary mortals know of your virtues? But if there is truth in the world, then such virtues will surely be judged above.

Hearing Becharam Babu’s words, Bardababu hung his head in embarrassment, then said humbly, “Sir! Please do not praise me so much—I am a most insignificant person—what knowledge do I have, or what religion of mine is worth mentioning?”
Benibabu said, “Gentlemen, let us leave these matters for now. Let us discuss what should be done for the master’s illness.”
Bardababu replied, “If you all agree, I can go to Calcutta and bring a doctor by afternoon. In my opinion, it is no longer wise to rely on Brajanath Ray.”

Premnarayan Majumdar, who was standing nearby, said, “Doctors do not understand the pulse very well—they kill people at home, and it is not right to dismiss the kaviraj entirely. Let one illness be seen by a doctor, and another by the kaviraj.”
Benibabu said, “That can be decided later. For now, let Bardababu go and fetch the doctor.”

Without bathing or eating, Bardababu set off for Calcutta. Everyone said, “Sir, it is quite late—please eat a little before you go.” He replied, “That would only cause delay, and everything might be ruined.”

Babu Ram Babu lay on his bed, ceaselessly asking, “Where is Mati? Where is Mati?” But there was no sign of Matilal’s tuft of hair—he was off in the garden, reveling in a picnic with his companions, paying no heed even after hearing of his father’s illness. Seeing this behavior, Benibabu sent someone to the garden to fetch him, but Matilal sent back a message, falsely claiming, “I have a terrible headache; I will return home after some time.”
At two hours past noon, Babu Ram Babu’s fever reached its crisis, and his pulse became utterly erratic. The kaviraj, after examining his hand, said, “The master must be moved—”

Duty—He is elderly, venerable, and most honorable; it is only proper to do whatever may ensure his well-being in the afterlife. No sooner had these words been spoken than the entire household burst into tears, and all the relatives and neighbors, supporting Baburam Babu, brought him out to the verandah of the house. At this moment, Borda Babu arrived, bringing a doctor with him. The doctor, after feeling the pulse, said, “You have called me at the very end—what can a doctor do if he is summoned only when the patient is about to be sent to the banks of the Ganges?” Saying this, the doctor departed.

All the people of Baidyabati surrounded Baburam Babu, each one asking, “Sir, do you recognize me—can you tell who I am?” Benibabu said, “Why trouble the patient so much—what is the use of such questions?” The Swastyayani Brahmins, having finished their rituals, came bearing flowers of blessing, only to see that their divine rites had had no effect whatsoever.

Seeing Baburam Babu’s labored breathing, everyone took him to the Baidyabati ghat. There, after drinking Ganges water and breathing the gentle air, he regained a little consciousness. The crowd gradually thinned. Ramlal sat by his father’s side. Bordaprasad Babu stood before Baburam Babu and, after a while, softly said, “Sir! Now, with all your heart, meditate upon the Supreme Lord—without His grace, there is no deliverance for us.”

Hearing these words, Baburam Babu gazed at Bordaprasad Babu for a few moments and began to weep. Ramlal wiped away his tears and gave him a little milk with a blade of kusa grass. Somewhat revived, Baburam Babu said in a faint voice, “Brother Bordaprasad! Now I realize that in this world, apart from you, I have no friend left—I have committed grave misdeeds, led astray by the evil counsel of others. Whenever I recall those deeds, it feels as if my soul is burning in fire—I am a great sinner—what answer shall I give? And will you ever forgive me?” Saying this, Baburam Babu clasped Bordaprasad Babu’s hand and closed his eyes.
The friends and relatives nearby began to chant the name of God, and, in full consciousness, Baburam Babu departed from this world.

chapters.title: The Funeral Farce
paragraphs: Upon his father’s death, Motilal took his place on the family throne. Not for a moment did his companions leave his side. Now, his chest swelled with pride—he began to imagine that, after so many years, everything would proceed in grand style, with pomp and splendor. Motilal felt a flicker of sorrow for his father, but his friends said, “Big Babu! Why the long face? Who lives forever with their parents? Now you’re the lord of the manor.”

Grief, for a fool, is but a name—he who never brought joy to his parents, who tormented them in countless ways, how deeply can he mourn his father? If he feels anything at all, it is as fleeting as a shadow, and never does he remember his father with reverence, nor does he feel any urge to perform any act in his memory. Motilal’s sorrow for his father was soon buried under a pressing desire to know exactly what property and wealth remained. On the advice of his companions, he double-locked every door, chest, and strongbox, and sat tight. In his mind, there was always the fear that, should his mother, stepmother, brother, or sister get their hands on any money, it would be lost forever.

His friends were always saying, “Big Babu! Money is a precious thing—one can’t trust even one’s own father with it. The younger Babu may go about wrapped in the cloak of religion, preaching the truth, but if he gets the chance, even his guru spares no one. We’ve seen plenty of such hypocrisy. Anyway, the eldest Babu surely knows some tricks—must have spent some time in Kamakhya, otherwise how did he manage so many tricks at the master’s deathbed?”

A few days later, Motilal began to pay formal visits to relatives and acquaintances. Those who are always ready to meddle, to play the go-between, who drift about like jalebis on a platter, went around spreading all sorts of talk—words that float in the air, never quite touching the ground, so that, twisted this way or that, they can mean anything. Some said, “The master was a remarkable man—leaving behind such sons must be the fruit of great merit. He was a man of his kind, and his death was just as extraordinary, Babu. All these days you were hidden behind the mountain, now you must take heed—the burden of the household has fallen on your shoulders.”

There are certain rituals to be performed—one must uphold the name of one’s father and grandfather, that is an inherited duty. One should perform the shraddha according to one’s means; there is no need to start dancing just because ten people are whispering in your ear. Ramchandra himself offered pinda to Bali—so there’s no use lamenting over the matter, but doing nothing at all is hardly commendable either. Babu! Do you know the reputation of the late master? Even today, at the mere mention of his name, tigers and cows drink water together in peace. But does that mean everything will proceed in the most orthodox, extravagant fashion?—Even if you get arrested, you’ll have to answer to people’s gossip. Motilal understands none of these tangled affairs. The relatives, with all the warmth of kinship, express their concern, but their real aim is to orchestrate a grand spectacle so they can strut about and flaunt their authority—that is their true desire. Yet if you ask them directly, they dodge and evade. One says, “If you don’t perform the sixteen rites with silver, it won’t be proper”—another says, “If you don’t host a great feast, your honor will be at stake”—yet another says, “If you don’t welcome a married couple, the shraddha will be insignificant”—someone else says, “If you don’t invite a number of scholars and send off the poor with gifts, it will be a terrible disgrace.” Thus, a great commotion ensues—who wants rules?—who wants to argue?—who listens to decisions?—everyone fancies himself the village chief—everyone is his own master—everyone has five tales of his own to tell.

Three days later, Beshibaba, Becharam Babu, Banchharam Babu, and Bakreshwar Babu arrived. They sat before Motilal like venomous cobras robbed of their jewels—rosary in hand, lips trembling as they muttered prayers; many other conversations were taking place, but their minds were elsewhere—they stared at the wall, eyes rolling, lost in thought—unable to settle on any decision.

At the sight of Benibabu and the others, Thakchacha sprang up and began to greet them with great humility. Such meekness had never been seen in Thakchacha before. When a snake is subdued, its pride vanishes. Benibabu took Thakchacha’s hand and said, “What are you doing? You are an elder of the family—why such deference to us?” Banchharam Babu said, “Let that be—time is short, and nothing has been arranged yet—what do you say should be done?”

Becharam Babu said, “Babu Ram’s estate is quite substantial—some property should be sold off to pay the debts—it is not proper to incur more debt for the sake of a lavish shraddha.” Banchharam: What are you saying! First, we must listen to what people will say, only then can we think about saving our property and assets. Should our honor and reputation just float away in the floodwaters?
Becharam: That advice is terrible—I would never give such counsel, would I, Beni brother? What do you say?

Beni: When there are so many debts, and even if we sell off all the property and assets it’s doubtful whether the debts will be repaid, then taking on more loans is nothing short of theft. Because how will those debts ever be paid back?

Banchharam: That’s all English thinking—these big people just parrot whatever the English say—one hand giving, the other taking, always putting a spanner in the works of any good deed, and ending up like a broken idol of Mangalchandi. That’s not the way of a gentleman. I myself don’t have the means to give alms, but if someone else is willing to donate to ten Brahmin scholars, why should I interfere? Besides, everyone has their own loyal Brahmins and scholars—they too want to receive invitations and gifts—they have to make a living as well.
Bakreshwar: You’re right—there’s a saying: “Let the body go, but let the honor stay.”

Becharam: Baburam’s family has fallen into a ring of fire—I can see they’ll be finished soon enough. Our duty is to say what will truly help in the end—taking on more debt just to buy a name is a fool’s errand. I don’t keep such sycophantic Brahmins who would slit another’s throat just to fill their own bellies. What kind of business is this! Enough! Let’s go, Beni brother! I must be off—saying this, he took Beni Babu by the hand and got up.

When Beni Babu and Becharam left, Banchharam said, “Peace to your troubles! These two understand nothing—they just stir up confusion. It’s a relief to talk with someone sensible! Thakchacha, come here—what do you think?”

Thakchacha: I really enjoy talking with you—but those others, they’re all big talkers—I’m afraid of their kind. Everything you’ve said is true. When a man loses his respect and power, life itself is lost. You and I will handle the lawsuits and legal matters and cut through all the trouble—what’s there to be afraid of?

Matilal has a reckless nature—no sense of income or expense—he doesn’t know the first thing about managing property. He has great faith in Banchharam and Thakchacha, because they are both veterans of the courts...

The scheming fellows, with all their cunning and connivance, began to coax and cajole in such a manner that Motilal finally declared outright, “You gentlemen take charge of these affairs and see to their execution as you see fit. Whatever papers you need me to sign, I shall do so at once.” Banchharam Babu said, “Bring out your father’s will and hand it to me. In the will, only you are named as executor—your cousin was left out because he is mad. If we present this will in court, you will be confirmed as the sole executor. Then, with your signature, the property can be mortgaged or sold.” Motilal opened the box and produced the will.

Afterwards, when Banchharam had finished the court formalities, he brought a moneylender along with the necessary documents and the cash to the house at Baidyabati. Motilal, upon seeing the money, immediately signed all the papers. As he reached to put the bag of coins into his box, Banchharam and Thakchacha interjected, “Babuji! If the money stays in your hands, it will be spent in no time. If we keep the funds, perhaps some of it might be saved. Besides, you are too good-natured—too bashful; if anyone asks, you won’t be able to refuse. We, on the other hand, can give or withhold as we see fit.” Motilal thought this was wise—after the funeral, how would he get money for expenses? Now that his father was gone, he could no longer simply ask and receive. So he agreed to their proposal.

A grand commotion broke out over Baburam Babu’s funeral rites. The sound of pounding rice for offerings, the aroma of clarified butter, the buzzing of flies, the smoke from damp wood, the arrival of all sorts of goods—the house was filled with the clamor of people. Every priest, shopkeeper, and market official, every Brahmin in the district, donned a pair of new silk dhotis and smeared their foreheads with Ganges clay, coming and going in droves for their share of the offerings. And as for the scholars—Tarkabagish, Vidyaratna, Nyayalankar, Bachaspati, and Vidyasagar—their numbers were endless; day and night, Brahmin pundits and teachers poured in, as if a cobbler’s festival had broken out during a cattle plague.

The day of the funeral feast arrived. The assembly was filled with Brahmin scholars from all corners, and all the relatives, kinsmen, and friends were seated. Before them lay a sea of silver offerings—horses, palanquins, brass vessels, brocades, utensils, and piles of cash. Kirtan was being sung at the side, while in the midst of it all, poor Becharam Babu sat deep in thought, lost in contemplation. Outside the house, the beggars, musicians, drummers, and the ever-hungry crowd were gathered in full force. Thakchacha was prowling about, too wary to sit in the assembly. The teachers— They are taking snuff and discussing scriptural matters among themselves—their particular talent is that whenever they gather, it is impossible for conversation to remain calm; sooner or later, some commotion inevitably arises. One professor brought up a knotty point from the Nyaya Shastra: “The relation of vyapti, as distinguished by the property of ‘ghatatva’ (pot-ness), is externally observed in smoke, and in smoke is fire.”

A scholar from Orissa said, “The vyapti, when joined and distinguished, is the competitor; the vyapti is the mountain, called fire by name.” A scholar from Kashi-Jora interjected, “What sort of talk is this? The sentence hasn’t been properly constructed—you’re breaking the pot and calling the mountain fiery, and the smoke’s crown you’re knocking off with a stick!”

A Bengali scholar chimed in, “The vyapti distinguished by the pot is the competitor; in smoke is fire, in fire is smoke—how can there be smoke without fire?” Thus the debate raged on—face to face, it was on the verge of turning into a scuffle. Thakchacha thought, “Better to settle this before disaster strikes.” Quietly approaching, he said, “I say, why are you all fighting over a jug and a lamp’s wick? I’ll give you two jugs.”

At this, a hot-tempered Brahmin professor from Chattopote stood up and shouted, “Who are you, you rascal? Why is a Yavana at a Hindu shraddha? What’s this? Is this the presiding officer at a widow’s shraddha or what?” With that, the abuse began, and from words it escalated to shoving and stick-waving.

Banchharam Babu rushed in and declared, “If you create a ruckus and ruin the shraddha, you’ll see—I’ll bring a summons straight from the big court. Is this how you let boys beat you up?” Bakreshwar said, “Of course! And the one performing the shraddha isn’t some ordinary boy, he’s Paresh Pathar.” Becharam added, “That’s well known—wherever Thak and Banchharam preside, there’s bound to be trouble.”

chapters.title: The New Master
paragraphs: It will never be enough—nonsense! The commotion refuses to die down. The likes of Reo Bhat and others are still bustling about, sometimes getting a whipping, and shouting, “Well done with the funeral feast, eh!” At last, the gentlemen present at the gathering, witnessing this spectacle, began to remark, “Who performs whose funeral rites? The Brahmin dies, and the shroud-cutter eats his fill.” It’s best to slip away now—why lose one’s dignity over a mess of sour tamarind?

21. Motilal’s Inheritance of the Estate and Babudom, His Ill-Treatment of His Mother, Departure from His Mother and Sister’s House, Forbidding His Brother from Returning Home, and the Brother’s Departure to Another Land.

At Baburam Babu’s funeral, people did not feel much reverence, just as thunder does not always bring rain. Many oily heads received more oil, but the dry scalps cracked for lack of it. The professors’ only skill was argument; the city-wise Brahmins of the “friends’ circle” won with their cunning. The professors, owing to their many strict habits, had become rigid in nature—they followed their own inclinations and never said “yes” to any bargain. The city-bred Brahmins, on the other hand, were seasoned by urban life—they spoke to please the babus, struck when the iron was hot. For them, every job was a job, every curry was curry. So is it any wonder they received the highest honor everywhere? The professors sat with their purses tightly shut—whether the Brahmin pundits and beggars received a grand send-off or a paltry one, they cared only for their own reward. The one act that had caught everyone’s eye and could not be ignored was loudly proclaimed, but there was no balanced consideration of pros and cons. Such management is merely cutting a ribbon to win applause.

The commotion of the funeral feast gradually subsided. Bancharam and Thakchacha began to flatter Motilal in their own peculiar way. Motilal, weak of character, was easily swayed by their honeyed words and began to believe that there were no relatives in the world as dear as these two.

To enhance Motilal’s sense of importance, one day they said, “Now you are the master; it is your duty to sit on the late master’s seat. Otherwise, how will his position be maintained?” Hearing this, Motilal was overjoyed. In his childhood, he had heard a little of the Ramayana and Mahabharata, so now it began to seem to him— Just as Ramachandra and Yudhishthira were enthroned with great pomp and ceremony, so too must I be seated upon the ancestral seat. As soon as Bancharam and Thakchacha saw this proposal, Moti Lal’s face began to glow with delight—so much so that the very next day, they fixed an auspicious date, invited all the relatives and acquaintances, and installed Moti Lal upon his father’s seat of authority. News spread through the village by the beat of the town crier’s drum: “Moti Lal has inherited the seat!” This tidbit began to circulate in the market, at the bathing ghat, in the fields, everywhere.

A sharp-tongued Brahmin, upon hearing the news, remarked, “Inherited the seat, you say? That’s a tall claim! And whose seat is this, anyway? Is it the seat of Jagat Seth, or that of Debidas Balmukund? A man of substance, even if he attains high office or wealth, does not sway or stagger; but one who is empty within, if his fortunes rise, wobbles like floodwater. Such was the state of Moti Lal’s mind.

Day and night, it was nothing but games and amusements, noise and music, laughter and merriment, endless revelry and frolic, feasts and gatherings, all flowing on like an unceasing stream. The number of his companions never dwindled—on the contrary, like the demon Raktabija, they seemed to multiply every day. But what’s so surprising about that? Where there’s rice, there’s never a shortage of crows; and the mere scent of molasses brings forth an army of ants in a trice.

One day, Bakreshwar came along the road and spoke at length to Moti Lal about the importance of mindfulness. But Moti Lal knew Bakreshwar’s tricks all too well, ever since childhood. So he replied, “Sir! The way you’ve looked after me, you’ve already ruined my prospects for the next world. As a boy, I never failed to spit at you when you came near—why do you torment me still?” Bakreshwar, crestfallen, slunk away with a pitiful mew.

Moti Lal was intoxicated with his own pleasures. Bancharam and Thakchacha would come by now and then, but there was little interaction with them. They managed all collections and payments through legal documents, and would occasionally hand something to the young master as a token. As for the household expenses, there was no accounting—no oversight of the family either. Who stayed where, who ate what—no one knew, and no one cared. As a result, the family members began to suffer, but Moti Lal was so lost in his lordly airs that he paid no heed to their complaints.

There is no greater torment for a virtuous wife than the grief of a husband’s neglect. If there is a worthy son, that sorrow is somewhat alleviated. But if the son is unworthy, it is as if ghee is poured upon the fire of her anguish...

Because of Motilal’s misbehavior, his mother became deeply distressed—yet she never showed it on her face. After much deliberation, one day she came to Motilal and said, “My son! Whatever was written in my fate has come to pass. Now, for the few days I have left, let me not have to hear your harsh words. I cannot bear the reproaches of people. Please, take a little care of your younger brother, your elder sister, and your stepmother—they often do not get even a full meal in a day. My son! I do not say this for myself, nor do I burden you with any responsibility.”

Hearing this, Motilal’s eyes grew red with anger. He said, “Why do you keep whining and nagging a hundred times over? Don’t you know, I can do whatever I please now? And what harsh words have I ever spoken?” With these words, he slapped his mother hard and shoved her aside.

After a long while, his mother got up, wiped her tears with the end of her sari, and said, “My son! I had never heard of a child striking his mother, but even that has come to pass in my ill-fated life. I have nothing more to say, except this: may you fare well.” The next day, without saying a word to anyone, she left the house, taking her daughter with her.

After their father’s death, Ramlal had tried hard to maintain good relations with his brother, but he was insulted in various ways. Motilal always thought, “If I give him half of the property, I won’t be able to act like a big man; but if I don’t act like a big man, life is not worth living. Therefore, I must do whatever it takes to cheat my brother out of his share.” With this plan in mind, and following the advice of Bancharam and Uncle Thakchacha, Motilal forbade Ramlal from entering the house. Barred from setting foot in the family quarters, and after much reflection, Ramlal left for another land without meeting his mother, sister, or anyone else.

chapters.title: The Trading Scheme
paragraphs: Motilal saw that his mother had left the house, his brother had gone, his sister too had departed. Calamity’s peace! After so many days, the coast was finally clear—no more nagging, no more endless scolding—now, with just a single glare, all work would be done, and “by force, Dhananjaya!” All that was well and good, but the family coffers were running dry—what to do now? How would the babudom continue? He could no longer juggle those petty moneylenders. Even the pawnshop-walas had stopped lending. And right ahead was the grand Snan Yatra festival—he’d have to hire a barge, pay the dancers, place orders for sweets and confections, and procure charas, ganja, and liquor too—the arrangements weren’t even half done.

Lost in such worries, Motilal sat brooding when Bancharam and Thakchacha arrived. After a few words, they asked, “Bada Babu! Why so glum? When you look downcast, we too feel downcast—you’re at an age when you should always be cheerful. Why the hand on your cheek? Shame! Sit up straight.”

Motilal, softened by these sweet words, poured out all his troubles. Bancharam said, “Why fret so much about that? Are we just here to cut grass? Today we’ve come up with a grand plan—within a year, you’ll clear all your debts and be able to put your feet up and live like a true gentleman, generation after generation. The scriptures say, ‘In trade resides Lakshmi’—it’s in business that people prosper. I’ve seen so many fellows—ragged, patched-up, half-wits, fools—who, just by dabbling in trade, have become fat and rich. Just seeing them makes my eyes burn. We’re grinding away at just one job—isn’t that a hard fate? Chandi Charan gathers dung, Rama rides a horse.”

Motilal: “That’s a fine idea—I always need money. But does trade grow in the market, or is it born in the office? Or can you buy it at the sweet shop? Unless I have an Englishman’s agent, my business won’t flourish.”
Bancharam: “Bada Babu! You just sit back on your cushion, leave all the work to us. Our butler knows an Englishman’s friend, Jan Sahib…”
Recently returned from England, it is he who must be put forward and made the manager. But that fellow is riddled with rot when it comes to business.

Thakchacha: I’ll be right there with him, side by side. There’s no job in the court, goods, criminal cases, or business that I haven’t handled. My Shena understands all this well. Babu, my only regret is that my credentials have yet to be recognized—my references haven’t been made public. I’m not the sort to stay quiet—if I find an enemy, I grab him, bite him, and thrash him to the ground. Give me a business deal, and I’ll handle it like Rustam the Great.
Motilal: Thakchacha—who is Shena?
Thakchacha: Shena is your Thakchachi—what else would she be? Her face is like a jailer’s, but her mind is sharp as an angel’s. She understands everything.

Banchharam: Let’s leave that for now. We’ll have to supply Jan Sahib with ten or fifteen thousand rupees, but there’s no harm in that. I’ve decided that if we mortgage the Kotolpur estate, we can raise the money. The mortgage paperwork will be handled at our sahib’s office—the expenses won’t be much—about four or five hundred rupees, and another five hundred for the moneylender’s clerks and staff. Those rascals are born enemies—one jab from them and the whole deal could fall apart. In every business, you have to grease the wheels and clear the obstacles before you can rescue your fortune. I won’t delay any longer; I’m taking Thakchacha and heading to Calcutta—my head is burning with urgency. Barababu! You must consult Tarkasiddhanta Dada, pick an auspicious day, and set out for my house in Sonagazi at once. You’ll have to stay in Calcutta for a while, and then, when you return to this Baidyabati ghat with seven ships laden with treasure like Chand Sadagar, and the drums sound your arrival, then the young and old, the maidens and matrons, will marvel at your return and shower you with praise. Ah! May that day dawn soon!
With these words, Banchharam set off with Thakchacha.

Motilal recounted all these events to his companions in detail. Hearing it, the friends clapped their armpits and broke into a dance—their nightly rations, which had nearly been cut off, now seemed secure again. There was every hope that the old allowances would soon be restored. In haste,

With much commotion, Man Gobind came running at full tilt and arrived at the school of Tarkasiddhanta, panting for breath. Tarkasiddhanta was a venerable old man, taking snuff—sneezing with a loud “fench fench”—coughing “khok khok”—surrounded by his pupils. In front of him lay several palm-leaf manuscripts; with his spectacles perched on his nose, he glanced at the texts, then dictated lessons to the students. The cows had not been fed their straw, so they were mooing restlessly. From inside the house, the Brahmani shouted, “When men grow old, they lose all sense! He’ll pore over almanacs and scriptures day and night, but won’t spare a glance at the household chores.” The students, overhearing this, nudged each other and exchanged sly looks.

Annoyed, Tarkasiddhanta grabbed his stick and was about to storm out to silence his wife, when Man Gobind caught hold of him and pleaded, “Oh Tarkasiddhanta uncle! We’re all going on a trading expedition—please choose an auspicious day for us.” Tarkasiddhanta contorted his face in disgust and grumbled, “Go eat roasted taro! Always calling me for nonsense at the oddest hours. Going trading, are you? May your father’s homestead be ruined—what need have you for auspicious dates? The day you lot leave will be a blessing for everyone—everyone will breathe easy and go bathe in the Ganges. Go on, go! The very day you leave this place will be the most auspicious.”

Receiving this “blessing,” Man Gobind returned, face fallen, and announced that tomorrow was a good day. Instantly, the house erupted in a flurry of preparations. Someone picked up the majorab of the sitar, someone else thumped the baya drum to check if it was in working order, another slapped the tabla with his palm, testing its tone, while someone else tightened the dhol’s cords. One smeared resin on the bow of the beyal, another packed up bundles and bags, someone else rolled up charas, ganja, even knives and sticks into a bundle, while another carefully stowed away bullets and gunpowder. Someone else took stock of the provisions, making sure nothing was lacking. Thus, the whole day and night passed in restless bustle—fetch this, bring that, check this, listen to that, “Hey you there, hurry up!”—the preparations went on in a great hullabaloo.

News spread through the village: the babus were setting off on their trading expedition. Next morning, all the shopkeepers, vendors, beggars, paupers, and many others lined the road, watching. Meanwhile, the young babus, like drunken elephants, marched to the ghat with a thunderous “paiyis paiyis” sound. Many Brahmin scholars, engaged in their morning rituals, turned at the commotion and were utterly dumbstruck.

chapters.title: The Failed Merchant
paragraphs: Seeing them so frightened, the young babus burst into mocking laughter and began pelting them with handfuls of Ganges mud, bits of broken pottery, and clumps of dirt. The Brahmins, their midday rituals ruined, departed muttering “Govinda! Govinda!” under their breath. The babus clambered into their boat, and all together broke into a raucous chorus of “Sakhi Sambad.” The boat, riding the ebb tide, sped swiftly down the river, but the babus could not sit still—one clambered onto the roof, another tugged at the anchor rope, a third wielded the oar, and yet another struck sparks with a flint.

After a little while, they encountered Dhanamala. Dhanamala was a notorious chatterbox—she called out, “You’ve already burned the whole village to ashes, and now you’re trying to set the Ganges on fire as well?” The babus, irritated, shouted back, “Shut up, you shrew! Don’t you know we’re all off to become merchants?” Dhana retorted, “If you lot ever become merchants, may the noose of trade strangle you all!”

Motilal, with his retinue, arrived at Sonagazi and drove away a certain Guru Mahashay; the babus’ antics grew ever more outrageous, and in fear of falling into debt through their trading ventures, they soon departed.

At the dargah in Sonagazi, Kuni and Buni had made their home. All around, the place was thick with moss and wild creepers, nests of crows and mynas in every corner. The womenfolk brought their water pots to the stream, the children shrieked and played, and not a speck of lime dust could be found anywhere. At night, only the howls of jackals and the barking of dogs could be heard, and one wondered if anyone in the place even bothered to light lamps at dusk.

Nearby, a certain Guru Mahashay taught a group of boys, each with a slate tied around his neck. Whether the boys learned anything or not, the mere sound of the cane sent terror through their hearts. If a boy so much as raised his head or dared to sneak a mouthful of puffed rice from his pouch, the cane would come down on his back in an instant. Such is human nature: wherever there is authority, it must find a way to assert itself, or else its pride feels diminished. Thus, Guru Mahashay, eager to display his power, would gather passersby from the road. Whenever there was an audience, he would raise his voice to its highest pitch, and the more people gathered, the more his sense of command swelled. Is it any wonder, then, that the boys received severe punishment for the slightest offense? Guru Mahashay’s school was little better than the abode of Yama himself—always the sound of “whack, smack, thwack!” and cries of “Oh Guru Mahashay, I’ve finished my lesson!” and the endless recitation of names.

Someone’s ears were being boxed, someone was made to stand on bricks, someone else had their hands twisted, another was hung from the well’s pulley, yet another was doused with water—one punishment or another was always being meted out. The only one who managed to keep Sonagazi’s secrets was that very guru-mahashay.

At the far end, a couple of beggars would linger, spending their whole day begging. In the evening, exhausted from their labors, they would lie down and sing softly. Such was the state of Sonagazi. But from the moment Motilal made his auspicious arrival, Sonagazi’s fate turned on its head. Suddenly, it was all “the neigh of horses, the slap of the tabla, the crackle of fried bread”—uproarious revelry, day and night. Sweets and confections, rosewater and attar, hashish, ganja, and liquor flowed so freely that many were left reeling.

It’s hard to recognize people in Calcutta—many are chameleons in disguise. At first, they appear in one form, and later reveal another. The root of it all is money—money changes everything. Human nature is so weak that it worships wealth as something extraordinary. If people hear that someone has a lot of money, they’ll do everything in their power—body, mind, and speech—to curry favor with him, leaving no stone unturned in saying or doing whatever it takes.

For this reason, all sorts of people began to flock to Motilal. Some, like the brash Brahmins of Ula, would bluntly state their intentions; some, like the crafty folk of Krishnanagar, would weave elaborate tales and display their cunning, only revealing their true purpose after much delay and in the subtlest of ways. Others, like the cautious Bengalis from the east, would tread carefully—at first presenting themselves as disinterested and free from greed, while their real motives lay submerged in the depths of the Dwaipayana lake, only surfacing after a long time, when it became clear that their visits were motivated by nothing more than “a little bit of gold.”

Anyone who came to Motilal would snap their fingers when they yawned, say “Bless you” when he sneezed. If he called out “Hey!” they’d respond with an even louder “Hey!”—and to everything, good or bad, they’d reply, “Yes sir, whatever you say is right.”

From dawn till two hours past midnight, people thronged to Motilal—there was not a moment, not an instant, not even a blink of time when some new visitor wasn’t arriving, sitting, or leaving. The clatter of their shoes made the drawing room stairs tremble; tobacco was brought in constantly, and the smoke billowed out like a steamer’s funnel. The servants could no longer keep up with rolling the tobacco—they began to flee.

The invitations are being sent out. Day and night, there is dancing, singing, music, laughter, grand boasting, buffoonery, mimicry, jokes, banter, mock quarrels, playful scolding, jostling and slapping in jest, picnics, intoxication—all follow one after another in endless succession. It is as if, overnight, Motilal has suddenly become a full-fledged babu.

In this crowd, the importance of the revered tutor dwindled to nothing—he who was once a great bird has now shrunk to a mere sparrow. Occasionally, there would be a little commotion about the boys’ lessons—hearing of it, Motilal would say, “Why is this fellow still making a fuss here? I freed myself from the torment of the tutor in my boyhood itself, why should he be near me again? Get rid of him at once.” No sooner had these words been uttered than the young babus, within a day or two, made the tutor disappear with the help of bricks and tiles, and thus the school was dissolved. The boys, delighted to be free, ran home at full speed, waving toddy leaves and making faces and rude gestures at the tutor.

Meanwhile, Mr. John opened a house of his own—named it the John Company. Motilal became the accountant, Bancharam and Uncle Thak were the officials. For the sake of money, the sahib fawned over the accountant, and the accountant, along with his companions, would, around two or three or four in the afternoon, chew betel leaf and, with red eyes, pay a visit to the bungalow, strut about for a while, and then return home. The sahib had not a penny to his name—once he had been a butler at another sahib’s house, but now he rented a house in Chowringhee, bought all sorts of furniture and paintings to decorate it, and acquired fine carriages, horses, and dogs on credit. He even trained racehorses and began to gamble on the races. After some time, the sahib got married, wore a gold watch-chain and a diamond ring, and began to circulate in polite society. Seeing all this show, many were convinced that Mr. John had become wealthy, and so, in dealing with him, they entertained not the slightest suspicion. But a few shrewd men, knowing his true nature, kept their distance—they never got too close.

Many merchants in Calcutta earn their living through agency business—either by arranging the chartering of ships, or by buying and selling company papers or goods, and for this they receive a commission, a certain percentage as agency fee.

Many others, using their own money, carefully study the markets here and elsewhere before venturing into trade. But those who take up such work must first learn the business of trading—otherwise, nothing good can come of it.

Jan Saheb had not the slightest sense or understanding. He believed that simply buying goods and sending them off would surely bring profit. His real intention was to enjoy the fruits of another’s labor and become a great man overnight. He thought of trade as nothing more than a gamble—fire ten shots, and surely one of them will hit the mark. The Saheb was ignorant, but his mutsuddi was even worse—a complete blockhead. He had neither learning nor common sense, nor could he grasp the basics of business. Entrusting him with any task was like sending a cow to slaughter.

Moneylenders, brokers, and government agents were always bringing him samples of goods, discussing the ups and downs of prices, and giving him news of the markets. When it came to business matters, he would fall into utter confusion, staring blankly and saying nothing in reply—perhaps fearing that if he spoke, his ignorance would be exposed. All he would say was, “Go to Banchharam Babu or Thakchacha.”

There were one or two clerks in the office who kept all the accounts in English. One day, Motilal decided it would be good to understand the English cashbook. He sent for the book from the clerk, glanced through it here and there, then set it aside. Motilal used to sit in the downstairs room of the office—a rather damp place. The cashbook, left there for months, became moldy and began to rot. The young gentlemen of the house started tearing out the pages, rolling them into wicks, and using them daily to clean their ears. In a few days, all the pages were gone, leaving only the cover behind. Later, when the cashbook was sought, it was discovered that only the shell remained—the bones and skin had been sacrificed for the greater good! Jan Saheb, lamenting, cried, “Where is the cashbook? Oh, the cashbook!” but kept his sorrow to himself.

Jan Saheb, without restraint or discretion, began purchasing all sorts of goods and sending them off to England and other countries. He had no idea what the demand was or what the prices would be—he never bothered to find out. Seizing this opportunity, Banchharam and Thakchacha swooped down like kites, and soon...

Their bellies grew fat—nothing could quench their thirst with little—they ate day and night. Today, “Let’s eat the elephant’s fodder from the elephant stable,” tomorrow, “Let’s eat the horse’s feed from the horse stable”—the two of them would sit together in secret, plotting such schemes. They knew very well that such days would not last for them—the spring of profit was setting, and the autumn of loss would soon dawn. Therefore, they thought, “Let’s not waste a single moment.”

Within a year or two, terrible news came about the sale of their goods—there was loss in everything, not a penny of profit to be found. Mr. John saw that the losses would amount to nearly a hundred thousand rupees—this news struck him like a blow to the chest, and he stood frozen in shock. Besides, he himself had been spending nearly a thousand rupees a month, and on top of that, there were many debts at the bank and with moneylenders. For several months, the office had been running on borrowed time and borrowed money, but now, the boat of outward respectability sank with a resounding splash. Word spread that John’s company had failed. The sahib, taking his wife with him, departed for Chandannagar. That city was under the French—even now, debtors and accused in criminal cases flee there to escape the reach of the law.

Meanwhile, the moneylenders and other creditors surrounded Motilal. Motilal looked around and saw emptiness on all sides—not a single paisa in hand—he was surviving on advances from the pawn-brokers, but now, what could he say or do? He had no idea. Every so often, he craned his neck to see if Bansharam Babu or Uncle Thakchacha might appear, but trusting in his elder brother was like holding a knife to his own side—those two incarnations of trickery had already fled at the first sign of trouble. When their names were mentioned, the creditors said, “The papers are all in Motibabu’s name; we have no dealings with those two—they were only clerks, nothing more.”

With such chaos, Motilal, along with his followers, fled in disguise at night to Baidyabati. Hearing the seven volumes of his misdeeds, the people there clapped their hands and said, “Well done!” and added, “It’s still going on, day and night—the man who was so wicked as to cheat his own mother, brother, and sister—who never ceased his sinful ways—if this isn’t his just reward, then what is the meaning of virtue and vice?”
Meanwhile, the next day, Premnarayan Majumdar was bathing at the ghat in Baidyabati—

chapters.title: The Forger’s Downfall
paragraphs: Seeing Tarkasiddhanta, someone said, “Sir, have you heard? The Bitlals, having lost everything, have come running back here out of fear of the warrant—yet they show no shame in displaying their faces! Baburam left behind a fine pestle for the destruction of the family line.” Tarkasiddhanta replied, “The village had cooled down in the absence of those rascals—have they come back again? Ah, Mother Ganga, if only you would show a little mercy, we might yet be saved.”

Many other Brahmins were bathing; upon hearing the news of the return of the young babus, their teeth began to chatter. They thought to themselves, “It seems we shall have to offer today’s bath and daily rites to Srikrishna himself.” The shopkeepers and merchants, glancing toward the ghat, said, “Well! We’d heard that Moti Babu would return with all his wealth, beating the drums in triumph—now, never mind the wealth, we can’t even spot a single fisherman’s dinghy.” Premnarayan said, “Don’t be anxious—Moti Babu, owing to the troubles of Kamala and Kamini, has ended up in the southern cremation ground. The Babu is a man of great piety—a blessed son of the Goddess. Soon you’ll see dinghies, wealth, and ships, and while you’re still frying puffed rice and lentils, you’ll hear the sound of the drums.”
The matter of a pure heart, Thakchacha’s forged warrant, Barda Babu’s sorrow, Motilal’s fear; the meeting and conversation of Becharam and Banchharam.

A foul morning breeze was blowing—the fragrances of champak, shefali, and jasmine wafted through the air. The birds were chirping, their eyes bright with excitement. Because of the matchmaker, Benibabu was deep in conversation with Barda Babu at home. From the south, a pack of dogs began barking, and the street boys came running, shouting “ho ho!” When the commotion eased a little, the shrill voices of “Go away!” and “Don’t go to the Gopis’ house, I warn you!” floated to their ears in a wave of comic delight.

Benibabu and Barda Babu got up and saw that Becharam Babu of Bahubazar was approaching—lost in song, whistling continuously. The dogs were barking, the boys were shouting, and the residents of Bahubazar, annoyed, were shooing them away. As Becharam drew near, Benibabu and Barda Babu rose and respectfully welcomed him, offering him a seat. After exchanging pleasantries, Becharam Babu placed his hand on Barda Babu’s shoulder and said, “Brother!” From childhood, I have seen many kinds of people—indeed, many of them possess many virtues. But whether I call them good or bad, with their faults and merits, that is another matter. Yet, such humility, simplicity, courage in matters of faith, and pure-heartedness towards others as you possess—I have not seen in anyone else. I myself try to walk humbly, it is true, but at times, when I see the pride of others, my own pride is roused—and as soon as pride arises, anger follows, and in anger, my pride swells all the more. I spare no one—whatever comes to mind, I say it then and there. But in my own faults, I am not so simple—I do not wish to confess my misdeeds openly; I feel that if I admit them, I will be diminished in the eyes of others. In matters of faith, my courage is very little—though I know well in my heart what ought to be done, I lack the courage to always act according to my convictions. To keep a pure heart towards others is most difficult—I know well that, having taken human birth, one should always strive for the good of others, never for their harm, but to put this into practice is most arduous. If someone utters even a harsh word, my heart turns away from them—I immediately see them as a thoroughly bad person. But even if someone wrongs you, your heart remains pure towards them—in other words, you never turn away from doing them good, even if they do you harm. And if someone slanders you, you are not disturbed by it—is that not a rare virtue?

Borda: One sees only good in those one loves, and only faults in those one cannot bear to see. What you have said is all kindness—these are the words of your affection, not of my own merit. To keep one’s heart pure at all times, in all matters, towards all people—this is nearly impossible for a human being. Our hearts are filled with anger, envy, jealousy, and pride—can these be restrained so easily? To purify the heart, humility is essential—but often, one sees only false humility in people. Some are humble out of fear, some out of distress or misfortune—that sort of humility is fleeting. For humility to endure, we must have this firm conviction in our minds: He who is the Creator alone is great—He alone is wise—He alone is pure and faultless; we are here today, gone tomorrow—what strength or wisdom do we possess? If our errors, bad judgments, and misdeeds are punished, then what cause have we for pride? Such humility...

When anger, envy, malice, and pride are diminished in the mind, then one’s heart becomes pure towards others—then one no longer wishes to flaunt one’s learning, intelligence, wealth, or position to irritate others—then the sight of another’s prosperity no longer breeds jealousy—then one feels no urge to slander or think ill of others—then, even if wronged by someone, anger or resentment does not arise—then the mind is absorbed only in self-purification and the welfare of others. But to reach such a state is difficult without long practice. Nowadays, even a little knowledge gives rise to foreign conceit: “What I say—what I do—is the best; what others say or do is worthless.”
Becharam: Brother! Hearing these words soothes my soul—I always wish to converse with you.

As this conversation was going on, Premnarayan Majumdar came hurrying in with news that the Calcutta police were arresting Thakchacha on account of a forged promissory note case. Upon hearing this, Becharam Babu exclaimed, “Serves him right!” and was overjoyed. Borda Babu fell silent and began to ponder.
Becharam: Why are you still thinking? When such a wicked man is sent to jail, the country breathes easier.
Borda: The sorrow is that the man, for all his life, has done nothing but evil deeds—if he is imprisoned now, his family will starve to death.

Becharam: Brother! If you weren’t so virtuous, why would people revere you? Thakchacha never missed a chance to harm or slander you—he constantly maligned and insulted you—he even filed false murder charges against you—he made special efforts to forge that promissory note—yet you harbor not a trace of anger or resentment towards him, nor do you know what revenge means. If, in seeking revenge, the man or his family fell ill, you would be the first to bring medicine and nurse them back to health. Even now, you are worrying about his family—brother! You may be a Kayastha by birth, but I would gladly take the dust of such a Kayastha’s feet and place it on my head.

Borda: Sir! Please do not praise me so much—among the people, I am but a very... Lowly and insignificant am I. I am not worthy of your praise, sir—if you keep repeating such words, my pride may steadily swell.

Meanwhile, at Baidyabati, the police sergeant, constables, and the daroga had tied Thakchacha’s hands behind his back and were dragging him along, shouting, “Move! Move!” as they hauled him away. The street was crowded with onlookers—some said, “As you sow, so you reap”; others muttered, “I won’t believe it till the rascal boards the ship”; yet others whispered, “I fear he might turn out to be a snake in the grass.” Thakchacha walked with his head hung low—his beard fluttered in the wind, his eyes glared fiercely—he tried to slip the sergeant a coin to loosen his bonds, but the sergeant, with his big belly, simply pocketed the coin without a second thought. Thakchacha pleaded, “Take me once to Motibabu—bring him my letter and set me free—then I’ll appear in court myself.” The sergeant replied, “You talk too much—say another word and I’ll slap you.” At this, Thakchacha joined his hands and began to beg and plead. The sergeant paid no heed, bundled Thakchacha onto a boat, and after two prahars and four hours, delivered him to the police station—only to find the officers had already left for the day, so Thakchacha had to spend the night wandering in the Benigarden lock-up.

On the other side, hearing of Thakchacha’s misfortune, Motilal’s heart skipped a beat. He feared that this thunderbolt might soon strike him as well—if the trickster has been caught, surely I’ll be next, there’s no doubt. Perhaps the Company itself has gotten wind of the affair—whatever the case, it’s best to be cautious. Resolving thus, Motilal shut the main gate of the house tight. Ramgovinda said, “Badebabu! Thakchacha has been arrested for fraud—if there were a warrant for you, the house would have been surrounded long ago. Why are you so afraid for nothing?” Motilal replied, “You don’t understand! In bad times, even a roasted fish can slip from your grasp. If I can just get through today, tomorrow at dawn I’ll depart for my estate in Jessore. I can’t stay in this house any longer—so many troubles, so many obstacles, so many fears, so many nuisances—and now my purse is empty.” No sooner had he finished speaking than there came a sharp knock at the door—“Open up! Who’s there?” voices called out. Motilal whispered, “Quiet—just as I feared, it’s happening.” Managobinda peered down from above and saw—

A peon was pushing at the door—just then, Tipu rushed in and said, “Boro Babu! Leave at once, perhaps an old warrant has come up because of Thakchacha—sparks from the fire are still flying. If you can’t find a quiet place, then do as Duryodhan did in the pond by the back gate—hide under water, only your nose above the surface.” Dolgovinda said, “Why are you panicking just seeing the waves? First, try to understand what’s going on. Let me ask—well, Mr. Peon! Which court have you come from?” The peon replied, “I’ve brought a letter from Jan Sahib—here, take the letter,” and with a flourish, tossed it up onto the table. “Thank heavens! I’m saved! Now I can breathe again,” everyone exclaimed in relief.

Immediately, from the back, Haladhar and Gadadhar began chanting, “Bhobe tran karo!”—Save us, Lord! The young gentlemen were like autumn clouds—now rain, now sun, now heat, now joy. Motilal said, “Hold on, let me read the letter—maybe we’ll get another chance to get back to business.” As Motilal opened the letter, all the young men crowded around—many heads together, but not a single one could decipher the inked words; reading the letter became quite an ordeal. After a long while, someone fetched a man from the nearby De family’s house, and from him they finally learned the gist: Jan Sahib was nearly starving—he desperately needed money.

Mangobinda said, “That scoundrel! So much money was wasted on him, and still he’s not satisfied—now he dares ask for more?” Dolgovinda said, “It’s best to keep the English on your side—their luck is strange; sometimes you dig up dirt and find gold.” Motilal said, “Why are you all grumbling? Even if you cut me, there’s no blood; even if you twist me, there’s no flesh.”

Just then, from the direction of Bali, Becharam Babu was passing by in the evening in a rattling hackney carriage, singing at the top of his voice, “That ash-smeared hair, Everywhere you look, in every pot and pan, All the knots are tangled there.” He was heading north, while from the south, Banchharam was driving his buggy at full speed. Both were dressed in their finest, so each mistook the other for someone important and craned their necks to get a better look. The moment Banchharam caught sight of Becharam’s silhouette, he lashed his horse furiously. Becharam, in turn, quickly grabbed the side of his carriage, stuck his head out, and shouted, “Hey Banchharam! Hey Banchharam!” at the top of his lungs. With all this shouting and commotion, the buggy came to a halt and the hackney carriage rattled up close. Becharam Babu called out, “Banchharam! You—”

chapters.title: The Indigo Dispute
paragraphs: Fate has marked you as a man—your skull of fortune blazes like Ravana’s ten heads. Once, you managed to ruin the merchant business in a single sweep—now your dear Uncle Thak is off again. Who knows, perhaps he’ll manage to cook up another mess, only this time with some lawyer’s trickery, and drag you straight to ruin. Did it never cross your mind that, in the end, you’ll have to die? Bancharam, thoroughly exasperated, pursed his lips, twisted his moustache into a knot, and, to vent his irritation, gave his horse a sharp prod and rode off at a gallop.
25. Motilal sets off for the Jessore estate with his retinue— Description of estate management; clash with the indigo planter and the planter’s acquittal in court.

Of all Baburam Babu’s properties, the Jessore estate was the most coveted. During the ten-year settlement, much of that estate lay fallow—the revenue was uncertain, the land mostly uncultivated. Later, as those lands were reclaimed, they were distributed by the bigha, and soon the estate was in such fine shape that hardly a single katha remained uncultivated or fallow. For a few years, the tenants worked the land diligently, and with the bounty of their harvests, they managed to make ends meet. But, following Uncle Thak’s advice, when pressure was brought to bear on many tenants, they began to lose heart. With so many revenue-free landholders’ plots being confiscated, and as they had no formal deeds, they merely came and went, offered their respects and little gifts, and eventually slipped away for good. Many smallholders, battered by fraud and oppression, relinquished their rights to their land for nothing, fleeing to seek better fortune under another’s authority.

Because of this, though the estate’s income rose for a year or two, Uncle Thak would swagger about, twirling his moustache, and boast to Baburam Babu, “See what a fine steward I am!” But “the ways of justice are subtle indeed”—before long, many tenants, gripped by fear, packed up their cattle and seed and departed. Their lands became a burden to distribute; everyone began to worry: “We’ll toil away, break our backs farming, and if we manage to make a couple of rupees, the landlord will swallow it up by force or trickery—so what’s the point of holding on to these rights?” Even the estate manager, for all his coaxing, could not persuade the tenants to stay. Much land remained unclaimed—no one would take it, not even at a reduced rent, and after deducting expenses, it was impossible to collect the revenue. The manager was constantly...
