They would send word to the landlord, and the landlord Sudamat would write a stern letter: “If the revenue is not collected, you will lose your bread—no excuses will be entertained.” Sometimes, a timely scolding, given with discernment, gets the work done. But where trouble is not subject to threats, what use is a scolding? The manager, caught in a fix, began to run things in a haphazard, makeshift manner. Meanwhile, as two or three years’ revenue from the estate fell into arrears, the whole property was mortgaged. To save the situation, Baburam Babu would write bonds and take loans to pay the government’s revenue on time.

Now, Motilal arrived at the estate with his entire entourage and took up residence. His intention was to squeeze money out of the estate, pay off the debts, and restore the old grandeur. But Babu had never so much as glanced at the estate’s papers; he had no idea what a letter was, what a “goswara” meant, or what “jamawasil baki” referred to. The manager would say, “Sir! Please have a look at the files.” But instead of casting his eyes on the piles of papers, Babu would gaze out at the creepers and foliage around the office courtyard.

The manager would say, “Sir! At present, the ‘khodkasta’ tenants are so many, and the ‘paikasta’ so many.” Babu would reply, “I don’t want to hear about ‘khodkasta’ or ‘paikasta’—I’ll make everyone ‘ek-kasta’ (all the same)!”

News spread that the eldest Babu had arrived at the estate office, and all the tenants came rushing in, thinking, “That wretched fellow has finally come—perhaps after all these years, our luck will turn.” So, with delighted hearts and smiling faces, the rough-haired, skinny-bellied, and sunken-cheeked tenants came near, offering their greetings with “Robdhan” and “Salaam.”

Motilal, with a jingling sound, fell silent and grinned broadly. Seeing the Babu in good spirits, the tenants began to pour out their complaints. One said, “So-and-so broke the boundary of my land and ploughed it.” Another said, “So-and-so tied a pot to my date palm and stole the sap.” Another, “So-and-so let his cows loose in my garden and ruined everything.” Yet another, “So-and-so’s ducks ate my paddy.” Someone said, “I haven’t received my title deed in three years.” Another, “I’ve paid the assessment money, please return my deed.” Someone else, “Let me cut down the babla tree and sell it to repair my house—please grant me a remission.” Another said, “My land transfer hasn’t been recorded, so I can’t pay the greeting fee.” Yet another, “The survey has reduced the area of my joint land—my revenue assessment for the season…”

If not, then at least try to investigate. Motilal, understanding not a jot or tittle of all these matters, sat there like a painted doll. The companion babus, picking up a word or two, made jokes and laughed, filling the office hall with their merriment. In the midst of it all, someone began to sing, “The bird flies away, flapping its wings.” The manager sat as stiff as wood, while the tenants, hands on their heads, slumped to the ground in despair.

Where the master is sharp, the servants’ tricks do not go far. Seeing Motilal’s utter ignorance, the manager gradually revealed his true colors. Many cases were brought forth, but the babu could not make head or tail of any of them. The manager threw dust in his eyes and fulfilled his own desires, while the tenants realized that appealing to the babu was as futile as crying in the wilderness—the manager was the all-powerful lord!

In Jessore, the indigo planters’ oppression had greatly increased. The tenants were unwilling to grow indigo, for rice and other crops brought more profit. And once a man went to the indigo factory and took an advance, his fate was sealed. The tenants would struggle desperately to cultivate indigo and repay the advance, but the account’s plough only deepened year after year, and the bellies of the factory’s overseers and other officials were not easily filled. Thus, a tenant who once tasted the nectar of the indigo planter’s advance would never again willingly approach the factory, but if indigo was not produced, there would be grave trouble. Every year, loans were taken from some Calcutta merchant’s factory; if indigo was not produced now, the debt would increase, and later the factory itself might have to close. The other Englishmen who managed the factories were of little consequence back in England, but here they strutted about like princes—if the factory’s business was disrupted, they feared they might be reduced to mere rats again. For this reason, they took every care, in every way, at all times, to ensure indigo was produced.

Motilal, with his companions, was making a great commotion—the manager, spectacles perched on his nose, sat at his desk writing and chewing betel. At that moment, a few tenants came running, shouting, “Sir! That factory scoundrel has ruined us! The wretch himself has come to our fields and is ploughing up our sown land, and has seized all our ploughs and oxen—Sir! What is this rascal doing—” He ruined the whole crop. The scoundrel ran a harrow through our ripened paddy. The estate manager, hearing the commotion, quickly gathered a hundred or so farmhands and rushed to the spot, only to find the indigo planter’s overseer standing there—on his head a pith helmet, a cigar clamped between his lips, a gun in hand—shouting orders. The manager approached and tried to reason with him, but the overseer barked back, “Drive them out! Beat them!” At once, men from both sides began swinging their sticks. The overseer himself charged forward, almost ready to fire his gun. The manager slipped away and hid behind a bamboo fence. After a brief spell of stick-fighting and brawling, the landlord’s men fled, a few of them wounded. The overseer, puffed up with his own strength, swaggered back to the indigo factory, while the battered tenants ran home crying, “What a disaster! What a disaster!”

The indigo sahib, after stirring up the trouble, returned to his bungalow, popped open a bottle of foreign soda, mixed it with brandy, and began to sing “Taza Bataza” at the top of his lungs—his dog running and playing before him. He knew well enough that bringing him to heel would be no easy task; the magistrate and the judge were frequent guests at his table, and with such close company, the police and court officials treated him like the god of death himself. Even if there was an inquiry, he would never be tried for murder or any serious crime in a district court. If a black man killed someone or committed a grave offense, he’d be tried and sentenced at once in the local courts. But if a white man did the same, the case would be sent to the Supreme Court, where witnesses and plaintiffs, worn out by expense, trouble, and wasted time, would be forced to give up, and so, even in the higher courts, such men would slip through the cracks.

And just as the indigo planter had expected, so it happened. The next morning, the police inspector arrived and surrounded the landlord’s office. Weakness is a terrible curse—no one dares stand up to the strong. Motilal, seeing the situation, retreated into his house and bolted the door. The manager came forward, struck a hasty bargain, and managed to get many of the captives released. The inspector was making quite a racket, but as soon as he got his bribe, it was as if water had been thrown on a fire. Afterwards, he filed a report to the magistrate, carefully covering both sides—greed on one hand, fear on the other. The indigo planter busied himself with all sorts of arrangements, and the magistrate became ever more convinced that the indigo planter, being an Englishman and a Christian, could never do anything wrong.

chapters.title: The Prison
paragraphs: Only the dark-skinned folk commit all sorts of misdeeds. Meanwhile, the serestadar and the peskar, having taken extra bribes from the indigo planter, began to suppress the depositions of the opposing party and read out only those statements that favored their own side, gradually twisting and turning the needle as they pleased. At this juncture, the indigo planter began his speech: "I have come to this place and am doing all manner of good for the Bengalis—I am spending especially for their education and medicine—and yet, such accusations against me? Bengalis are terribly treacherous and quarrelsome." The magistrate, hearing all this, went off for his tiffin. After tiffin, having drunk copiously and smoked a cheroot, he returned to court. When the case was presented, the sahib, glancing at the papers as if they were a tiger, said to the serestadar, "Dismiss this case at once." At this order, the indigo planter's face puffed up in indignation, and he began to glare venomously at the naib. The naib, with downcast face, scratching his chin and shaking his belly, began to mutter, "It's become a burden to keep zamindari among Bengalis—the indigo planters' oppression has turned the land into a desert—the tenants are crying out in terror." The magistrates, at the request of their own kind, become subservient to them, and the way the law is twisted, there is always a sure escape route for the indigo planters. People say that the zamindar's tyranny is killing the tenants—that is a great mistake. The zamindars do oppress, true, but they do so while keeping the tenants alive, for the tenant is the zamindar’s eggplant field. The indigo planter is not like that—whether the tenant lives or dies matters little to him—as long as the cultivation of indigo increases, all is well—the tenant is merely the indigo planter’s true radish patch.

Thakchacha, in the Benigarden lock-up, reveals his own secrets in his sleep— Encounters with Banchharam and Batlay in the police station, The case is sent to the higher court, Thakchacha is imprisoned, His conversations with other prisoners in jail, And the theft of his food.

When fear and worry enter the mind, sleep does not come. Thakchacha grew exceedingly restless in the Benigarden lock-up, tossing and turning on a single blanket. He got up once or twice to check how much of the night remained. At the sound of a carriage or a human voice, he would think, "Perhaps it is dawn at last." Once or twice...

With a start, Bar sat up and asked the sepoys, “Brother! What time is it now?” Annoyed, they replied, “Arre, there are still two or three hours left before the cannon fires. Go back to sleep—why do you keep checking the time?” Hearing this, Thakchacha rolled about on his blanket. His mind was a whirlpool of thoughts—so many ideas, so many schemes, so many ways out. Sometimes he wondered, Why did I spend my whole life chasing after gambling and trickery? Where has all that money gone that I earned through such means? Sinful money never stays in hand; I see now, whenever I did wrong, I could never sleep at night, always afraid of being caught—if a leaf rustled, I’d think someone was coming to arrest me. My old friend Khodabux always warned me not to live such a deceitful life—he used to say it’s better to farm, to run a business, or to work an honest job; if you walk the straight path, there’s nothing to fear—both body and mind remain at peace. That’s how Khodabux lives happily to this day. Alas! Why didn’t I listen to him?

At other times, he wondered how he could escape the present danger. I must hire a lawyer or a counsel—without proof, I can’t be convicted—how will it ever come out where the forgery happened and who did it? How will it be revealed? Tossing and turning with such thoughts, dawn finally broke. Exhausted, Thakchacha fell asleep, and in his slumber, he began to dream about his own case—half-asleep, he started mumbling, “Careful! No one must see the paper, the pen, or the ink—they’re under the floor of the house in Sealdah—it’s safe, it’s safe—don’t you dare touch it—you must hurry to Faridpur—as soon as I’m free, I’ll meet you seven times.”

Morning had come—the sun’s rays glimmered on Thakchacha’s beard. The jailer of the Beniagarh lockup stood nearby, listening to all this, and shouted, “Scoundrel! Still lying there—get up! You’ve confessed everything yourself!” Thakchacha immediately sprang up, rubbing his eyes, nose, and beard, and began to mutter prayers on his rosary. He glanced slyly at the jailer, then closed his eyes for a moment. The jailer frowned and said, “So, you cover yourself with the cloak of religion, but your faith and your forgeries in Sealdah’s basement—your true colors will soon be revealed!”
At these words, Thakchacha began to tremble like a banana tree and said—

Oh, my! Mary Baiko has become very bold these days. That’s why I always keep my eyes open—I’m no fool. “Alright, you’ll understand everything in time—now get ready,” saying this, the orderly marched off.

Meanwhile, as the clock struck ten with a resounding *dong dong*, the police brought Thakchacha and the other accused before the authorities. Before nine had even struck, Banchharam Babu had been wandering about with Butler Sahib, circling the police station, all the while thinking to himself—If I can save Thakchacha this time, I’ll be able to get a lot of work out of him. The man is quite capable—he can speak, write, read, go here and there, handle affairs, lawsuits, and schemes—he’s good at everything. But this is my profession—if I don’t get paid, nothing gets done. I can’t go chasing wild buffalo while starving at home, and if I’ve sat down to dance, why should I keep my veil on? Thakchacha has taken advantage of many people, so what’s wrong if I take advantage of him? But eating crow’s meat requires a lot of cunning.

Butler Sahib, noticing Banchharam’s absent-mindedness, asked, “Bensa! What are you thinking about?” Banchharam replied, “Roso Sahib! I’m thinking about how money can find its way into my house.” Butler Sahib, walking a little ahead, said, “Acha—very good, very good.”

The moment Banchharam saw Thakchacha, he rushed over, grabbed his hand, and, squeezing his eyes as if about to cry, exclaimed, “What’s this! I heard the bad news yesterday and spent the whole night sitting up—I didn’t close my eyes even once. At the crack of dawn, I rushed through my prayers and rituals, picked flowers in a hurry, and came here with the Sahib. What’s there to fear? Is this a child’s game? A man faces ten kinds of trouble, and it’s only the big trees that catch the storm. But unless there’s an installment of money, nothing can be done—if not, perhaps Thakchachi could send a heavy piece of jewelry or two, and the work could proceed. For now, you’re safe, and later we’ll sort out the jewelry and all that.”

It’s hard to think clearly in times of trouble. Thakchacha immediately wrote a letter to his wife. Taking the letter, Banchharam glanced at Butler Sahib, winked, and smiled slightly. He handed the letter to a government servant and said, “You, hurry off to Baidyabati, get some heavy jewelry from Thakchachi, and bring it here or to the office for me to see. Make sure you’re very careful with the jewelry—don’t delay. Go and come back quickly—as if you never left.” The servant...

Annoyed, he said, “Sir! Is it just a matter of words, that you say it and it happens? Where is Calcutta—where is Baidyabati—and where is Thakchachi? I’ll have to wander around in the dark, haven’t even had a morsel to eat, let alone a full meal, nor have I poured a single jug of water on my head—how can I possibly return today?”

At this, Bancharam flared up and thundered, “These lowly folk are all the same, always independent—never listen to reason, unless you chase them with a broom, they won’t be subdued. People are searching all the way to Delhi, and you can’t even go to Baidyabati and settle a simple matter? If you’re so slow, I’ll have to point it out to you with my finger in your eye, and still you won’t understand?”

The servant, head bowed, said nothing—neither ‘Ram’ nor ‘Ganga’—just trudged along like a beaten horse, muttering to himself, “What is honor or dishonor to a poor man? For the sake of the stomach, everything must be endured. But when will the day come when this gentleman falls into a trap like Thakchacha? I’ve seen him put the knife to many a man’s throat—seen him strip many people of their land and home—seen him turn many a homestead into a haunt for crows and vultures. Oh father! I’ve seen many a clever lawyer, but none can match him. He fries pointed gourd but calls it ridge gourd; where a needle won’t go, he’ll send in a pestle. And then there’s the daily worship, the Dol and Durga festivals, the feasts for Brahmins, and all the religious observances. Such a Hindu, yet ashes on his face—the beginning and end, a scoundrel and a rogue!”
Here sat Thakchacha, Bancharam, and Butler, waiting; the case was not being called. The more time passed, the more their anxiety grew. It was five o’clock.

Just then, Thakchacha was brought before the magistrate. Arriving there, he saw that the pump used for drawing water from the Sealdah pond, along with a couple of the local workers, had been brought in as evidence. After the hearing, the magistrate ordered that the case be sent to the higher court, bail could not be granted, and so the accused must remain in the main jail.

No sooner had the magistrate given his order than Bancharam rushed forward, waving his hands, and declared, “What’s there to fear? Is this child’s play? It’s well known the case will go to the higher court—that’s what we want too!”
Thakchacha’s face shriveled with worry. The constables grabbed him by the hand, dragged him down, and sent him off to jail. Chacha walked off with a clatter, not a word on his lips—
He does not even raise his eyes to look, lest he meets someone—lest someone mocks him. Evening has fallen; at such a time, Thakchacha set foot in the prison.

In the big jail, those imprisoned for debt or civil cases are kept on one side, and those held for criminal cases are kept on the other. If the trial of these prisoners is concluded, they either serve their sentence there, or are sent to the harem, or to the dry cell, or else are shackled or hanged.

Thakchacha had to stay in the criminal ward. As soon as he entered, all the prisoners gathered around and sat encircling him. Thakchacha looked at them with a scowl—he could not spot a single acquaintance. The prisoners said, “Munshi-ji! Look here! Your fate is the same as ours now, so come, let’s all hang together.”

Thakchacha replied, “Ah, brothers! I have fallen into trouble for nothing—I neither eat nor touch anything, it’s just the twist of my fate.” A couple of old prisoners said, “Yes, indeed. Many get trapped by false charges.” But one brash prisoner piped up, “So your charge is false and ours are true, is that it? Hah! Are you a moneylender or Sarfaraz? Hey, brothers, be careful—this fellow is a sly one.”

At once, Thakchacha softened and made himself small, but they kept arguing over that remark for quite some time. Such is people’s nature—when there’s nothing else to do, they grab hold of some thread and make a ruckus out of idle talk.

The jail was locked up on all sides. The prisoners, having eaten, were preparing to sleep. Meanwhile, Thakchacha sat at one end, unwrapping some sweets tied up in a cloth, and was just about to put one in his mouth when, from behind, two mixed-race prisoners—mustache, hair, and eyebrows white, eyes red—burst out in a hideous laugh, “Ha ha ha!” They snatched the packet of sweets from his hand in a flash, waved it before him, and popped the sweets into their mouths one after another.

In the midst of chewing, they brought their faces close to Thakchacha’s and laughed, “Hee hee!” Thakchacha was utterly dumbfounded—quietly, he slunk over to his mat and lay down with a sigh, like a man who’s been struck and then robbed of the very blow.

chapters.title: The Great Trial
paragraphs: Banchharam’s Scurrying About, The Trial and Punishment of Thakchacha and Bahulya.

The paddy harvest had begun in Badar, the sickles were swinging—water everywhere, with makeshift platforms set up in the midst of it all. Yet the tenants found no respite—on one side the moneylender, on the other the landlord’s peons. If the harvest was good, they might manage two handfuls of rice, twice a day; if not, then fish, greens, and the hope of a day’s wage would have to suffice. In the lowlands, only the autumn rice was sown—most of the early crop grew in the marshes. True, Bengal’s soil yielded grain with ease, but blight, drought, pests, crabs, and the storms of Kartik often ruined the harvest; and then there was the paddy’s own blight—without careful tending, it could be lost to disease.

One morning, Bahulya, having inspected his own fields, sat on the veranda of his house, puffing on his hookah. Before him lay a pile of papers, and nearby sat two or three wretched tenants and some court officials. The talk was all of the magistrate’s law and lawsuits—someone was preparing a new document, another was coaching witnesses, yet another was opening the cash box and, in hopes of favor, showering Bahulya with all manner of flattery. Bahulya, meanwhile, seemed somewhat distracted—his gaze wandered here and there. Now and then he would bark out an idle order to his farmhands: “Hey, lift that gourd vine onto the trellis, spread those bundles of straw out in the sun.” At other times, he would glance around with a look of deep suspicion.

A man sitting nearby asked, “Maulvi Sahib! I’ve heard some bad news about Thakchacha—is there any trouble brewing?” Bahulya, unwilling to break his silence, stroked his beard, raised his hand, and replied with great sagacity, “Calamity dogs the heels of men—what use is it to fear?” Another chimed in, “That’s all very well, but that fellow is a sly one—he’ll wriggle out of trouble by his own wits.” Be that as it may, if no blame falls on you, we’ll be saved—here in this marshy Bhabanipur, you’re all we have left, our only hope and resource. Whether it’s strength or cunning, it’s all in you. If you weren’t here, we’d have had to pack up and leave long ago. By good fortune, you made me a few talismans, and since then I’ve managed to keep that landlord’s brat in check—he hasn’t dared trouble me since.

No—he knows very well that you are in my clutches. Bahulya, in his excessive delight, took a deep drag from his hookah, exhaled a cloud of smoke through his mouth, and let out a faint smile. Another man said, “If you want to take charge of land and property in the mofussil, there are two ways to keep the zamindars and indigo planters in check—first, seek the protection of someone like Maulvi Saheb; second, become a Christian. I have seen many tenants roam about like Gokul’s bull, invoking the name of the padre! Whether it’s for money or for influence, or for recommendations, the padre sahib always protects his ‘brothers.’ Not every tenant who joins the padre’s congregation does so with true faith, but whoever goes there certainly reaps many benefits. In lawsuits and disputes, the padre’s letter is a powerful tool.”

Bahulya replied, “That’s true—but a man loses his own days in the process, and that’s a great misfortune.” At once, everyone chimed in, “That’s right, that’s right; that’s exactly why we don’t go to the padre.”

As this light-hearted conversation was going on, suddenly the daroga, a few jamadars, and a police sergeant burst in, grabbed Bahulya by the hand, and said, “You rascal, you’ve committed seven frauds—there’s a warrant for your arrest!”

The moment they heard this, everyone nearby took fright and scattered in all directions. Bahulya tried to tempt the daroga and the sergeant with bribes, but they, fearing for their jobs, paid him no heed and dragged him away.

When this news reached Denga Bhabanipur, a crowd gathered, and the respectable folk began to say, “Punishment for wicked deeds will come, sooner or later. If a man could sin and live happily ever after, then creation itself would be a lie—such a thing can never be.”

Bahulya walked on with his head bowed—he was meeting many people along the way, but he looked at none of them. A couple of fellows, who had once or twice suffered at his hands, now emboldened by the situation, came up to him and said, “Maulvi Saheb, what’s this—are you in some kind of Vrindavan trance? Or have you gotten yourself into some serious trouble?”

Bahulya replied, “No, Ram, no Ganga, nothing at all,” and, crossing the Bansdroni ghat, arrived at Shaganj. There, a couple of Tipu-descended princelings, seeing him, said, “So, you’ve been arrested? Good! It’s much better when scoundrels like you are punished.”

All these words fell upon Bahulya like a blow upon a corpse. Humiliated beyond measure, he reached Bhabanipur—when, from a little distance, he noticed a group of people gathered on the left side of the road...

A crowd had gathered, standing in a circle. Approaching, Sarjan Bahulya stood nearby and asked, “Why are there so many people here?” Then, pushing through the throng, he entered the circle and saw a gentleman sitting with an injured man cradled in his lap—the wounded man’s head was bleeding profusely, the blood soaking the gentleman’s clothes.

Sarjan asked, “Who are you, and how did this man get hurt?” The gentleman replied, “My name is Bardaprasad Biswas. I had come here on some business, and by chance, this man was run over by a carriage and injured. That is why I am sitting here, supporting him. I am trying to arrange to take him to the hospital quickly—I had sent for a palanquin, but the bearers refuse to carry him, as this man is a ‘Hadi’ by caste. I do have a carriage with me, but the man is unable to climb into it. If I could get a palanquin or a duli, I am ready to pay whatever fare is needed.”

Such is the virtue of honesty that even the basest heart is moved by it. Witnessing Bardababu’s conduct, Bahulya was filled with amazement and began to reproach himself inwardly. Sarjan said, “Babu, Bengalis do not touch a Hadi. For a Bengali to go so far is no small matter. You must be a most extraordinary person.” Saying this, he left the injured man in the care of a constable, went to the police outpost, and, after some persuasion, managed to bring a palanquin. He then sent the Hadi to the hospital with Bardababu.

Previously, criminal cases in the higher courts were held once every two or three months; now, they occur somewhat more frequently. To dispose of criminal cases, two types of juries are formed there. First, the Grand Jury—who consider whether the police charges and other indictments are fit for trial, and inform the court accordingly. Second, the Petit Jury, who, based on the Grand Jury’s decision, try the case with the judge and declare the accused guilty or innocent.

In each session, that is, in the criminal court, fourteen people serve on the Grand Jury. Only those with property worth two lakhs of rupees, or those engaged in mercantile business, may serve on the Grand Jury. The Petit Jury is formed almost every day in session. When their names are called, the accused or the complainant may object at their discretion—that is, if they suspect anyone, they may have him replaced by another.

But once twelve petty jurors have sworn in, there’s no changing them. On the first day of the Sessions, three judges preside; when it’s a particular judge’s turn, he explains the charges—that is, the details of the cases for the session—to the grand jury. After the charge is given, the other two judges, whose turn it is not, leave, and the grand jurors retire to a chamber, where they write “true” or “not true” on each indictment according to their own judgment, and send them back. Only then does the trial begin.

Night is nearly over—a gentle breeze is blowing; in this cool and pleasant hour, Thakchacha is sleeping with his mouth wide open, snoring through his nose. The other prisoners have risen, some are smoking tobacco, and some, hearing that noise, are saying, “Eat burnt rice, man!” But Thakchacha, like Kumbhakarna, continues to sleep—“Hearing the thunder of his nose, the heart trembles.” After a while, the jailer arrives and tells the prisoners, “Get ready quickly, today everyone must go to court.”

Meanwhile, as soon as the Sessions open, within ten hours the grand veranda of the main court is packed with people—lawyers, counsels, plaintiffs, accused, witnesses, lawyers’ clerks, jurors, surgeons, orderlies, peons—a crowd of all sorts, bustling and jostling. Banchharam is walking about with the butler sahib, and whenever he spots a wealthy man, whether he knows him or not, he raises his hand to give a Brahmin’s blessing, just to show off his own status. But those who know him well are not fooled by his manners—after exchanging a word or two, they manage to escape from his hand before he can ask for some false favor.

Look, the prison cart has arrived—soldiers in front and behind, and as soon as the cart halts, everyone on the veranda leans forward to watch. The prisoners are taken from the cart and placed inside the dock in the room below the court. Banchharam hurries down, meets Thakchacha and Bahulya with great affection, and says, “You two are Bhima and Arjuna—don’t be afraid—is this something to be scared of, like a child’s slap?”

Within two hours, the center of the veranda is cleared—people stand to either side—the court peons begin to hush the crowd—“Quiet, quiet!”—everyone is craning their necks, for the judges are arriving. At that moment, the surgeon, peons, and orderlies appear, bearing maces, spears, ceremonial staffs, swords, and the silver-plated, crown-shaped insignia of the Emperor. After them, the sheriff and deputy sheriff appear, holding their staffs.

—appeared, and then three judges, clad in red coats, with grave faces and measured steps, ascended the bench and, saluting the counsels, took their seats. The counsels at once stood up and respectfully greeted them. The scraping of chairs, the murmuring and shuffling of people grew louder. The peons were hissing, “Chup!” The sergeants were going, “Hish!” The criers called out, “Oyez, oyez!” and thus the session began. Next, the names of the grand jurors were called, and they gathered together and appointed their foreman, that is, the chief grand juror. Now it was Mr. Russell’s turn. Casting his gaze upon the grand jury, he said:

“From the list of cases, it appears that forgery is on the rise in Calcutta, for I see five or six such cases on the calendar. Among them, the complaints against Thakchacha and Bahulya, as revealed in the depositions, show that they have been manufacturing forged company papers in Sealdah and selling them in this city for several years. Whether this case is fit for trial, you must first inform me. As for the other cases, examine the documents and do as duty requires—there is no need for me to say more on that.”

Receiving this charge, the grand jury withdrew into their chamber. Bancharam, with a gloomy face, kept glancing at Butler Sahib. Within ten or fifteen minutes, the indictment against Thakchacha and Bahulya was found to be true and sent up to the court. Immediately, the jail guard brought Thakchacha and Bahulya and stood them in the dock before the judge. As the petty jury was being empaneled, the court interpreter shouted:
“Mokajan, alias Thakchacha, and Bahulya! You are accused of making forged company papers. Did you do this or not?”

The accused replied, “What is ‘forged’ and what is ‘company paper’? We know nothing of these. We only know the fishing nets we use to catch fish—we are farmers. This is not our work—this is the work of the sahibs and babus.”
The interpreter, exasperated, said, “You people talk too much. Did you do this or not?”
The accused replied, “Our fathers and grandfathers never did such things.”
Now thoroughly irritated, the interpreter slapped his forehead and said, “Answer my question—did you do this or not?”

“No, we never did such a thing,” the accused finally replied. To this question— The purpose of the inquiry was this: if the accused confessed to their crime, there would be no further trial—they would be sentenced immediately. Then the interpreter said, “Listen—these twelve good men will sit as a jury and judge you. If anyone has any objection, speak now. If someone is removed, another will take his place.” The accused, understanding neither the good nor the bad of these words, remained silent.

Meanwhile, the trial began, and through the depositions of the plaintiff and witnesses, the government’s counsel clearly proved the forgery. Afterwards, the counsel for the accused, instead of presenting witnesses, tried to confuse the jury with clever cross-examinations and legal wrangling. When his speech ended, Mr. Russell explained to the jury the nature of the evidence and the marks of forgery, saying, “Jury, you have received these charges; now retire to the chamber and deliberate.” The jurors could not express their opinions unless they were unanimous.

At this juncture, Bancharam approached the accused to offer reassurance; a few words, good and bad, were exchanged, when suddenly there was a commotion—the jury was returning. They came and took their seats. The foreman stood up. The courtroom fell utterly silent—everyone craned their necks, ears straining to catch the verdict. The chief clerk of the criminal court, Clark Ab di Crone, asked, “Gentlemen of the jury! Are Thakchacha and Bahulya guilty or not guilty?” The foreman replied, “Guilty.”

No sooner had the accused heard this than their souls seemed to leave their bodies. Bancharam, flustered, rushed over and said, “Oh, you fools, guilty! Are we to be beaten by children? I’ll immediately petition for a new trial, a retrial!” Thakchacha stroked his beard and said, “Sir! Whatever is in our fate will happen; we can no longer supply money.” Bancharam, a little annoyed, said, “How much can I do, patching up the pot with leaves? In these matters, is it any use to just sit and cry and soak the earth?”

Meanwhile, Mr. Russell, flipping through his book, looked at the accused and pronounced this judgment: “Thakchacha and Bahulya! Your guilt has been clearly proven. Those who commit such crimes deserve severe punishment. Therefore, you are to go to the penal settlement and remain there for life.”
As soon as this order was given, the court guards took the accused by the hand and led them away. Bancharam followed behind.

chapters.title: The Honest Man
paragraphs: The Spoilt Child of a Wealthy House

Standing aside, he waited—someone said to him, “What’s this? Has your lawsuit gone up in smoke?” He replied, “That was only to be expected—I never get involved in such hopeless cases. I never take up lawsuits like these for anyone.”
28. The Honesty and Distress of Borda Babu Revealed to Beni and Becharam Babu, and a Conversation about Uncle Thok and Excess.

The house at Baidyabati gradually fell into darkness—there was no guardian left to look after it. The family members fell into dire straits—daily life became a burden. The villagers began to say, “How long can a sand embankment last? If this were a righteous household, the walls would have been built of stone.” Meanwhile, Motilal had disappeared—his whole retinue vanished too—no more pomp and circumstance could be heard. Premnarayan Majumdar was in high spirits—sitting on the veranda of Beni Babu’s house, snapping his fingers and singing, “Babla’s flowers have bloomed, O darling, you’ve named your puffed rice cakes golden and fair.”

Inside the house, Beni Babu, tuning his tanpura, was weaving a Hamir raga, singing with flourish and feeling, “Jasmine blooms, so does the champa,” his voice rising and falling with ornament and emotion. Meanwhile, Becharam Babu, taking up a song of Norchandri, was striding down the road, teasing all the street boys with, “Having come into the world, at first I found only a cage.” The boys cheered and clapped their hands. Becharam Babu, growing annoyed, shooed them away with a “Go on, now!”

Back in the days when Nadir Shah attacked Delhi, Emperor Muhammad Shah was so absorbed in music that even when Nadir Shah appeared before him, sword in hand, Muhammad Shah did not pause his musical revelry for even a moment—nor did he utter a word, but simply surrendered his throne without protest. But when Becharam Babu arrived, Beni Babu did not act so indifferent—he immediately set aside his tanpura, rose quickly, and respectfully offered him a seat.

After a few moments of polite conversation, Becharam Babu said, “Beni brother, after all these days, the deluge has come—Uncle Thok has fallen by his own misdeeds, and your Motilal too has been ruined by his own foolishness. Brother! You always used to tell me, unless a boy is taught wisdom and religion from childhood, disaster is sure to follow—Motilal is living proof of that. What more can I say of this sorrow? All this is Baburam’s fault—he had only the cunning of a clerk—clever with old women, but half-blind in everything else, bah!”

Beni: And what’s the use of lamenting over all this now? The decision was made long ago—when there was such neglect in Moti’s education and no way to keep him from bad company, that’s when the Ramayana was written from Ram himself. Whatever the case, it’s Bancharam who’s left to guard the house—Bakreshwar is all fuss and no substance. Never have I seen anyone so eager to flatter the sons of the rich under the guise of teaching—actual education for the children is a farce, day and night it’s just “laba-laba,” yet outwardly he pretends to be doing some grand work. Anyway, Motilal’s hopes for a reward from the Bawaji have not been fulfilled—he’s shouted “Give me water!” so loud he’s split the sky, but he’s never even seen a cloud of profit, let alone a shower. How could he expect rain?

Premnarayan Majumdar said, “Gentlemen, have you nothing else to discuss? The poets have gone—Kobikankan is gone, Valmiki is gone, Vyasa is gone—the talk of worldly affairs is over, and now only Baburami’s troubles remain, and he’s at death’s door. That Moti boy is as wicked as they come, and his fate is just as bad—let him go to the devil, I have no regrets for him.”

Hari, packing the tobacco, handed the hookah to Beni Babu and said, “That Bengali Babu is coming.” Beni Babu got up and saw Baradaprasad Babu hurrying over with his cane in hand. At once, Beni Babu and Becharam Babu stood up to greet him and offered him a seat. After the usual exchange of pleasantries, Barada Babu said, “Well, what was to happen has happened. Now, I have a request. I have lived in Baidyabati for many years, and so it is my duty to look after the people there as best I can. I don’t have much wealth, but if I consider the kind of man I am, the Lord has given me plenty. If I desire more, I’d only be blaming His justice, and that is not proper for any human being. Though it is my duty to care for my neighbors, due to my laziness and lack of foresight, I have not fulfilled that duty as I should have. Now—”

Becharam interrupted, “What are you saying! You’ve helped every poor soul in Baidyabati in every possible way—with food, with clothing, with money, with medicine, with books, with advice, with your own labor—you’ve left nothing undone. Brother! Your virtues bring tears to their eyes—I know all this very well. Why hide it from me?”

Borda: No, sir, I am not boasting—I am telling you the plain truth. If anyone has ever received help from me, it was so little that I feel ashamed to even recall it. Be that as it may, my request now is this: I have heard that Motilal’s and Thakchacha’s families are dying of hunger—their days pass in starvation. Hearing this has pained me deeply. That is why I have brought the two hundred rupees I had with me. If you could, without revealing my name, send this money to them by some means, I would be greatly obliged.

Hearing this, Beni Babu fell silent. After a moment, Becharam Babu looked at Borda, his eyes brimming with tears of reverence. Placing his hand on Borda’s shoulder, he said, “Brother! You alone have understood what true religion is—we have wasted our lives in vain. The Vedas and Puranas say that only the pure of heart can see the Supreme Lord—what can I say of your heart? Never have I seen a speck of impurity in you! May the Lord keep you as happy as your heart is pure. But have you had any news of Ramlal?”
Borda: A few months ago, I received a letter from Haridwar—he is well. He wrote nothing about returning.
Becharam: Ramlal is a fine boy—just seeing him soothes the eyes. Surely, he will do well—he has been saved by your good company.

Meanwhile, Thakchacha and Bahulya are crossing the seas together on a ship. The two are like a pair of jewels—where one sits, the other sits; where one eats, the other eats; where one sleeps, the other sleeps. They are always sharing tales of their misfortunes. Thakchacha, heaving a deep sigh, says, “Our fate is truly wretched—we are utterly ruined. No scheme comes to mind, all my plans have vanished from my head. My shop is gone—never met my wife again. I’m terribly afraid she’ll marry someone else.”

Bahulya replied, “Friend, forget all that—leave it behind. This world is but a journey—just coming and going—no one belongs to anyone. You have your tribe, I have my gang—let’s throw it all to the devil. Now let’s see what’s best for us. The wind is howling—the ship is listing to one side—a terrible storm is rising.”
Thakchacha, trembling with fear, says, “Friend! I’m terribly scared—I feel the end is near.” Bahulya...

chapters.title: Eviction from Home
paragraphs: He said, “What debts do we have left to pay the ferryman? We’re just sitting here, growing fat. Come, let’s stoop down and read the preface to Alami’s book. My tongue is as sharp as ever—if I drown, I’ll just shout the Pir’s name and swim for it.”
29. Seizing the House at Baidyabati—Bancharam’s Misconduct—The Family’s Distress and Eviction from the House—Borda Babu’s Kindness.

Bancharam Babu’s hunger could never be satisfied—he was forever scheming to snatch a little more, always plotting how best to twist things to his own advantage. Such constant scheming sharpened his cunning mind to a fine edge. Turning over all the events concerning Baburam in his head, he suddenly hit upon a splendid idea. Reclining against a bolster, he pondered for a long while, then slapped his thigh and exclaimed to himself, “Here’s a divine way to make some easy money! Baburam’s property in China Bazaar and the Bhadrasan house are mortgaged, and the term is up. If I get Heramba Babu to file a suit in court, I’ll be able to fill my belly for a few days at least.” Saying this, he flung his shawl over his shoulder, declared he was off to view the Ganges, and with his shoes slapping noisily, set out with the air of a man on a sacred mission—or perhaps a man ready to drop dead, so grave was his resolve—straight to Heramba Babu’s house.

No sooner had he entered the gate than he asked the servant, “Where’s the master?” At the sound of Bancharam’s voice, Heramba Babu came down at once. Heramba Babu was a simple, straightforward man—he answered everything with a “yes.” Bancharam took his hand with great affection and said, “Chowdhury Mahashay! Please, on my word, lend Baburam some money. His household and property are in ruins—his honor and reputation have gone with them. The elder son’s a monkey, the younger’s a lunatic—both have vanished without a trace. Now there are debts piling up, and other creditors are preparing to file suits. Who knows what troubles may follow? So I can’t keep silent any longer. Please, hand over the mortgage papers. We must file the suit at our office tomorrow itself. You only need to sign a vakalatnama.”
It’s natural to fear losing one’s money in such circumstances—everyone feels it. Heramba Babu was no villain, no trickster, so Bancharam’s words struck him right to the heart. At once...

"Yes," he replied, handing over the papers to him. Just as Hanuman, overjoyed after receiving the death-missive for Ravana, had sped back from Lanka with great haste, so too did Bancharam, tucking those papers under his arm like a sacred amulet, hurry home with the same eagerness and delight.

It had been almost a year now—the grand front gate of the Baidyabati house remained shut, the roof, walls, and fences stained with moss, and all around the place had grown thick with wild thorns and brambles. Inside the house, only Motilal’s stepmother and his wife, these two helpless women, resided. When necessary, they would slip out through the back door. Their days passed in great hardship—clad in soiled garments, and for fifteen days out of every month, they went unfed. The money they had received from Beni Babu had been spent entirely on repaying debts and a few months’ expenses, so now they suffered terribly and, helpless, pondered their fate.

Motilal’s wife would say, “Thakrun! Who knows what sins we committed in our past lives? I cannot say. I am married, yes, but I have never even seen my husband’s face—he has never once looked back at me. Whether I live or die, he never asks. Even if a husband is wicked, it is not a wife’s duty to speak ill of him—I do not blame my husband; it is my own cursed fate. What fault is his? I only say this much: the suffering I endure now would not seem so bitter if my husband were near.”
Motilal’s stepmother replied, “Child! There are none more wretched than us. To speak of our sorrows is to split the heart asunder. The destitute have no refuge but the Lord of the poor.”

As long as a man has wealth, servants and maids remain at his side, but when misfortune befalls, all abandon him. Only one old maidservant, out of affection, stayed with those two women—she herself survived by begging from door to door. One day, as mother-in-law and daughter-in-law were thus conversing, the old maid came in, trembling from head to toe, and said, “Oh my mistresses! Look out the window—Bancharam Babu has surrounded the house with a surgeon and a peon. Seeing me, he said, ‘Tell the women to leave the house!’ I asked, ‘Sir! Where will they go?’ At once, his eyes turned red and he shouted at me, ‘Don’t they know this house is mortgaged? Does the creditor throw his money into the Ganges? If they know what’s good for them, let them leave now—otherwise, I’ll have them thrown out by the throat!’”

No sooner had they heard the news than the mother-in-law and the daughter-in-law began to tremble in fear, their bodies shaking uncontrollably. Meanwhile, the sound of the main door being broken down filled the house; the street outside was teeming with people. Bancharam, swaggering about, was shouting, “Break it down, break the branches!” and waving his hands, proclaiming, “Who dares stop me from taking possession? Would I be beaten by a mere boy? This is the court’s order—I’ll break the house and seize it right now! Are honest men who lend money to be called thieves? Is this justice? The family must vacate the house at once!”

A great crowd had gathered. Among them, one or two, thoroughly exasperated, called out, “Oh Bancharam! There’s no greater scoundrel than you. It’s by your scheming that this house is lost. You’ve been leeching off this family all your life, stealing money hand over fist, and now you’re throwing these families out onto the street. Seeing your face is enough to make one take a ritual fast. Even hell won’t have room for you!”

Bancharam paid no heed to these words. Breaking down the door, he stormed into the house with his men, making straight for the inner quarters. At that moment, Motilal’s stepmother and wife, each clutching the hands of the old maidservant, cried out, “O Lord! Protect these helpless, suffering women!” Wiping their tears, they slipped out through the back door.

Motilal’s wife said, “Mother! We are women of a good family—we know nothing of the world. Where shall we go? Father has left with the whole household—no brother, no sister, no relatives—who will protect us now? O Lord! Our faith and our lives are in Your hands. Better to die of hunger than to lose our honor.”

After walking five or seven steps, they stopped beneath a banyan tree, lost in anxious thought. Just then, Babu Bardaprasad approached, his head bowed, his face clouded with sorrow, and said, “Oh! Do not lose heart. Think of me as your own son—I beg you, for the sake of your honor, come with me to my house. I have prepared a separate room for you. Stay there for a few days; we will find a way.”

Hearing Bardababu’s words, Motilal’s wife and stepmother felt as if they had found the shore after being cast into the sea. Overwhelmed with gratitude, they said, “Son! We wish we could remain forever at your feet. Who speaks such words at a time like this? Surely, in another life, you must have been our father.” Bardababu quickly helped them into a palanquin and sent them to his home. To avoid meeting anyone who might question them, he himself hurried back by winding lanes and alleys.

chapters.title: The Return Home
paragraphs: Good counsel and good company give rise to wisdom—some acquire it in youth, others only in later years. If wisdom does not come early, great disasters may follow. Just as a fire in the forest blazes uncontrollably, or a mighty wind, once it rises, sweeps away trees and buildings in its path, so too, if folly takes root in childhood, the vigor of youth makes it all the more dangerous. Examples of this abound everywhere. Yet, it is also seen that some people, after spending years in folly and vice, suddenly become pious in their later days. The root of such transformation is always good advice or good company. Sometimes, by chance, or due to some incident, or even a single word, a person may suddenly awaken—such transformations are rare indeed.

Motilal, returning from Jessore disappointed, said to his companions, “There is no wealth in my fate, and it is useless to seek it further. Now, let me travel for a while in the northwestern regions—will any of you come with me?” When Lakshmi smiles, companions flock unbidden—when there is money in hand, one need not even call, many come of their own accord. But in times of want, it is hard to find a companion. Those who stayed with Motilal did so for the sake of pleasure, amusement, and money—they showed affection, but in truth, they had not a drop of genuine love for him. When they saw that his fortunes had dried up, debts surrounded him on all sides, and even daily meals were a struggle, let alone the life of a gentleman, they thought, “What is the use of keeping up this friendship now? Better to slip away.” Motilal asked them such questions and saw that none gave any answer. All swallowed hard, hemmed and hawed, made various excuses, and cited other obligations. Disgusted by their behavior, Motilal said, “It is in adversity that one knows a true friend. After all this time, I have come to know you. Well, then, you may all go to your own homes; I shall travel the country alone.” The companions replied, “Boro Babu! Don’t be angry—why don’t you go ahead, and we’ll settle our own affairs and join you later.” At their words, Motilal no longer... Ignoring his ears, he set out on foot, and as a guest in strange places, begging for alms, after three months he finally arrived at Benares. In this state of adversity, left to his own solitary thoughts, his mind began to wander in many directions. He saw temples, ghats, and mansions built at great expense now falling into ruin—ancient, once-mighty trees with many spreading branches, now withered and decaying. He observed that rivers, mountains, and caves do not remain unchanged forever—inevitably, with time, all things alter and decay; everything is transient, everything is hollow. Mankind too is beset by disease, old age, separation, grief, and countless sorrows; pride, envy, pleasure, and enjoyment in this world are all as fleeting as bubbles on water.

Reflecting on these matters, Motilal would circumambulate the holy precincts of Benares every day, and in the evening, sit alone by the banks of the Ganges, pondering the frailty of the body, the essence of the soul, and his own character and deeds. Through such contemplation, the darkness within him began to lift, and memories of his past actions and present follies awoke sharply in his mind. With his thoughts thus transformed, he began to feel a deep disgust for himself, and from that disgust, a great anguish arose. He would constantly ask himself, “How can I find deliverance? When I recall the wicked deeds I have committed, my heart still burns as if in a wildfire.”

Immersed in such thoughts, he paid no heed to food or clothing, wandering about in a near-delirium. After some time spent in this distracted state, it so happened that one day he saw an elderly man sitting beneath a tree, absorbed in concentration—at times reading a book, at times closing his eyes in meditation. At first glance, it seemed this man was wise, having grasped the essence of knowledge and attained remarkable self-control. The very sight of his face inspired reverence.

No sooner had Motilal seen him than he approached, prostrated himself with full devotion, and stood respectfully nearby. After a while, the old man looked at Motilal and said, “My son! Judging by your appearance, you seem to be of gentle birth—but why are you so afflicted?”
Encouraged by these kind words, Motilal, without reservation, introduced himself and said, “Sir! You appear to be most learned—I am your humble servant. Please grant me some good counsel.”
The old man replied, “I see you are hungry—take some food and rest a while; afterwards, we shall talk of all things.” That day passed in hospitality—

Seeing the simple-heartedness of that ancient man, Motilal felt satisfied. It is human nature that unless mutual satisfaction arises, hearts do not open up; but if such contentment is born at the very first meeting, then the thoughts of each are soon revealed. If one person displays sincerity, the other, unless he is exceedingly deceitful, can never maintain his own duplicity. That elderly gentleman was deeply religious; pleased with Motilal’s guilelessness, he began to show him fatherly affection. Gradually, he revealed the spiritual intentions he harbored. He repeatedly said:

“My son! The essence of all religion is to worship the Supreme Being with heartfelt devotion, affection, and love—through body, mind, and soul. Always keep this in your thoughts, and practice it in mind, speech, and action. If this teaching takes firm root in your heart, the course of your mind will change entirely; then other religious observances will follow naturally. But to maintain unwavering love for the Supreme Being in mind, speech, and action at all times is exceedingly difficult—in this world, passions such as attachment, hatred, greed, and delusion constantly intrude and disrupt. Therefore, concentration and steadfastness are absolutely necessary.”

Motilal, accepting this advice, began to devote himself daily to meditation and worship of the Supreme Being, and took great care in self-examination and self-correction. After some time, this practice awakened in him a true devotion to God. Ah, what ineffable greatness lies in the company of the virtuous! The one who became Motilal’s guide was a jewel among the devout; is it any wonder, then, that Motilal’s mind should be transformed in his presence?

With single-minded devotion to the Supreme, Motilal’s heart grew fraternal toward all mankind. His affection for his father, mother, and family deepened, and his desire to relieve the sufferings of others and to do good increased day by day. At the mere sight or sound of anything contrary to truth and simplicity, he felt an alien discomfort. Motilal would always share his thoughts and past deeds with that elderly gentleman, and, expressing his remorse, would say:
“Guru! I am a wretch; the way I have behaved toward my father, mother, brothers, sisters, and others—sometimes I feel there is no place for me even in hell.”
The old man would console him, saying:

“My son! Persevere with all your might in the practice of virtue. Every human being commits sins of thought, word, and deed; our only hope of deliverance lies in the mercy of that Compassionate One. He who, with a contrite heart, earnestly strives for self-purification—”

It seemed as if he was never beaten. Motilal would hear all this, and, lowering his head, would ponder, and at times say, “Where have my mother, stepmother, sister, brother, wife—all of them gone? My heart is restless for them.”

The advent of autumn—the end of the long night—how wondrous is the beauty of Vrindavan! All around, groves of palm, tamal, sal, piyal, bakul, and countless other trees; above them, thousands upon thousands of birds singing in myriad voices—the breeze blowing gently—the ripples of the Yamuna playfully caressing the banks—cowherd boys and girls of Braj, wandering through the bowers and paths, playing the veena and singing hymns. At the end of the night, in every temple at the hour of the morning arati, the sound of a thousand conch shells and bells resounds. At Keshi Ghat, the turtles clatter and splash—on the trees, countless monkeys leap and bound—sometimes they tangle themselves in the plough, sometimes they stretch out languidly, sometimes, baring their monstrous faces, they pounce with a thud and snatch away people’s food.

In every forest, hundreds of pilgrims circumambulate—visiting various places, recounting the many pastimes of Sri Krishna. Meanwhile, the sun blazes fiercely—the earth is hot—traveling on foot is most arduous, so many pilgrims rest beneath the trees here and there. Motilal’s mother, holding her daughter’s hand, had been wandering, but overcome by exhaustion, she sat down in a secluded spot, laid her head in her daughter’s lap, and fell asleep. The daughter, with the end of her sari, wiped the sweat from her mother’s brow and began to fan her gently. The mother, feeling a little refreshed, said, “Promoda! My child, you rest a bit—I’ll sit up.” The daughter replied, “Ma! Your weariness gone is my weariness gone—lie down, let me rub your feet.” Hearing such tender words from her daughter, the mother, eyes brimming with tears, said, “Child! I live only to see your face—what sins did I commit in my past life, that I must endure such sorrow? I do not mind starving myself, but I cannot even feed you a handful of rice—that is my greatest pain! Where is there room to hold such grief? Where are my two sons? How fares my daughter-in-law? Why did I leave in anger? Moti struck me—he did, indeed, for what don’t children do in their father’s name? Now my heart always trembles for him and for Ram.” The daughter wiped her mother’s tears and tried to comfort her. After a while, the mother dozed off a little. The daughter, watching over her mother… Seeing her daughter asleep, the mother sat quietly, fanning her gently. Mosquitoes and gnats settled on the girl’s body, biting her, but the mother remained still, lest her movement disturb her daughter’s slumber. The affection and endurance of women is truly astonishing! It seems, in this matter, women far surpass men.

In her sleep, the mother dreamt that a young boy, clad in yellow garments, came near and said, “Mother, do not weep any longer—you are most virtuous. You have eased the suffering of many a wretched soul. You have never wished ill upon anyone, only good. Soon, all will be well—you shall have two sons and find happiness.”

Startled, the sorrowful mother awoke and opened her eyes, only to find her daughter beside her, and no one else. Without a word to the girl, she took her hand and, with great difficulty, made her way back to their little bower.

Mother and daughter would often converse. The mother would say, “My child! My mind is so restless. I am always thinking of returning home.” The daughter, seeing no other way, replied, “Mother, among our few possessions, we have a couple of garments and a water pot. If we sell these, what will become of us? Let us wait a few days. I shall work as a cook or a maid and save a little—then we shall have enough for our journey.”
Hearing this, the mother sighed deeply and fell silent, unable to hold back her tears. Seeing her mother so distraught, the daughter too became sorrowful.

Nearby lived a woman of Braj, who always looked after them. By chance, she arrived at that moment and, seeing their distress, offered words of comfort and listened to all their troubles. Moved by their suffering, the woman of Braj said, “Mother! What can I say? I have not a coin to my name. I wish I could give you everything I have to ease your pain. But let me suggest a way. I have heard there is a Bengali gentleman here in Mathura, who has earned some wealth through service and trade. He is most kind and generous. If you go to him and ask for help with your travel expenses, he will surely give it.”

Seeing no other recourse, the sorrowful mother and daughter resolved to follow this advice. Bidding farewell to the woman of Braj, they reached Mathura within two days. There, near a pond, they saw a group of sick, blind, crippled, wretched, and poor people sitting together, weeping. The mother approached one elderly person among them...

He asked the women, “Dear ones! Why are you crying?” One of the women replied, “Mother! There is a gentleman here—how can I describe his virtues? He visits the homes of the poor and the distressed, always ensuring they have food and clothing, and looks after them with great care. If anyone falls ill, he sits by their bedside himself, staying awake the whole night to give them medicine and nourishment. He shares in all our joys and sorrows. Just thinking of his goodness brings tears to my eyes. Blessed is the woman who bore such a son—surely she will enjoy heaven. Any place where such a man lives is a sacred place. But our wretched fate! That gentleman is now leaving this land, and we are weeping, wondering what will become of us after he is gone.”

Mother and daughter, hearing this, began to whisper to each other, “It seems our hopes have come to nothing—misery is written on our foreheads, who can erase the script of fate?” The old woman, noticing their downcast faces, said, “I think you are ladies of a respectable family, fallen on hard times. If you need some money, come with me right now to that gentleman—he helps not only the poor and distressed, but many respectable people too.” Mother and daughter immediately agreed, and following the old woman, waited outside the house while she went in.

Day was drawing to a close—the sun was setting, and the rays of the dying day turned the trees and the pond to gold. Where the mother and daughter stood, there was a small garden. All around, creepers climbed the fences, and in the center stood a platform. Inside the garden, two gentlemen, arm in arm like Krishna and Arjuna, were strolling together. By chance, their eyes fell upon the two women, and they hurriedly left the garden and approached them. Seeing the gentlemen, the mother and daughter grew shy, pulled their veils over their heads, and stepped back a little.

Of the two gentlemen, the younger one spoke gently, “Please consider us as your sons—do not be embarrassed. Tell us frankly why you have come here. If we can be of any help, we shall not fail in any way.” Hearing this, the mother, taking her daughter by the hand, stepped forward a little and briefly explained their situation. She had barely finished speaking when the two gentlemen turned to each other—

Looking among them, the youngest was so overcome by emotion that, crying "Mother! Mother!" he fell to the ground. Another, an older man, bowed at the feet of the grieving mother and, folding his hands, said, "Mother! Look—see who lies on the ground before you. He is the treasure of your sari’s end—he is your Ram. My name is Bardaprasad Biswas."

The moment the mother heard these words, she uncovered her face and said, "My son! What did you say? Could such fortune befall this wretched woman?" RamLal, regaining his senses, pressed his head to his mother’s feet and remained silent. The mother cradled her son’s head in her lap, shedding tears, and gazing upon his face, she watered her parched heart with the balm of consolation. The sister, too, wiped her brother’s tears and the dust from his body with the end of her sari, and sat quietly by.

Meanwhile, the old maidservant, not finding the young master inside the house, hurried out to the garden. There she saw the master lying on the ground, his head resting in the lap of an elderly woman—her companion from days gone by. "Oh mother, what is this? What has happened to the young master? Has he fallen ill? Shall I fetch the physician?" The old woman cried out in alarm. Bardaprasad Babu said, "Calm yourself—Babu is not ill. These two women are his mother and sister."

The old woman replied, "Babu, is it fitting to jest with the unfortunate? Babu is Lakshmipati, the lord of wealth, and these are beggars by the roadside. One comes with me and becomes his mother, another his sister—perhaps they are the daughters of some conjurer, come to bewitch us with their tricks. I have never seen such women—may their magic be undone, mother!" With these words, the old woman, muttering and grumbling, walked away.

Now, everyone having composed themselves, returned to the house. There, upon seeing her daughter-in-law and co-wife, the mother’s heart overflowed with joy. After learning of the family’s affairs, she said, "Come, Ram, let us go home. My mind is restless—I long to return to my own house." RamLal had already made preparations for the journey—boats and all were ready at the ghat. Obeying his mother’s wishes, he chose an auspicious day and set out with everyone. As they departed, the people of Mathura flocked to bid them farewell—a thousand eyes brimmed with tears, a thousand lips sang RamLal’s praises, a thousand hands were raised in blessing. The old woman who had been so vexed before now folded her hands and, approaching RamLal’s mother…
Alya began to weep, and until the boat passed out of sight, everyone stood on the banks of the Yamuna as if lifeless, their bodies devoid of spirit.

Meanwhile, there was no steady southern wind—the boat, carried swiftly by the current, soon arrived at Benares. Oh, what a spectacle Benares presents in the morning! How many Dvivedis, Chaturvedis, Ramats, Naimats, Shaivas, Shaktas, Ganapatyas, Paramahansas, and Brahmacharis are chanting hymns—how many Samavedis are reciting the mantras of the Kauthumas and the suktas to Agni and Vayu—how many women from Saurashtra, Maharashtra, Bengal, and Magadha, clad in garments of every hue, are circumambulating the temples after their ritual baths—how many shrines are fragrant with incense, frankincense, flowers, and sandalwood—how many devotees, crying “Hara Vishweshwar!” and clashing cymbals and drums, are moving about in a frenzy—how many blood-robed, trident-bearing Bhairavis, with wild laughter, are roaming the Bhairava temples in a mood of fierce devotion—how many ascetics, Udasis, and those with matted locks and upraised arms, their bodies smeared with ashes, are diligently engaged in subduing the body and senses—how many yogis, in secluded spots, are practicing rechaka, puraka, and kumbhaka for meditation—how many musicians, both skilled and rustic, are absorbed with veena, mridangam, rabab, and tanpura, lost in dhrupad, dharu, khayal, prabandha, chhanda, sorabandha, tarana, sargam, chaturang, and naqsh.

Ramlal and the others bathed at the Manikarnika Ghat and stayed in Kashi for four days. Ramlal was always with his mother and sister, and in the evenings, he would wander here and there with Barda Babu.

One day, while out sightseeing, they saw a charming hermitage ahead, where an elderly man sat gazing at the beauty of the Bhagirathi—the river, swift and lively, flowed on with a murmuring sound, and by virtue of its clarity, seemed to carry the variegated evening sky in its embrace. As soon as Ramlal approached the man, the latter, as if recognizing him from before, asked, “Well, how did you find the study of the Shuka Upanishad?” Ramlal, after looking at his face, bowed in greeting. The elderly man, a little embarrassed, said, “Ah, my mistake! I have a disciple whose face is exactly like yours. Thinking you were he, I addressed you so.” Afterwards, Ramlal and Barda Babu sat with him and engaged in various discussions on the scriptures.
Just then, a man, his face clouded with worry, came and sat nearby with downcast eyes. Barda Babu, observing him,

He said, “Ram! Do you see who it is? Your elder brother is right here.” No sooner had Ramlal heard these words than he was overcome with emotion, his hair standing on end. He looked at Motilal, and Motilal, recognizing Ramlal, started in surprise and embraced him tightly. For a moment, both stood in silence—neither could utter a word. In that instant, both brothers truly understood what it meant to be brothers.

After a while, Motilal, taking the dust from the feet of Borda Babu, joined his palms and said, “Sir! Only now, after all these years, do I realize what kind of person you are. Please forgive this wretch.” Borda Babu, taking both brothers by the hand, bade farewell to the elderly gentleman, and as they walked along the road, they shared and listened to all the stories of their past. Witnessing the transformation in Motilal’s heart through their conversation, Borda Babu expressed boundless joy.

When they reached the place where the rest of the family was staying, Motilal, standing a little distance away, called out in a loud voice, “Mother, where are you? Mother! Your prodigal son has returned—he is still alive, he is not dead. After all I have done, I hardly dare show my face to you. Now, my only wish is to behold your feet once before I die.”

The moment his mother heard these words, her heart brimmed with joy and her eyes filled with tears. She came near, and upon seeing her eldest son’s face, felt as though she had recovered a priceless treasure. The moment Motilal saw his mother, he fell at her feet, pressing his forehead to the ground.

After a while, his mother lifted him up by the hand and, with the edge of her sari, began to wipe away his tears. She said, “Moti! Your stepmother, your sister, and your wife are all here—go and meet them.” Motilal bowed to his sister and stepmother, and upon seeing his wife, memories of the past overwhelmed him. Weeping, he said, “Mother! As I have been a bad son and a bad brother, so too—” The Unworthy Husband—I am in no way deserving of such a virtuous wife. At the time of marriage, husband and wife take a kind of vow before the Almighty that they will love each other for life, that even in great adversity they will not separate—that the wife will never let her mind stray to another man, and the husband will never let his heart wander to another woman—such thoughts are grave sins. I have, however, committed many acts contrary to this vow. Then why has my wife not abandoned me? And my siblings—my brother and sister—how harshly have I treated them! And you, mother—there is nothing more precious in this world than a mother—I have caused you endless suffering. As a son, I have even struck you. Mother! Is there any atonement for all these sins? If only I could die soon, I would be freed from this wildfire burning in my heart. But it seems even death has died, for I see no sign of its messenger, disease. In any case, you all go home—I shall remain here in this hermitage with my guru and, through strict penance, give up my life.

Afterwards, Borda Babu, Ramlal, and his mother brought Moti Lal’s guru, explained everything at length, and brought Moti Lal back with them. Near Monghyr, as night fell and they boarded the boat, a man with the appearance of a boatman approached and began peering in, saying, “Fire! Fire!” Seeing his suspicious behavior, Borda Babu said, “Everyone be alert.” Then he climbed onto the roof of the boat and saw, hidden in a thicket, nearly twenty or thirty armed men lying in wait—if that fellow gave the signal, they would attack. At once, Ramlal and Borda Babu came out and began drilling with their guns. At the sound of gunfire, the dacoits fled into the forest. Borda Babu and Ramlal’s intention was to take swords in hand, pursue them, and capture one or two to hand over to the nearest police inspector, but the family forbade it.

Moti Lal, witnessing all this, said, “From my childhood, I have received nothing but bad education—my babudom has been my ruin. Ramlal practiced gymnastics, and I used to mock him for it—but today I have learned that unless a boy practices wrestling and gymnastics from a young age, he will never have courage. Just now I was terribly afraid—if Ramlal and Borda Babu hadn’t been there, we would all have been hacked to pieces.”

In a short while, everyone arrived at Baidyabati and entered Borda Babu’s house. Hearing of Borda Babu and Ramlal’s return, all the villagers came from every direction to pay their respects—joy blossomed in every heart, every face glowed with delight, and all, with auspicious longing, showered prayers and blessings upon them.

The next day, Heramba Chandra Chowdhury Babu came and said, “Ram Babu! I did not understand at first—on Bancharam’s advice, I took possession of your ancestral house. I am deeply sorry that I drove your family out and occupied the house. Your extraordinary virtue has moved me—now I am returning the house to you at once, please go and live there in comfort.”

Ramlal replied, “I am greatly obliged to you. If you truly wish to return the house, we would be grateful if you would accept whatever is rightfully yours.” When Heramba Babu agreed to this proposal, Ramlal immediately paid him and had a deed drawn up in both brothers’ names. With his family, he returned to their ancestral home, and lifting his eyes in gratitude, said in his heart, “O Lord of the Universe! What can you not accomplish?”
Afterwards, Ramlal was married, and the two brothers, in great harmony, became the source of their mother’s and the family’s happiness, spending their days in utmost joy.

Borda Babu, by the grace of the elders, went to Badarganj for business affairs. Becharam Babu sold off his property and, becoming a true “Becharam” (the destitute one), went to live in Benares. Benibabu, for a time, indulged in idle pleasures without learning, then turned his attention to the legal profession. Bancharam, after many schemes and tricks, died suddenly by a stroke of lightning. Bakreshwar, ever the flatterer and sycophant, wandered about making a show of himself. Thakchacha and Bahulya, having gone to Pulipalme to cheat people, found their gambling ground cut from under them, and after much suffering, both died. Thakchachi, seeing no other way, became a bangle-seller, wandering the lanes singing the song of the bangle-seller, “Churiyaler Churiya.” Haldhar, Gadadhar, and the other Braj boys, seeing Motilal’s changed ways, set out to seek other Captain Babus. Jan Sahib, taking up insolvency, began working as a broker. Premnarayan Majumdar, donning the garb of a sadhu, went about singing, “Mahadev’s secret thoughts, O devotee, read the book—”
"Who knows!"—uttering this, he began to wander about Navadwip, shouting at the top of his voice.

Pramoda’s husband had taken wives in many places, but now, finding himself empty-handed, he came to the physician’s house and, perched on the shoulders of his brothers-in-law, feasted only on fried lentil cakes, ghyaaru, tajpheni, pomegranate, sago, and jalgoja. After eating these, he started singing tappas at full volume.
What happened after that remains to be told—“My tale is done, the pea plant is spun.”
